title: No Passenger Airbag for Dogbert

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Dogbert, come look at our new car!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It has all of the most important safety features.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You got your anti-lock brakes, your reinforced bumpers, your automatic seatbelts and your driver-side air bag.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I didn't hear "passenger side air bag" in that list.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It turns out that it's only economical to save the person who makes the buying decision.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But I got a baby seat in case you want to use that.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Well, thank you for letting me choose between humiliation and death.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I've got a better idea.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ooh... just wait until my turn.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Watch me ram that cop car.

setting: Outside next to Dilbert's new red car, then inside the car
situation: Dilbert proudly shows Dogbert his new car and lists its safety features, but it lacks a passenger-side air bag. Dilbert explains that only the buyer's safety was worth paying for and offers Dogbert a baby seat instead. Dogbert declines the humiliating option and ends up driving the car, planning to ram a cop car.
punchline: Dogbert, offered only a baby seat in place of a passenger air bag, takes revenge by taking the wheel and announcing he'll ram a police car, leaving the driver-side-protected Dilbert in the passenger seat.
summary: After learning his friend's new car protects only the driver, a slighted Dogbert seizes the steering wheel and plans some reckless payback.

title: Dogbert Obeys the Fitness Television

transcript.speaker: TV
transcript.text: ... and that's the CNN weather report.

transcript.speaker: TV
transcript.text: Hey! Don't just sit there watching TV all day! Give me thirty tummy crunches!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: One, two...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's been nothing but mixed messages since Ted married Jane.

setting: Dogbert's living room, in front of the television
situation: Dogbert is lounging in his armchair watching the CNN weather report when the broadcast switches to an exercise show. The fitness instructor on screen orders viewers to stop sitting around and do thirty tummy crunches. Dogbert dutifully starts exercising.
punchline: Dogbert complains that the TV is sending mixed messages, which is just what happens when you take orders from a television that goes from weather report to workout drill without warning.
summary: A dog lounging in front of the TV gets barked at by an exercise show and, grumbling about mixed signals, starts doing sit-ups.

title: Dogbert's Cognitive Dissonance Morale Consulting

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why should I hire you as my consultant?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll use my special process of cognitive dissonance to improve employee morale.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How does it work?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: When people are in an absurd situation, their minds rationalize it by inventing a comfortable illusion.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay, go do it.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Isn't it strange that you have this dead end job when you're twice as smart as your boss?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The hours are long, the pay is mediocre, nobody respects your contributions, and yet you freely choose to work here.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: It's absurd! No, wait... There must be a reason... I must work here because I love the work.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I love this job.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Next!

setting: Office, the Boss's desk and an employee's cubicle
situation: Dogbert pitches himself to the Boss as a consultant who can raise morale through cognitive dissonance, and the Boss hires him. Dogbert then reminds a blond employee how bad his job is and how unreasonable it is that he stays. The employee talks himself into believing he loves the work, and Dogbert moves on to the next victim.
punchline: Dogbert's morale 'improvement' is just tricking employees into rationalizing a terrible job, so they end up delusionally happy without anything actually getting better.
summary: A canine consultant makes workers content by pushing them to invent a flattering story about why they put up with a lousy job.

title: Dogbert's Jail for the Rich

transcript.speaker: Wealthy Inmate
transcript.text: Checking in.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your record says you stole three billion dollars from investors.

transcript.speaker: Wealthy Inmate
transcript.text: Ha ha ha ha ha ha

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I guess you've learned your lesson.

transcript.speaker: Wealthy Inmate
transcript.text: Whoa! Looks like my jail term is almost over!

setting: Entrance and office of Dogbert's Jail for the Rich and Famous
situation: A well-dressed businessman carrying a briefcase checks in at Dogbert's Jail for the Rich and Famous. Dogbert reads his record, which says he stole three billion dollars from investors, and the man laughs it off. When Dogbert remarks that he has learned his lesson, the man happily notes that his jail term is nearly over.
punchline: The jail's idea of punishing a three-billion-dollar thief is so absurdly lenient that the sentence ends within minutes of his arrival, mocking how rich white-collar criminals escape real consequences.
summary: A wealthy fraudster arrives at a cushy prison for the elite and finds his sentence is over almost as soon as it begins.

title: Saving Money Cutting Own Hair

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What happened to your head, Dave?

transcript.speaker: Dave
transcript.text: I'm cutting my own hair now.

transcript.speaker: Dave
transcript.text: I'm not too far along the old learning curve, but at least I'm saving money.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How much did you save?

transcript.speaker: Dave
transcript.text: Not counting the divorce and therapy?

setting: Office break area
situation: Dilbert asks a coworker named Dave about his badly cut hair. Dave explains he has started cutting his own hair to save money and admits he is still learning. When Dilbert asks how much he saved, Dave reveals the hidden costs of the decision.
punchline: Dave's savings on haircuts are wiped out by the divorce and therapy his terrible self-cut hair supposedly caused, a deadpan exaggeration of false economy.
summary: A coworker with a botched haircut brags about his savings, then undermines himself by mentioning the personal fallout it caused.

title: Dilbert's Hair Growth Experiment Results

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dilbert's Lab

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Any luck with your hair growth formula?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Define "luck."

setting: Door to Dilbert's home laboratory, then inside the lab
situation: A closed door labeled Dilbert's Lab opens and Dilbert steps out. His hair and body are now covered in sprouting bristles, spiky and wild. Dogbert asks whether his hair growth formula had any luck, and Dilbert answers with a question.
punchline: Dilbert's experiment grew hair everywhere except where he wanted it, so his sarcastic request to define "luck" shows the formula went badly wrong.
summary: After testing his own hair tonic, a bristly, hairy Dilbert deflects his dog's question about the results with a dry quip.

title: Dilbert Gets Called Ugly

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: Most handsome men are self-centered jerks.

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: But you're different... You're...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Considerate?

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: Ugly.

setting: A restaurant table during a dinner date
situation: Dilbert sits across a table from a woman with curly hair on a date. She remarks that handsome men tend to be self-centered jerks, then says Dilbert is different. Dilbert hopefully guesses she is about to call him considerate, but she says he is ugly.
punchline: What sounded like a compliment turned out to be an insult, as Dilbert is set apart from handsome jerks only by being ugly rather than by any good quality.
summary: A date seems to be praising Dilbert as unlike other men, but her actual reason for the distinction is his lack of good looks.

title: Big Ed Bumps Into Coffee Drinkers

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Look out! Big Ed is hulking backwards waving his arms again!

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: BUMP

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Big people can be so annoying.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I just wish he wouldn't refer to us as debris.

setting: Office break area
situation: Wally and Dilbert stand holding coffee cups while Wally warns that Big Ed is backing toward them and waving his arms. Big Ed bumps into them and spills their coffee all over them. They end up flat on the floor, upside down and soaked, complaining about him.
punchline: Big Ed is so oblivious and oversized that he treats his coworkers as debris in his path, and they casually grumble about it after being knocked flat.
summary: A huge coworker backs into two men holding coffee and sends them sprawling, leaving them to grumble from the floor.

title: Dilbert's Perfect Woman Owns Cats

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Somewhere out there is the woman who is perfect for me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But how will I recognize her? How will I know she's the one?

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Meanwhile, somewhere "out there"...

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Okay, I agree that it seems like cats own people, but it's not actually the law.

setting: A grassy hillside outdoors
situation: Dilbert stands and then sits on a rock on a hillside, musing to Dogbert that a perfect woman must exist somewhere and wondering how he will recognize her. A caption cuts to the woman 'out there,' sitting on a rock with an orange cat, defending the idea that cats own people.
punchline: The woman Dilbert dreams of turns out to be a devoted cat person who is already half-convinced that cats own their humans, hinting she is a poor match for him.
summary: While Dilbert daydreams about meeting his ideal woman, we see her elsewhere, a cat-obsessed woman insisting that cats owning people isn't technically a legal fact.

title: The Lazy Beaver Rents

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I always thought you beavers were busy all the time.

transcript.speaker: Beaver
transcript.text: That's a common stereotype. I'm actually quite lazy.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: How do you build your beaver home?

transcript.speaker: Beaver
transcript.text: I rent.

setting: Outdoors on a grassy hillside
situation: Dogbert sits on the grass chatting with a beaver who is holding a coffee mug. Dogbert remarks that beavers are supposed to be industrious, and the beaver admits he is actually lazy. When Dogbert asks how he builds his home, the beaver reveals he just rents one.
punchline: The beaver proves his laziness by skipping the famous beaver dam-building and simply renting a home like any other tenant.
summary: A relaxed beaver dismantles the hardworking beaver myth by admitting he pays rent instead of building his own lodge.

title: Neither a Lover Nor Killer

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The guys in the office decided that somebody must kill Floyd the budget manager because he's so mean to us.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They want me to kill him. But I can't do it. I'm a lover, not a killer.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Technically, you're neither.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is that my fault?

setting: Dilbert's home, sitting in an armchair
situation: Dilbert tells Dogbert that his coworkers have decided someone must kill Floyd, the mean budget manager, and they have chosen him to do it. He protests that he cannot because he is a lover, not a killer. Dogbert dryly points out that he is technically neither.
punchline: Dogbert's deadpan reply insults Dilbert by implying he is neither a successful lover nor a killer, and Dilbert's defensive response concedes the point.
summary: Pressured by coworkers to eliminate a nasty budget manager, Dilbert claims to be a lover rather than a killer, only to have his dog dismiss both labels.

title: Financial Advisor Moves In, Churns

transcript.speaker: Financial Advisor
transcript.text: Hi! I want to be your financial advisor.

transcript.speaker: Financial Advisor
transcript.text: I've come to live with you. We'll eventually form a lifelong bond of trust and friendship.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I liked it better when you guys just took our money.

transcript.speaker: Financial Advisor
transcript.text: I recommend a strategy called "churn."

setting: Dogbert's front door and then inside his home
situation: A smiling financial advisor with a suitcase shows up at Dogbert's door and announces he wants to be his financial advisor. He then moves in, promising a lifelong bond of trust and friendship. Dogbert complains that he preferred the old arrangement, and the advisor cheerfully recommends a strategy called churn.
punchline: The advisor's friendly relationship-building is just a setup for churning, excessively trading a client's account to generate commissions, so he is still just taking the client's money.
summary: A cheerful investment salesman invades a dog's home to cultivate trust, only to reveal that his real plan is to drain the account through excessive trading.

title: Incan Monkey God Writes Report

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gee, Tim, you look awful.

transcript.speaker: Tim
transcript.text: I've been working for five days without any sleep to finish this report.

transcript.speaker: Tim
transcript.text: At first I had a mental block. But on the fourth day I was visited by an Incan monkey god who told me what to write.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wow, lucky break.

transcript.speaker: Tim
transcript.text: Now I just have to find somebody who can translate his simple but beautiful language.

setting: Office
situation: Dilbert, holding a coffee cup, tells a coworker named Tim that he looks awful. Tim, sleep-deprived after five days of working on a report, explains that an Incan monkey god visited him and dictated what to write. Dilbert reacts as though this is good luck, and Tim says he now only needs someone to translate the god's language.
punchline: Tim's hallucination-fuelled report is written in an unintelligible divine language, so the sleep-deprived work is effectively useless, yet he and Dilbert treat it as a lucky break.
summary: An exhausted coworker credits a hallucinated deity for his report, which turns out to need a translator before anyone can read it.

title: Dilbert Admits Letting Floyd Die

transcript.speaker: Coworker (woman)
transcript.text: We heard you killed Floyd, our unbearable co-worker, yesterday.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No. I was there, but he choked on his own bile.

transcript.speaker: Coworker (woman)
transcript.text: What did you do - perform first aid? Call an ambulance?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't know firstaid.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh... Can I use your phone?

setting: Office, among coworkers
situation: Three coworkers approach Dilbert, who is holding a coffee mug, and say they heard he killed their unbearable coworker Floyd. Dilbert denies it, saying Floyd choked on his own bile while he was there. When asked whether he gave first aid or called an ambulance, he says he doesn't know first aid, then awkwardly asks to borrow a phone, implying he never called for help.
punchline: Dilbert's request to use a phone reveals he simply stood by and let Floyd die, never even calling an ambulance, which makes his denial of killing him ring hollow.
summary: A man accused of causing a hated colleague's death insists he's innocent, then gives himself away by asking to borrow a phone.

title: Dogbert Haggles Over Lenin's Body

transcript.speaker: Street Vendor
transcript.text: Pssst! Dog! Would you like to purchase Lenin's body?

transcript.speaker: Street Vendor
transcript.text: Twenty bucks. He's in great shape... the king of commies... not available in stores.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...and you talked him down to ten dollars?

transcript.speaker: Soldier
transcript.text: Do you like it better against this wall?

setting: A street in Russia
situation: A vendor in a tall fur hat offers to sell Dogbert the body of Lenin, carrying it hunched over his shoulder, and names a price of twenty dollars. Dogbert haggles, and Dilbert later reacts to the reduced price of ten dollars. A uniformed soldier is shown with Dogbert, implying Dogbert has had the vendor arrested or threatened with a firing squad.
punchline: Dogbert's negotiating technique was to have the vendor threatened with execution against a wall, which is how he got the price cut in half.
summary: A street peddler tries to sell Dogbert an embalmed Soviet leader, and Dogbert's bargaining turns out to rely on armed intimidation.

title: Technically All You Can Eat

transcript.speaker: Sign
transcript.text: All you can eat $7.00

transcript.speaker: Restaurant Worker (off-panel)
transcript.text: Hey! Stop!

transcript.speaker: Restaurant Worker
transcript.text: You owe us another $14.

transcript.speaker: Restaurant Worker
transcript.text: You deliberately put more than you could eat on your plates.

transcript.speaker: Restaurant Worker
transcript.text: Technically, our agreement is "all you can eat," not "all you can waste."

transcript.speaker: Restaurant Worker (thought)
transcript.text: Mom wanted me to be a lawyer, but I said "No, food services is where I'm needed."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I believe this is your department, Dogbert.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Technically, it's all you CAN eat, not all you DO eat.

transcript.speaker: Restaurant Worker (thought)
transcript.text: Ooh... he's good.

setting: An all-you-can-eat restaurant entrance
situation: Dilbert and Dogbert try to leave a $7.00 all-you-can-eat restaurant when a worker stops them and demands $14 more, claiming they deliberately overloaded their plates with food they couldn't eat. The worker argues the deal is 'all you can eat,' not 'all you can waste.' Dilbert hands the dispute to Dogbert, who counters with an even more technical reading of the phrase.
punchline: Dogbert out-lawyers the worker's pedantic reading by arguing the sign only promises what you CAN eat, not what you actually DO eat, leaving the would-be lawyer turned food worker impressed.
summary: A buffet employee's legalistic complaint about wasted food is defeated by Dogbert's even sharper hair-splitting over the wording of the offer.

title: Translator Prank Gives Alien the World

transcript.speaker: News Reporter
transcript.text: The leaders of the world met today to consider the demands of Dogbert the space alien.

transcript.speaker: U.N. Delegate
transcript.text: All in favor of letting the alien run the world, raise your hand.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Meanwhile in the translators' booth, a reckless prank is being played.

transcript.speaker: Translator
transcript.text: He says "Who wants my parking space by the elevator?"

setting: A television news report, the United Nations assembly hall, and the translators' booth
situation: A news reporter announces that world leaders are meeting at the U.N. to consider the demands of Dogbert, a space alien. The chair asks everyone in favor of letting the alien run the world to raise a hand. In the translators' booth, a translator is mistranslating the alien's demand as an offer of a prized parking space, tricking the delegates into voting yes.
punchline: The world leaders hand over global control because a prankster translator turned the alien's demands into an offer of a coveted parking spot near the elevator, showing how eagerly people will grab a petty perk.
summary: A mischievous interpreter gets the entire planet to surrender to an alien by pretending the invader is giving away a good parking spot.

title: Dogbert's Advertising Company Insults Customers

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm going to open the "Dogbert Advertising Company."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Apparently, people will believe just about anything that makes them feel good.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hey, don't underestimate our intelligence.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I could never underestimate your intelligence.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Apology accepted.

setting: Dilbert's living room, with Dilbert in an armchair
situation: Dogbert announces he will start an advertising company, explaining that people will believe anything that makes them feel good. Dilbert, reading a newspaper, objects and tells him not to underestimate their intelligence. Dogbert replies that he could never underestimate it, and Dilbert takes this as an apology.
punchline: Dogbert's reply is actually an insult, since it implies Dilbert's intelligence is so low it can't be underestimated, but Dilbert is too gullible to notice and accepts it as an apology, proving Dogbert's point.
summary: A scheming dog's backhanded remark about the gullible public is proven right when his friend mistakes an insult for an apology.

title: Dogbert Blames Dilbert For Failing

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I've made little progress toward my goal of being supreme ruler of Earth.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Obviously it's not my fault. Somebody else must be to blame.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hate it when he just stares.

setting: Dilbert's home or office, with Dogbert on a green cushion and Dilbert at a computer
situation: Dogbert sits on his cushion thinking about how little progress he has made toward ruling the Earth. He concludes it can't be his fault and that someone else must be to blame. In the last panel Dilbert, working at his computer, thinks about how much he hates it when Dogbert just stares at him, implying he is the target of the blame.
punchline: Dogbert's silent staring at Dilbert is him quietly assigning blame for his own failure to conquer the world, and Dilbert is the one who suffers for it.
summary: A dog with world-domination ambitions decides his lack of success must be someone else's doing, and his human housemate feels the weight of that unblinking gaze.

title: Dogbert Makes Desk From Lenin

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I didn't approve of you buying Lenin's body to begin with...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And I certainly don't approve of you making a desk out of it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you listening to me?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Hey, if I flip him over I can use his nostrils as a pencil holder!

setting: Dilbert's home or office, with Dogbert working on the furniture
situation: Dilbert scolds Dogbert for purchasing Lenin's preserved body and then turning it into a desk. Dogbert, hammer in hand and busy with the construction, ignores the lecture. He happily announces a new design feature instead.
punchline: Dogbert is so absorbed in the macabre desk project that he ignores Dilbert's moral objections and gleefully plans to use the corpse's nostrils as a pencil holder.
summary: While Dilbert protests the purchase of a famous corpse, Dogbert cheerfully carries on building furniture out of it.

title: Security Guard's Daydream Reality Check

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It must be great to be a security guard.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You have the entire day to let your mind transport you to magic realms of wonder and creativity.

transcript.speaker: Security Guard
transcript.text: I wonder what balsa wood tastes like.

setting: Office building lobby with a reception desk
situation: Dilbert walks past the security guard's desk and, in thought bubbles, envies the guard for having all day to daydream about magic realms of wonder and creativity. The final panel reveals the guard's actual thoughts, which are mundane and silly.
punchline: Dilbert's romantic assumption about the guard's rich inner life is deflated by the guard's actual thought, a random musing about what balsa wood tastes like.
summary: A man idealizes a guard's idle hours as a source of imaginative bliss, only to learn the guard is pondering the flavor of lightweight timber.

title: Boss Stamps Cancelled on Backs

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My consultant advised me to handle the lay-offs in a direct, professional way.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So, throughout the day I'll be sneaking up on people and stamping "cancelled" on their backs.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Let me see if I understand...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hey! Is that the Goodyear blimp?

setting: Office, in front of a group of employees
situation: The Boss announces that on his consultant's advice he will handle lay-offs in a 'direct, professional way' by sneaking up on employees and stamping 'cancelled' on their backs. As an employee starts to question the plan, he points and shouts about the Goodyear blimp to distract her so he can stamp her.
punchline: The supposedly direct and professional layoff method is actually a sneaky, childish trick, and the Boss immediately resorts to a cheap distraction ploy to carry it out.
summary: A manager's consultant-approved plan for firing people turns out to be a sneak attack with a rubber stamp, complete with a classic look-over-there diversion.

title: Dogbert's Terrible Marriage Counseling Advice

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I can see your problem.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I recommend massive plastic surgery for both of you... and your personalities are bad, too; pretend to be other people.

transcript.speaker: Client
transcript.text: Should we try to communicate more?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: No, that's just begging for trouble.

setting: Marriage counselor's office
situation: Dogbert, posing as a marriage counselor, sits behind a desk and tells a couple he can see their problem. He prescribes massive plastic surgery and pretending to be other people. When one of them asks if they should communicate more, he dismisses the idea as inviting trouble.
punchline: The counselor's advice is to become different people entirely and to avoid the one thing real counselors recommend, communication, because it would only cause trouble.
summary: A canine therapist tells a bickering couple to remake their faces and personalities rather than ever talking to each other.

title: Dogbert Calls Science Cultish

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Evolution must be true because it is a logical conclusion of the scientific method.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: But science is based on the irrational belief that because we cannot perceive reality all at once, things called "time" and "cause and effect" exist.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's what I was taught and that's what I believe.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Sounds cultish.

setting: Outdoors on a rocky hillside
situation: Dilbert and Dogbert sit on rocks outdoors. Dilbert asserts that evolution must be true because it follows logically from the scientific method. Dogbert argues that science itself rests on an irrational assumption about time and cause and effect, and when Dilbert says he believes it because that is what he was taught, Dogbert calls that cultish.
punchline: Dilbert's defense of science, that he believes it simply because he was taught it, is exactly how a cult member would justify their beliefs.
summary: A debate about evolution turns when a skeptical dog points out that his friend's faith in science sounds just like blind belief in a cult.

title: Lightbulb Joke at Performance Review

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm going to use humor to ease the tension during your annual job performance appraisal.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How many engineers does it take to change a lightbulb?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't know.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wait... I'll say three.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well, that's consistent with your appraisal.

setting: The Boss's office during an annual performance review
situation: The Boss announces he will use humor to ease the tension of Dilbert's annual appraisal and tells the classic 'how many engineers' lightbulb joke. Dilbert first says he doesn't know, then guesses 'three.' The Boss responds that the answer matches the poor rating he is about to give.
punchline: The Boss's reply turns Dilbert's wrong guess into an insult, implying his appraisal is just as poor and that the boss's joke was a setup for criticism rather than comic relief.
summary: A manager's attempt at a lighthearted joke before a review ends up as a passive-aggressive dig at the employee's performance.

title: Dogbert's Tax Preparation Confusion Scam

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Tax preparation $5.00

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: I need some help...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Sit down.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: I always fooled around during math classes. Now I can't do my own taxes.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: We can prattle about your inadequacies later.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll do your taxes and talk at the same time so you really feel dumb.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Hmm... Simply multiply the standard deviation of the cosine of your depreciation and integrate the resulting polynomial... There.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: According to this, you owe your tax preparer an additional two thousand dollars.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Confusion - it works for the IRS and it can work for you.

setting: Dogbert's makeshift tax preparation desk
situation: A bald customer in a yellow shirt approaches Dogbert's $5 tax preparation booth admitting he never paid attention in math class. Dogbert insults him, then rattles off nonsensical mathematical jargon while supposedly doing his taxes. He then announces the customer owes him an extra two thousand dollars and ends up with a pile of cash.
punchline: Dogbert exploits the customer's math ignorance with meaningless technobabble to con him into paying far more than the advertised fee, justifying it by comparing his tactic to the confusing tax code the IRS uses.
summary: A con-artist canine bamboozles a math-averse client with absurd formulas and bills him a fortune for a cheap tax service.

title: Money Buried in Bags Fund

transcript.speaker: Financial Advisor
transcript.text: That's our new "Strategic Diversification Fund."

transcript.speaker: Financial Advisor
transcript.text: Our lawyers put your money in little bags, then we have trained dogs bury them around town.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do they bury the bags or the lawyers?

transcript.speaker: Financial Advisor
transcript.text: We've tried it both ways.

setting: Restaurant or meeting table with coffee cups and papers
situation: Dilbert sits across a table from a financial advisor who is pitching a new investment product. The advisor casually explains that the fund consists of lawyers putting clients' money in bags for trained dogs to bury around town. Dilbert asks whether the bags or the lawyers get buried, and the advisor says they've done both.
punchline: The supposedly sophisticated investment fund is absurdly primitive, and the advisor's cheerful admission that they have tried burying lawyers too implies both incompetence and a dark disregard for the clients' money.
summary: A smiling money manager reveals that his fancy-sounding fund is really just cash hidden in holes by dogs, and cheerfully admits that lawyers have been buried too.

title: Alien Abduction Was Just a Movie

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I didn't remember being abducted by aliens until you hypnotized me. But now I remember they looked like "E.T."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I remember being in a dark room with rows of seats. They fed us a popcorn-like substance. My feet were stuck to the floor.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I recall being disgusted that they charged me six dollars to enter the ship.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That's why you suppressed the memory.

setting: Dogbert's office, with Dilbert seated across the desk
situation: Dilbert recounts the memories he recovered after Dogbert hypnotized him, claiming he was abducted by aliens who looked like E.T. As he reads his notes, the details (dark room, rows of seats, popcorn, sticky floor, paid admission) make it clear he is actually describing a trip to the movie theater. Dogbert, acting as hypnotherapist, deadpans that this is why he suppressed the memory.
punchline: Dilbert's recovered alien-abduction memory is plainly just a bad movie-theater experience, and Dogbert's deadpan reply treats the overpriced ticket as the real trauma.
summary: A hypnotized man's recollection of being taken aboard an alien spacecraft turns out to match an overpriced night at the cinema in every detail.

title: Ratbert Pitches Himself as Pet

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Forget Dogbert; I can be your new best friend!

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Rats are twice as good for cuddling. And you should see me catch a frisbee!

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Here, scratch behind my ears. You'll find me most appreciative!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You sound like me on a date.

setting: Dilbert's desk at the office
situation: Ratbert, standing on Dilbert's desk, tries to persuade Dilbert to adopt him as a replacement for Dogbert. He lists his advantages as a pet: cuddling, catching frisbees, and being scratched behind the ears. Dilbert replies that Ratbert's desperate sales pitch sounds just like himself on a date.
punchline: Ratbert's needy, eager-to-please begging for affection reminds Dilbert of his own awkward, desperate behavior when dating.
summary: A pleading little rat auditions for the role of best friend, and his neediness strikes his prospective owner as uncomfortably familiar.

title: Ratbert Won't Be A Little Rat

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: You've never accepted me in your family because I'm a little rat.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: But I'll be testing a drug at the lab that will change that. No more little rat.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You won't be a rat?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Don't tell me it's the "rat" part that bothers you...

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle
situation: Ratbert complains to Dilbert, who sits at his computer, that Dilbert's family has never accepted him because he is a little rat. He announces he will be testing a drug at the lab that will change that. Dilbert asks if he won't be a rat, and Ratbert wryly responds as if the 'rat' part is what bothers Dilbert.
punchline: Ratbert has misheard or misread the issue: he assumes the problem is his size ('little'), while Dilbert is clearly bothered by the 'rat' part, and Ratbert's last line is a pointed, sarcastic jab at that.
summary: A tiny lab-bound pet announces a drug trial meant to cure his unwelcome status, only to be asked whether he'll stop being a rodent at all.

title: Credit Card Application Includes Cavity Search

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'd like to apply for a "Bank of Ethel" credit card.

transcript.speaker: Ethel
transcript.text: Sit down and shut up.

transcript.speaker: Ethel
transcript.text: It's 21% interest plus surprisingly high annual fees. We'll do a credit check and a full body cavity search.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...And I had to smile the whole time because they were filming it for their television ads.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You have to admire their attitude.

setting: A bank desk, then Dilbert's home
situation: Dilbert applies for a Bank of Ethel credit card and is rudely told to sit down and shut up by the bank clerk. She announces a 21% interest rate, high fees, and a credit check plus full body cavity search. Later Dilbert, standing in polka-dot boxer shorts, tells Dogbert he had to smile throughout because the humiliating process was being filmed for television ads.
punchline: The bank's contempt for customers is so extreme that it turns an invasive cavity search into advertising material, which Dogbert sarcastically calls admirable attitude.
summary: A man seeking a credit card endures abusive terms and a humiliating physical search, all while being secretly recorded for the bank's commercials.

title: Dogbert Tricks Insecure Woman Into Self-Insult

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's easy to make insecure people insult themselves.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Good morning, ma'am. You look thin and sexy today!

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Sexy?! Ha! I'm a whale... a whale with a bad hairdo!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Next.

setting: Outdoor sidewalk with grass behind it
situation: Dogbert walks down a sidewalk and thinks that insecure people are easy to manipulate into insulting themselves. He greets a passing woman with an exaggerated compliment about being thin and sexy. She immediately reacts by calling herself a whale with a bad hairdo, and Dogbert happily moves on to his next target.
punchline: Dogbert's flattery is a deliberate experiment that proves his claim, since the insecure woman responds to a compliment by savagely insulting herself, and he cheerfully looks for the next victim.
summary: A scheming dog offers a flattering greeting to a stranger just to watch her respond with harsh self-criticism, then skips off in search of someone else to try it on.

title: Dogbert Babysits, Terrorizes Toddler for Fun

transcript.speaker: Mother
transcript.text: Thanks for agreeing to baby-sit, Dogbert.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: No sweat.

transcript.speaker: Baby Bret
transcript.text: Doggie-bert!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Sit down, Bret.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You're in your most innocent and impressionable years.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: As an adult, it is my duty to fill your sponge-like brain with incredible nonsense for my own entertainment.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your parents are really space aliens.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: They're just fattening you up so they can eat you!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The slaughterhouse is a place they call kindergarten!!

transcript.speaker: Father
transcript.text: Thanks, Dogbert. Did you change him?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Probably.

setting: A family's home living room
situation: Dogbert agrees to babysit a toddler named Bret and decides to use the job for his own amusement. He tells the impressionable child that his parents are space aliens fattening him up to be eaten, and that kindergarten is a slaughterhouse. When the father returns and pays him, he asks if Dogbert changed the baby.
punchline: Dogbert's cheerful 'Probably' answers the diaper question while hinting that he has indeed changed the child, now traumatized by his lies.
summary: A babysitting dog gleefully fills a gullible toddler's mind with terrifying fabrications and then collects his fee from the unsuspecting dad.

title: Past Inventions Don't Count Toward Appraisal

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Tell me what you've accomplished this year so I can write your performance appraisal.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The inventions I made last year -- that you thought were worthless, will generate twelve million in license fees next year!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So, no real accomplishments THIS year?

setting: The Boss's office, during a performance appraisal
situation: The Boss asks Dilbert to list his accomplishments so he can write the annual performance appraisal. Dilbert points out that inventions the Boss once dismissed as worthless will bring in twelve million dollars in license fees. The Boss ignores the success and fixates on the fact that nothing was accomplished this year.
punchline: The Boss dismisses a huge payoff from Dilbert's earlier work on a technicality, showing how managers never admit they were wrong and care only about the current review period.
summary: A manager brushes off a multimillion-dollar windfall from an employee's earlier inventions because it technically happened in the wrong year.

title: Supercomputer Predicts Evil Squirrel Kidnapping

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Here's the full script of the rest of your life. My supercomputer model predicted it.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Well, according to this I'll be kidnapped by evil squirrels and forced to work in their nut mines.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They get me too.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I didn't know that evil squirrels had nut mines.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's probably too late to do anything about it.

setting: Dilbert's home, with Dogbert on a chair and later at a desk
situation: Dilbert hands Dogbert a thick book containing the supposed script of the rest of his life, generated by his supercomputer model. Dogbert reads that he will be kidnapped by evil squirrels and forced to work in their nut mines, and Dilbert says the same fate awaits him. They discuss it calmly and conclude it's too late to prevent it.
punchline: The supercomputer's absurdly specific prediction is accepted without question, and the characters resign themselves to the fate instead of doubting the model or trying to avoid it.
summary: A man's computer forecast of a friend's entire future turns out to include a bizarre squirrel abduction, which both of them meekly accept as unavoidable.

title: Dogbert Eavesdrops for Inside Trading

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I've decided to become an inside trader of stocks.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Inside trading is illegal. Besides, where will you get your information?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Shhh... I hear a board meeting starting in San Francisco.

setting: Dilbert's living room
situation: Dogbert, perched on a footstool, tells Dilbert he plans to become an inside trader of stocks. Dilbert, reading the newspaper in his armchair, points out that it is illegal and asks where Dogbert would even get the information. Dogbert then listens intently and claims he can hear a board meeting starting far away in San Francisco.
punchline: Dogbert's absurd claim that he can literally overhear a distant corporate board meeting shows he intends to get his illegal inside information by eavesdropping, brushing off Dilbert's objections.
summary: A scheming dog plans to profit from confidential corporate secrets and boasts that his hearing is good enough to pick up a boardroom discussion across the country.

title: Dogbert Lobbies for Canine Tax Rebate

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: So, Mister President, a tax rebate for dogs is the only fair way to stimulate the economy.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Because then you get a Keynesian free market multiplier effect to boost your GNP up the supply side of the curve.

transcript.speaker: The President
transcript.text: Are you positive that dogs can vote?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Now, R-E-E-L him in...

setting: The President's office
situation: Dogbert sits at a large desk facing the President, pitching a tax rebate exclusively for dogs as the fair way to stimulate the economy. He backs it up with a string of economic jargon. The President asks whether dogs can even vote, and Dogbert privately thinks about reeling him in like a fish.
punchline: Dogbert's real motive is political: he wants the rebate because he is angling for votes, and he is playing the President like a fish on a line while hiding it behind impressive-sounding economic buzzwords.
summary: A scheming dog baffles a president with economic jargon to win a special tax break for canines while secretly manipulating him.

title: Dogbert Pitches Hangover Beer Slogan

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the Ad Man

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: We must turn the negatives of your product into perceived benefits.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The new slogan will be "Shmultz Beer: You know it's working because your head pounds."

transcript.speaker: Beer Executive
transcript.text: Can you work some bikinis into this concept?

transcript.speaker: Beer Executive
transcript.text: We're very lonely men.

setting: Advertising pitch meeting in a conference room
situation: Dogbert, working as an ad man, presents a flip-chart pitch to two beer company executives. He explains that product negatives should be recast as benefits and proposes a slogan celebrating the hangover headache, illustrated by a dazed drinker. The executives ignore the slogan and ask for bikinis to be added, admitting they are lonely.
punchline: The beer executives are indifferent to the clever slogan about hangovers and only care about adding bikini-clad women, revealing the clients' own lonely, shallow motives.
summary: An ad consultant spins a beer's hangover into a selling point, but his clients only want swimsuit models in the campaign.

title: Mensa Networking Reaches the Garbage Man

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You joined what?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Mensa. It's a group of people with genius IQs.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm hoping it will be a good way to network and enhance my career.

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: I heard you joined our Mensa group... I hope you can make it to the Career Expo.

setting: Dilbert's office, then outside by a trash can
situation: Dilbert tells Dogbert he has joined Mensa, the society for people with genius IQs, hoping it will help him network and advance his career. In the last panel a garbage man emptying a trash can says he heard Dilbert joined 'our' Mensa group and invites him to the Career Expo.
punchline: Dilbert's hoped-for career networking turns out to be with garbage men, implying that Mensa members are underemployed and that high IQ does not translate into career success.
summary: A man hoping a genius society will boost his career finds that its members include sanitation workers.

title: Can-O-Matic Fires Staff Randomly

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: As your consultant, I recommend the "Can-O-Matic" to reduce staff levels.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Disguised as a restroom stall, the Can-O-Matic randomly fires people by slapping a pink slip on their backs and catapulting them out of the building.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But I won't get to see the expressions on their faces.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Well, we could fling them past the security cameras here...

setting: Office conference area with a flip chart on an easel
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, presents a flip-chart pitch for the Can-O-Matic, a restroom-stall-disguised device that fires employees at random by sticking a pink slip on them and launching them out of the building. The Boss approves of the concept but complains he won't get to watch his victims' reactions. Dogbert offers to route them past the security cameras so he can watch.
punchline: The Boss's only objection to a cruel, random firing machine is that he would miss seeing his employees' shocked faces, and Dogbert cheerfully accommodates his sadism.
summary: A consultant pitches a booby-trapped bathroom stall that randomly ejects workers from the company, and the manager's sole complaint is missing the show.

title: Dogbert's Driving School Scare Tactics

transcript.speaker: Student
transcript.text: Sign me up, little doggie-dude.

transcript.speaker: Sign
transcript.text: Dogbert's Driving School

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: We'll begin with a film about gruesome highway accidents. It is intended to shock you into driving safely.

transcript.speaker: Student
transcript.text: Really? People get shocked by THIS?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll be following your car in a helicopter.

setting: Dogbert's Driving School office
situation: A young man in a red cap enrolls at Dogbert's Driving School. Dogbert announces a shocking film about gruesome highway accidents, and the student casually eats a snack while watching, unfazed. Dogbert responds with a more ominous plan for his driving lessons.
punchline: Since the gory film fails to scare the student, Dogbert threatens to escalate to menacing surveillance, following his car in a helicopter.
summary: A driving student shrugs off a grisly safety film, so the school's canine owner promises a far more intimidating form of supervision.

title: Knee-Jerk Liberal Reflex Test

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Hold still while Doctor Dogbert whacks your knee.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Aak... Crime is society's fault... Raise taxes to feed the poor... Stop nuclear research... Save the...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Apparently you're a knee-jerk liberal. You can live a normal life but you'll be annoying at parties.

setting: A doctor's examination room
situation: Dogbert, playing a doctor, stands on a stool and taps a seated patient's knee with a reflex hammer. Instead of a leg twitch, the patient blurts out a string of liberal political talking points. Dogbert diagnoses him as a knee-jerk liberal and says he can live normally but will be annoying at parties.
punchline: Taking the phrase 'knee-jerk liberal' literally, the reflex test produces political slogans instead of a kick, and the diagnosis is merely that he'll be tiresome at social gatherings.
summary: A pretend physician literally tests a man's reflexes and finds that his knee triggers automatic political rants rather than a kick.

title: Judge Keeps Declaring Courtroom Ties

transcript.speaker: Judge
transcript.text: Mister Dogbert, you made a good argument in your petimony suit against Dilbert...

transcript.speaker: Judge
transcript.text: But Dilbert had some good points, too... I call it a tie.

transcript.speaker: Judge
transcript.text: Third tie this week... Maybe it's me...

setting: A courtroom, with the judge seated at the bench
situation: A judge hears a lawsuit brought by Dogbert against Dilbert and praises both sides before ruling the case a tie. In the last panel he thinks to himself that this is his third tie this week and wonders whether he is the problem.
punchline: The judge slowly realizes that his habit of splitting the difference and calling everything a tie suggests he is simply indecisive and unable to make a ruling.
summary: A wishy-washy judge declares yet another case a draw and finally wonders if his own indecisiveness is to blame.

title: Bluffing Latin Before the Judge

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: At the petimony trial

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your honor, I request that Dogbert's suit against me be dropped...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...on the grounds that there's no habeas corpus, no lo contendre, and no e pluribus unum.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: With luck, he doesn't know Latin either.

transcript.speaker: Judge
transcript.text: Bailiff, club this man.

setting: A courtroom during a trial
situation: Dilbert, defending himself against a lawsuit filed by Dogbert, asks the judge to dismiss the case. He strings together impressive-sounding Latin phrases that are misused or invented, hoping the judge won't notice. The judge sees through the bluff and orders the bailiff to club him.
punchline: Dilbert's gamble that the judge is as ignorant of Latin as he is backfires, and the judge answers his pseudo-legal jargon with violence.
summary: A defendant tries to dodge a lawsuit by bluffing with nonsense Latin, only to have the judge order him beaten.

title: Booby-Trapped Sidewalk Flings the Mailman

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've received death threats because of my new patent. So I augmented our home security system.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The sidewalk is rigged to give an electric shock, thus disarming the intruder. Then a spring catapults him to the city landfill.

transcript.speaker: Mailman
transcript.text: Aagh! Fling

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The mail is here.

setting: Dilbert's home living room
situation: Dilbert explains to Dogbert that he has upgraded his home security after receiving death threats over a new patent. The sidewalk shocks intruders and then catapults them to the landfill. A mail carrier approaches, gets zapped and flung, and scattered letters rain down outside the window.
punchline: Dilbert's overzealous security system can't tell a harmless mail carrier from a killer, so the mail is delivered by the carrier being flung away, scattering letters everywhere.
summary: A man's lethal home defenses, built to stop assassins, instead launch the unsuspecting letter carrier into the distance.

title: Donuts Versus Co-Worker and Bear

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: At the "Rivers and Trees" management course.

transcript.speaker: Instructor
transcript.text: We'll start with a trust-building exercise.

transcript.speaker: Instructor
transcript.text: You have one minute to decide to eat these donuts or to save your co-worker from the bear.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Okay, who wants to be on the donut option working committee?

transcript.speaker: Bald Man
transcript.text: Oops... problem solved.

setting: Outdoor wilderness management training course in a forest clearing
situation: At a management retreat, an instructor sets up a trust-building exercise in which participants must choose within one minute between eating donuts or saving a co-worker who is hanging from a rope and about to be reached by a bear. Instead of acting, a woman asks who wants to join a working committee on the donut option. By then the time has run out and the co-worker's fate has been settled.
punchline: The managers respond to a life-or-death choice by forming a committee, so they waste the minute and the problem solves itself the grim way, showing how bureaucracy paralyzes decision-making.
summary: Managers on a corporate retreat answer a rescue-or-snack dilemma by organizing a committee and run out the clock while a bear closes in.

title: Government UFO Cover-Up Logic

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: General, I don't understand why the government is trying to cover up all the U.F.O. encounters.

transcript.speaker: General
transcript.text: People would lose faith in their government if they knew aliens were abducting people and we were helpless to stop them.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: So, to maintain confidence in the government, you use our taxes to kill the citizens who find out?

transcript.speaker: General
transcript.text: Is that so bad?

setting: A military office with a table, chairs and coffee cups
situation: Dogbert sits across a table from a military general and asks why the government hides UFO encounters. The general explains that people would lose faith if they learned aliens were abducting people and the military couldn't stop it. Dogbert sums up the policy as using taxpayer money to kill citizens who find out, and the general casually asks if that's really so bad.
punchline: The general admits the cover-up involves killing citizens with their own tax money, and shrugs it off as no big deal, showing how far officials will go to protect public confidence.
summary: A general calmly justifies silencing citizens who discover alien abductions, treating murder as a reasonable price for keeping the public trusting its leaders.

title: Dogbert Becomes Supreme Ruler of Earth

transcript.speaker: TV Newscaster
transcript.text: In a surprise decision, the United Nations voted to make Dogbert - the space alien - the supreme ruler of Earth.

transcript.speaker: TV Newscaster
transcript.text: More on that later. But first, science offers new hope for people with freckles...

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert holds his first press conference

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Hu-ha-ha! Hu-ha-ha!

transcript.speaker: Reporter
transcript.text: Not a good sign.

setting: Dilbert's living room watching TV, then a press conference podium
situation: Dilbert watches a TV news report announcing that the United Nations has made Dogbert, a space alien, the supreme ruler of Earth. The newscaster quickly moves on to a trivial story about freckles. At his first press conference, Dogbert laughs maniacally from the podium while a worried reporter looks on.
punchline: The world has just been handed to an evil-laughing alien dictator, yet the media treats it as a minor item, and Dogbert's villainous laughter confirms the reporter's fear that this is a bad omen.
summary: News of Earth's new alien overlord is brushed aside for freckle science before Dogbert cackles ominously in front of the press.

title: Aliens Playing Hide the Pellet

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We can only speculate why aliens keep abducting people.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They often probe people's body cavities. Sometimes they implant small objects. It must be some form of highly advanced medical research.

transcript.speaker: Alien 1
transcript.text: How about another round of "hide the pellet"?

transcript.speaker: Alien 2
transcript.text: Okay. I can use my nose prober.

setting: Dilbert's home or office, with a cutaway to aliens
situation: Dilbert muses to Dogbert that alien abductions, with their probing and implanting of small objects, must be advanced medical research. The final panel reveals the aliens themselves casually playing a game called 'hide the pellet', with one planning to use a nose prober.
punchline: What humans assume is sophisticated scientific research is actually just aliens amusing themselves with a juvenile game.
summary: A man theorizes that alien abductions serve lofty scientific goals, but the aliens are shown simply playing a silly game with their victims' orifices.

title: Roofer Admits He's Unreliable, Gets Hired

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The roof is leaking there. Can you fix it tomorrow?

transcript.speaker: Roofer
transcript.text: Well, like all members of my profession, I'm unreliable. However, I could give you a quote and then never show up or return your calls.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're hired. Nobody else would even show up for the quote.

transcript.speaker: Roofer
transcript.text: I depend on repeat customers.

setting: Outside Dilbert's house, beneath a leaking roof
situation: Dilbert points to a leak in his roof and asks a roofer to fix it the next day. The roofer candidly admits that his profession is unreliable and that he might give a quote and then vanish. Dilbert hires him anyway because no other roofer would even show up to quote.
punchline: Dilbert is so desperate for any contractor that he hires the one who openly admits he won't show up, and the roofer's closing remark about depending on repeat customers is absurd given how unreliable he is.
summary: A homeowner with a leaky roof hires the only contractor who bothers to turn up, even though the man cheerfully confesses he will probably flake.

title: Meat Lobby Fights Nutrition Pyramid

transcript.speaker: Lobbyist
transcript.text: We must use all of the resources of the "cow and egg" lobby to counter the latest threat from the vegetarians.

transcript.speaker: Lobbyist
transcript.text: Somehow they've managed to link food with health... They invented a "nutrition pyramid" chart and got schools to use it...

transcript.speaker: Teacher
transcript.text: Kids, this is a little different from the way I learned it...

setting: A lobbyist's office, then a school classroom
situation: A powerful lobbyist for the meat and egg industry rallies two aides to fight a pyramid chart promoted by vegetarians, complaining that it links food to health. In the last panel a teacher presents a distorted food pyramid that puts meat at the top with a skull and crossbones, and gravel and bugs alongside milk and beer.
punchline: The industry's counterattack is so heavy-handed that it produces an obviously absurd propaganda chart, showing how lobbying twists information that schools teach children.
summary: An industry lobbyist grumbles about a health chart threatening his business, and a teacher then unveils a bizarrely rewritten version of it for her pupils.

title: Boss Shocks Himself With Cattle Prod

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's see if my idea of using an electric cattle prod will boost employee productivity.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: ZAP!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Mental note: Hold rubber end.

setting: Office cubicle
situation: The Boss stands behind Dilbert, who is working at his computer, and announces he will test an electric cattle prod as a way to increase productivity. He grabs the wrong end of the prod and gives himself a violent shock, leaving him charred and frazzled with his hair standing on end. Dilbert is untouched.
punchline: The Boss's cruel productivity scheme backfires on him because he is too clueless to hold the prod by its insulated handle.
summary: A manager's plan to motivate staff with a livestock zapper ends with him electrocuting himself instead.

title: Boss Doesn't Recognize His Employees

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's begin by going around the table and introducing ourselves.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm Dilbert. I've worked for you for five years.

transcript.speaker: Albert
transcript.text: Albert, six years.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Alice, I've worked for you for ten years.

transcript.speaker: Sally
transcript.text: Sally, eight years.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I knew these people looked familiar.

setting: Conference room meeting table
situation: The Boss opens a meeting by asking everyone around the table to introduce themselves. Dilbert, Albert, Alice and Sally each state how many years they have worked for him, ranging from five to ten years. The Boss, in a thought bubble, remarks that the people looked familiar.
punchline: The Boss has managed these employees for years yet has to be told who they are, and only vaguely realizes he has seen them before, showing how out of touch he is.
summary: A manager asks his long-serving staff to introduce themselves and privately concludes that their faces seem familiar.

title: Crime as a Dating Strategy

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why do women write letters to guys who are in prison?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe if I commit a crime I can go to prison just long enough to improve my social life.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Why not do a personals ad instead?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's more of a last resort.

setting: Dilbert's living room, sitting on the couch
situation: Dilbert sits on his couch and wonders aloud why women write letters to prisoners. He decides he could commit a crime and serve a short sentence to improve his dating prospects. Dogbert suggests placing a personals ad instead, but Dilbert says that is more of a last resort.
punchline: Dilbert considers going to prison a more acceptable way to meet women than placing a personals ad, which shows how desperate and awkward his social life is.
summary: A lonely engineer weighs a brief stint behind bars as a smarter way to meet women than advertising for a date.
