transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Woman (thought)
transcript.text: What's going on here?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert (thought)
transcript.text: Good. It looks like the window of opportunity is still slightly open.

setting: A grassy hillside outdoors
situation: Dilbert's girlfriend tells him she wants them to be just friends, and he calmly agrees. Disappointed that he gives in so easily, she keeps demoting the relationship, from friends to acquaintances to a fired ex-butler, and he agrees every time. At the end she grows suspicious while Dilbert privately concludes that the relationship might not be over.
punchline: By agreeing to every increasingly insulting demand, Dilbert shows he is willing to accept any humiliation to keep a sliver of hope alive, while she can't stand that her bargaining isn't meeting resistance.
summary: A woman tries to push her boyfriend into a breakup, but his endless agreeableness only makes her demands more absurd while he quietly hopes for another chance.

title: Ratbert's Most Dangerous Cosmetics Test

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: What product are we testing today, Doc?

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: We'll be testing the safety of cosmetics. This will be your most dangerous assignment.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Sometimes I hate this job.

transcript.speaker: Catcaller
transcript.text: Hey baby!!

transcript.speaker: Catcaller
transcript.text: Whoa!! Whoa!!

setting: Research laboratory, then an outdoor sidewalk
situation: Ratbert, working as a lab test subject, asks the doctor what product they are testing today. The doctor says it is cosmetics safety testing and warns it will be Ratbert's most dangerous assignment. In the last panel Ratbert walks down the street wearing the makeup, getting catcalled by unseen men.
punchline: The danger of testing cosmetics is not toxic chemicals but the unwanted catcalls Ratbert gets when he walks outside wearing makeup.
summary: A lab rat expects a hazardous experiment but discovers the real risk of makeup testing is being whistled at by strangers on the street.

title: Dilbert Threatens Elves With Flyswatter

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: "We the elves make the following demands..."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wouldn't it be funny if I just slapped your pointy hats flat?

transcript.speaker: Elf
transcript.text: I cannot believe what passes for funny around here.

setting: Dilbert's desk or office, with tiny elves on the desktop
situation: Dilbert reads a list of demands from a group of tiny elves standing on his desk while Dogbert watches. Dilbert picks up a flyswatter and muses aloud about flattening their pointy hats. The elves, unimpressed and stomping away in a line, complain about the sense of humor in the office.
punchline: The elves, who are about to be swatted, are more offended by Dilbert's bad joke than by the threat itself, turning the threat into a complaint about the office's low standard of humor.
summary: Tiny elves present their ultimatum to a flyswatter-wielding Dilbert, who responds with a menacing quip that leaves them criticizing his idea of comedy.

title: Dilbert's Fiber Optic Competitor Warning

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There... I think I've invented a way to send vast amounts of data without fiber optic cables.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's a simple application of J.S. Bell's theorem.* He showed that if you break up a molecule and change the spin of one electron, the spin of the other electrons originally joined will immediately change too, no matter where they are.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: *Really, no kidding

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What do you think the fiber optic industry will give me for this?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: A horse's head in your bed.

setting: Dilbert's office desk, with Dogbert seated across from him
situation: Dilbert tells Dogbert he has invented a way to transmit huge amounts of data without fiber optic cables, explaining it using Bell's theorem and entangled electron spins. He then asks what the fiber optic industry will give him for his invention. Dogbert answers with a reference to a threatening mob warning.
punchline: Dogbert implies the fiber optic industry will respond to a disruptive invention with mafia-style intimidation, alluding to the horse's head scene in The Godfather.
summary: An inventor eager for a reward learns that threatening his established industry could earn him menace rather than money.

title: Date Falls For The Waiter

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: I must warn you that I have an obsessive personality.

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: If I spend a moment with a man I fall completely in love. I think of only him. I... I become his slave.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you saying...

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: Yes. I'm in love with our waiter.

setting: A restaurant table during a dinner date
situation: Dilbert sits across from his date at a restaurant. She warns him that she has an obsessive personality and falls completely in love with any man she spends a moment with. When Dilbert starts to ask what she means, she confirms she has fallen for their waiter instead of him.
punchline: Dilbert braced for a confession of obsessive love for himself, but the date's obsession has landed on the waiter, who spent more time with her than Dilbert did.
summary: A woman on a dinner date cautions her companion about her tendency to obsess over men, then reveals her fixation is on the server.

title: Dilbert Doubts His Own Happiness

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I thought I was happy...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then I thought what if I only THINK I'm happy but I'm not. Maybe I've been hypnotized and don't even know it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Worrying about it made me unhappy, which means I must NOT be under hypnosis, so I'm happy.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Maybe I only THINK you're talking but really I'm happy.

setting: Outdoor walking path through grassy hills, then a rock where Dilbert sits
situation: Dilbert strolls along a path with Dogbert and talks through a chain of reasoning about whether he is truly happy or merely hypnotized into thinking so. He concludes that because worrying made him unhappy, he must not be hypnotized and is therefore happy. Dogbert answers by applying the same shaky logic to Dilbert's speech.
punchline: Dogbert mocks Dilbert's circular, overthinking logic by suggesting he only thinks Dilbert is talking while really being happy, implying he has tuned out the whole rambling monologue.
summary: A man talks himself in circles about whether his contentment is real, and his dog answers with a deadpan parody of the same reasoning.

title: Dilbert Smitten by Biographer Kitty

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What happened to you?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Kitty Kelly was here to write your biography. She was all over me. I think she took my watch.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I never trust anybody named "Kitty."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think I love her.

setting: Dilbert's home or office
situation: Dilbert stands rumpled, with his shirt disheveled and lipstick kisses all over his face, and Dogbert asks what happened. Dilbert explains that biographer Kitty Kelly came to write Dogbert's biography, was all over him, and probably stole his watch. Dogbert says he distrusts anyone named Kitty, but Dilbert, still covered in kisses, says he thinks he loves her.
punchline: Dilbert has clearly been seduced and robbed, yet he is so smitten by the attention that he declares his love for the thief.
summary: A lipstick-smeared Dilbert admits a visiting biographer swindled him and then swoons over her anyway.

title: Dogbert's Distracting Driving Lesson Simulator

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: With your right hand, insert a CD into the stereo... Good.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Now signal left! Answer the car phone! Defrost the rear window! Honk if you love fishing!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Fortunately, we're only in the driving simulator.

transcript.speaker: Car Salesman
transcript.text: Do you boys want to take it for a test drive?

setting: Inside a car in a dealership showroom
situation: Dogbert, acting as a driving instructor in a car marked 'Student Driver', pelts Dilbert with a string of simultaneous tasks: insert a CD, signal, answer the car phone, defrost the window and honk. Dilbert grows frantic and overwhelmed. The final panel reveals the car is just a demo model in a dealership, and a salesman approaches to offer a test drive.
punchline: Dilbert's panicked multitasking was all for nothing because they were merely sitting in a showroom car, and Dogbert's 'lesson' was really a prank on him.
summary: A flustered student gets bombarded with in-car chores by his dog instructor before it turns out they never left the showroom floor.

title: Churn 'N' Burn Mutual Funds

transcript.speaker: Financial Adviser
transcript.text: I recommend our "Churn 'N' Burn" family of mutual funds.

transcript.speaker: Financial Adviser
transcript.text: We'll turn your worthless equity into valuable brokerage fees in just three days!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it risky?

transcript.speaker: Financial Adviser
transcript.text: Are you kidding?! We have actual brochures!

setting: Financial adviser's office, seated at a table
situation: Dilbert meets with a financial adviser who pitches a mutual fund family called "Churn 'N' Burn." The adviser cheerfully admits the fund converts the client's equity into brokerage fees within days. When Dilbert asks if it is risky, the adviser offers the existence of brochures as proof of legitimacy.
punchline: The adviser answers a question about risk by pointing to printed brochures, implying that glossy marketing material substitutes for safety, while the fund openly exists to generate fees by draining the client's money.
summary: A cheerful investment salesman openly promises to convert a client's savings into commissions, then treats sales brochures as proof the product is safe.

title: Lab Rat Plans Revenge on Researchers

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: All week I've been watching violent movies at the lab.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: A group of parents are studying me to see if I become inured to violence.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Are you?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Yeah. I'm planning to gnaw the parents to death tomorrow.

setting: A stone wall outdoors, with a pink sky behind
situation: Ratbert tells Dogbert that he has spent the week watching violent movies in a laboratory while a group of parents observes him, to find out whether he becomes desensitized to violence. When Dogbert asks if it is working, Ratbert calmly says he plans to gnaw the parents to death the next day.
punchline: The experiment's subject has indeed become desensitized to violence, as the parents feared, and he is about to demonstrate it on the researchers themselves.
summary: A test animal casually reveals that the screen-violence study on him has worked, and the observers are about to learn it the hard way.

title: Dogbert Denies Respecting Ratbert

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Dogbert, sometimes I think you're the only one who respects me.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Wrong.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Maybe I should drop it while there's still some ambiguity.

setting: Dogbert's red armchair at home
situation: Ratbert sits on the arm of an armchair next to Dogbert and says he feels Dogbert is the only one who respects him. Dogbert flatly replies that he is wrong. Ratbert then thinks to himself that he should stop the conversation before the answer becomes any clearer.
punchline: Dogbert bluntly rejects the idea that he respects Ratbert, so Ratbert decides to quit while he can still pretend the answer is uncertain.
summary: A hopeful little pet fishes for a compliment from his cynical companion and gets shot down in a single word.

title: Worcestershire Sauce Frostbite Cure

transcript.speaker: Pilot
transcript.text: I've survived several jet crashes this year, so listen to me.

transcript.speaker: Pilot
transcript.text: The best way to prevent frostbite is to rub Worcestershire sauce on your body and whack yourself repeatedly with a meat tenderizer.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I wonder why he had enough of these for everybody?

transcript.speaker: Survivors
transcript.text: Whack whack

setting: Snowy mountainside near a crashed jet
situation: Crash survivors stand in the snow while a portly pilot, who claims to have survived several jet crashes, gives them frostbite-prevention advice. He tells them to rub Worcestershire sauce on themselves and hit themselves with a meat tenderizer, and the group obediently does so. Dilbert, doing it too, wonders why the pilot happened to have enough supplies for everyone.
punchline: The pilot's absurd advice, which conveniently involves seasoning and tenderizing the survivors' bodies, hints that he is a serial crash survivor because he eats the other passengers.
summary: Stranded plane-crash survivors blindly follow a pilot's bizarre advice to season and pound themselves, oblivious that they are being prepared as a meal.

title: Dogbert's Ping-Pong Gun Family Game

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I bought a gun that shoots ping-pong balls!

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Ptoink

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I love games that involve the whole family.

setting: Dilbert's home, at his desk
situation: Dogbert announces he has bought a gun that shoots ping-pong balls while Dilbert sits working at his desk. Dogbert immediately fires it and hits Dilbert in the forehead with a ball. Dogbert then walks away with the gun, musing happily about games for the whole family.
punchline: Dogbert's idea of a family game is shooting Dilbert in the head with a toy gun, so Dilbert is the unwilling target of the fun.
summary: Dogbert gleefully pelts a distracted Dilbert with a toy gun and calls it wholesome family fun.

title: Ratbert Turns Clueless Around 360 Degrees

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Ratbert, I brought you a copy of the "Dogbert Clueletter," the newsletter for clueless people.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: No thanks. I used to be clueless but I turned that situation around 360 degrees.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: "Dogbert's clues to conversational geometry..."

setting: Ratbert's living room, with Ratbert sitting on a maroon ottoman
situation: Dogbert offers Ratbert a copy of his newsletter for clueless people, called the Clueletter. Ratbert declines, claiming he fixed his cluelessness by turning it around 360 degrees, which is a full circle back to where he started. Dogbert then reads aloud from the newsletter's article on conversational geometry.
punchline: Ratbert's claim of turning things around 360 degrees shows he is still clueless, since a full rotation leaves him exactly where he began, and Dogbert's newsletter is conveniently ready with a lesson on geometry.
summary: A boastful rodent thinks a complete spin counts as a reversal, so a canine publisher happily reaches for the right issue of his self-help sheet.

title: Dilbert Meets Dogbert's Laughing Game

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I know you're only trying to make me THINK you've played a prank on me!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Hoo-ha-ha hoo-ha-ha

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, two can play this game, my friend.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Is this a bad time to visit?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Hoo-ha ha, hoo-ha-ha

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hoo-ha-ha, hoo-ha-ha

setting: Dilbert's home living room
situation: Dilbert accuses Dogbert of merely pretending to have pulled a prank on him. Dogbert just keeps laughing in a sinister way. Dilbert decides to play the same game and mimics the laughter, so Ratbert arrives to find both of them laughing maniacally.
punchline: Dilbert tries to beat Dogbert at his own bluffing game by laughing mysteriously too, ending up looking just as unhinged and baffling a visitor.
summary: Dilbert tries to out-bluff a smugly cackling Dogbert by laughing right back, leaving a visiting Ratbert wondering what is going on.

title: Government Assassin Hampered by Budget Cuts

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The government sent a general to kill me for talking about my encounter with space aliens.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I was scared at first. But when you think about the government's track record, well, my odds are pretty good...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Especially after all the budget cutbacks.

transcript.speaker: General
transcript.text: Dang it! Where's my air support?!!

setting: Dilbert's home or living room
situation: Dilbert calmly explains to Dogbert and the uniformed general standing beside him that the government has sent the general to kill him for talking about meeting space aliens. Dilbert reasons that the government's poor track record gives him good odds, especially after budget cutbacks. The general, on his radio, angrily demands to know where his air support is.
punchline: The government's incompetence and budget cuts are so pervasive that even its assassination attempt is undermined by missing air support, just as Dilbert predicted.
summary: A man targeted by a military hitman for his alien story takes comfort in the government's famed inefficiency, and his confidence is confirmed when the officer's backup fails to show.

title: Sales Training Encourages Illegal Quota Hitting

transcript.speaker: Trainer
transcript.text: Welcome to sales training.

transcript.speaker: Trainer
transcript.text: As you know, our company makes overpriced, inferior products. We try to compensate by setting high sales quotas.

transcript.speaker: Trainer
transcript.text: We don't ASK you to act illegally, but it's pretty much the only way to reach quota. Okay, that's it for training. Any questions?

setting: Training room at the office
situation: A sales trainer addresses a classroom of new salespeople, including Dilbert. He cheerfully admits the company's products are overpriced and inferior, so management sets very high quotas to compensate. He then hints that the quotas can only be met by illegal behavior, while stressing that nobody is officially asking for it.
punchline: The company gets plausible deniability by never explicitly requesting illegal acts while setting quotas that can only be met by breaking the law.
summary: A sales trainer candidly admits the firm's lousy products force unreachable quotas and winks at law-breaking as the only way to meet them.

title: Engineering Is the Company's Snot

transcript.speaker: Marketing Person
transcript.text: Think of the company as a person. We in marketing would be the "brains."

transcript.speaker: Marketing Person
transcript.text: The sales department would be the "body."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's engineering?

transcript.speaker: Marketing Person
transcript.text: The snot.

setting: An outdoor path in hilly countryside, where a marketing person in a yellow robe and a laurel wreath walks with Dilbert
situation: A marketing representative in a toga-like robe and laurel wreath walks with Dilbert and compares the company to a human body. Marketing is the brains and sales is the body. When Dilbert asks where engineering fits, the marketer cheerfully calls it the snot.
punchline: The marketing person casually insults engineering by assigning it the most disgusting role in the corporate body, revealing how little marketing values the people who build the product.
summary: While strolling along a path, a smug marketing employee explains the company as an anatomy metaphor and gives Dilbert's engineering department the least flattering part.

title: Date With Puppetitis Sufferer

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I haven't dated much since I came down with puppetitis.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: It's a rare disorder that makes your hand act like a puppet.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's weird.

transcript.speaker: Woman's hand
transcript.text: He hates us! We must kill him!

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Not yet, Ginger!

setting: Restaurant table during a dinner date
situation: Dilbert is on a dinner date with a woman who explains she has a rare disorder called puppetitis that makes her hand behave like a puppet. When Dilbert calls it weird, her hand speaks up in a puppet voice, saying he hates them and they must kill him, and she scolds the hand, named Ginger, to wait.
punchline: The woman's apparent medical condition turns out to include a murderous hand puppet, and her 'Not yet, Ginger!' implies she is an active participant in the homicidal plan.
summary: A man's blind date reveals a strange affliction, then her hand proves it by plotting his demise while she merely asks it to hold off.

title: Ratbert Fakes Drug Reaction Again

transcript.speaker: Scientist
transcript.text: Just take one, Ratbert.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Aaargh!! I'm changing! I'm changing!

transcript.speaker: Scientist
transcript.text: It wasn't funny the first hundred times I gave you a Tic-Tac either.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Let's try it again!

setting: Laboratory
situation: A lab scientist offers Ratbert, his test subject, a pill to take. Ratbert immediately flops onto the lab bench, thrashing and screaming that he is changing. The scientist is unimpressed, explaining that Ratbert has pulled this stunt with harmless Tic-Tacs a hundred times already.
punchline: Ratbert has been faking dramatic reactions to harmless mints so often that the scientist no longer believes his act, and Ratbert cheerfully wants to keep doing the bit.
summary: A lab rat theatrically pretends to mutate after swallowing a pill, but the researcher has seen the same prank far too many times to react.

title: Dogbert's Date-A-Base Search Fails Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll search my date-a-base for women who want a nice guy and don't care about looks.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: All I'm getting are some quotes from guests on "Donahue," but they don't seem sincere.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Maybe if I expand the search to include all primates...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why did you add "don't care about looks"?

setting: Dilbert's home, at a computer desk
situation: Dogbert uses his computer database to search for dates for Dilbert, specifying women who want a nice guy and don't care about looks. The search returns only insincere talk-show quotes, so Dogbert suggests widening the search to all primates. Dilbert, standing nearby, asks why the 'don't care about looks' criterion was added at all.
punchline: Dogbert's search only works if the pool includes non-human primates, implying Dilbert is so unattractive that only an animal would overlook his looks, and Dilbert takes offense at the criterion that was added on his behalf.
summary: A dog's computer matchmaking for his unlucky owner turns up nothing human, so he proposes dating apes and insults his owner's appearance along the way.

title: Ratbert's Apple Bribe Backfires

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Snack time, Dilbert! I brought an apple so you will like me!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Nice try, Ratbert. But I don't want to eat something that was touched by a rat.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: The worst part is that's why I didn't eat it myself.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle
situation: Ratbert, a small pet rat, hauls a big apple over to Dilbert's desk, hoping to win his affection with a snack. Dilbert, seated in his chair, refuses to eat anything a rat has handled. Ratbert walks away hugging the apple and laments that the same logic kept him from eating it himself.
punchline: Ratbert's gift is unwanted because he handled it, and he realizes he can't eat it either, leaving him with a snack nobody will touch.
summary: A little rat tries to buy a friend's affection with fruit, only to discover his own contact has spoiled it for everyone, including himself.
themes: trying too hard to be liked

title: Dogbert Runs As Communist

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I've decided to run for President of the United States.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm hoping my charisma will unify a divided political party.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're running as a Democrat?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: No, Communist. I want to have a chance.

setting: Dilbert's living room, with Dilbert in an armchair and Dogbert on a footstool
situation: Dogbert announces to Dilbert that he is running for President of the United States, relying on his charisma to unify a divided political party. Dilbert assumes he means the Democrats, but Dogbert says he is running as a Communist.
punchline: Dogbert claims the Communist party gives him a better chance than the Democrats, a sarcastic jab at the Democratic Party's divisions and prospects in the 1992 election.
summary: A self-assured dog declares his presidential bid and picks the one party he thinks offers him better odds than the Democrats.

title: Dogbert Offers Head on Platter

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I heard you're looking for a hit man to eliminate an inventor named Dilbert.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: For a million dollars I can deliver his head on a platter.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Does it have to be on a platter?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I've tried using those Tupperware lettuce crispers, but it loses a lot of the drama.

setting: The Boss's office, with Dogbert seated across the desk
situation: Dogbert pitches himself as a hit man to the Boss, who wants an inventor named Dilbert eliminated. He quotes a million dollars and promises to deliver Dilbert's head on a platter. When the Boss asks whether a platter is required, Dogbert explains he has tried a Tupperware lettuce crisper instead.
punchline: Dogbert's only concern about decapitating Dilbert is presentation, having tested kitchen storage containers and found that they lack the drama of a proper platter.
summary: A scheming dog offers to murder an inventor for a fortune and fusses over the serving dish for the grisly delivery.

title: Dogbert's Insulting Smart Pills Gift

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I bought some "smart pills" for you. They're made from Chinese herbs.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I saw a news story about these... and naturally I thought of you.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I've discovered the perfect gift item.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle
situation: Dogbert approaches Dilbert at his desk carrying a small bag and announces he has bought him herbal smart pills. He adds that a news story made him think of Dilbert, implying Dilbert needs help being smart. In the last panel Dogbert walks away alone, pleased with how his gift idea worked out.
punchline: Dogbert's 'thoughtful' gift is really a backhanded insult, since buying smart pills because you thought of someone implies they are stupid, and he is proud of finding such a perfect way to say it.
summary: Dogbert presents his coworker with brain-boosting supplements, cheerfully insulting his intelligence under the guise of a kind gift.

title: Inventing Traditions: Nose-Sausage Day

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The problem with modern society is that we have no traditions.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We should create some traditions for future generations.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: How do you create a tradition?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, you just do something ridiculous every year at the same time.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Eventually other people join in and then it's a tradition.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Ooh, how about "Annual Nose-Sausage Day"? You dress in colorful robes and stick sausages in your nose!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes, yes... and we'll do a squirrel dance and shout "Kaloo-kalah" at the sun!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Or maybe not.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You lost me with the squirrel dance.

setting: Grassy hillside with a low stone wall
situation: Dilbert and Dogbert sit on a stone wall overlooking green hills while Dilbert laments that modern society lacks traditions. Dogbert asks how to create one, and Dilbert says to do something ridiculous every year. Dogbert proposes a silly ritual involving sausages in the nose, and Dilbert enthusiastically escalates it with a squirrel dance, which finally goes too far for Dogbert.
punchline: Dogbert happily suggests the absurd nose-sausage ritual himself but draws the line at the squirrel dance Dilbert adds, showing how arbitrary the line between a 'tradition' and plain silliness is.
summary: While brainstorming ways to invent a lasting custom, two friends dream up an increasingly bizarre ritual until one decides the other has gone a step too far.

title: Warden Dogbert Executes Prisoners for Profit

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Attention, prisoners! This is Warden Dogbert speaking!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: My jail has not been profitable. I've decided to have you all executed to reduce operating costs.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The "Joke of the Day" program seems wasted on these people.

setting: A prison yard, with prisoners in orange robes
situation: Dogbert, acting as prison warden, addresses the prisoners through a megaphone. He announces that because the jail is unprofitable he will have everyone executed to cut operating costs. The prisoners stand grimly, and Dogbert muses that his 'Joke of the Day' program is wasted on such a humorless audience.
punchline: Having just announced mass executions as a cost-cutting measure, Dogbert is baffled that the prisoners don't appreciate his jokes, showing how cold and detached he is from the human cost of his budget decisions.
summary: A cost-obsessed canine warden decides to kill off his inmates to save money, then wonders why they aren't laughing.

title: Elbonian Light Bulb Joke Fails

transcript.speaker: Elbonian 1
transcript.text: How many left-handed Elbonians does it take to change a light bulb?

transcript.speaker: Elbonian 1
transcript.text: None! Left-handed Elbonians don't have any light bulbs!

transcript.speaker: Elbonian 2
transcript.text: What's a light bulb?

transcript.speaker: Elbonian 1
transcript.text: I guess it would be funnier if we knew that.

setting: Muddy Elbonian village outside a hut
situation: Two tall-hatted, bearded Elbonians stand in the mud. One tells a 'how many left-handed Elbonians does it take to change a light bulb' joke and delivers the punchline. His companion doesn't know what a light bulb is, so the joke falls flat.
punchline: The Elbonians are too primitive to have light bulbs, so the joke makes no sense to them and they admit it would only be funny if they understood it.
summary: Two villagers tell a light bulb joke but neither has ever seen a light bulb, so the humor collapses.

title: Elbonians Discover Weapons in Civil War

transcript.speaker: Television
transcript.text: The tiny nation of Elbonia has erupted in civil war.

transcript.speaker: Reporter
transcript.text: What caused you to turn your weapons on your own people?

transcript.speaker: Elbonian 1
transcript.text: Weapons? We can use weapons?

transcript.speaker: Elbonian 2
transcript.text: Well, no wonder it was taking so long.

setting: Dogbert's living room watching TV, and a news report from the hills of Elbonia
situation: Dogbert watches a TV news report announcing that Elbonia has erupted in civil war. A reporter interviews two bearded Elbonians in tall hats, asking why they turned their weapons on their own people. The Elbonians reveal they didn't know they were allowed to use weapons.
punchline: The Elbonians' civil war has been dragging on only because they had been fighting without weapons, until the reporter's question taught them they could use them.
summary: A news interview inadvertently gives warring Elbonians the bright idea of arming themselves, escalating their conflict.

title: Boss Shreds Report, Then Necktie

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Here's my report. It's some of my best work.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hate that porto-shredder.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Say, is that a silk necktie?

setting: Office, the boss's work area
situation: Dilbert hands his boss a report he's proud of. The boss, wearing a portable paper shredder strapped to his waist, feeds the report straight into it. Dilbert grumbles about the device, and the boss cheerfully asks whether Dilbert's necktie is silk, with the shredder now aimed at it.
punchline: The boss destroys the report without reading it, then turns his shredder on Dilbert's necktie, showing that Dilbert's work is worthless to him and that his own whims are dangerous.
summary: A manager with a wearable paper shredder destroys an employee's proudest work unread and then eyes the man's tie as the next victim.

title: Dogbert Exposes the Diamond Scam

transcript.speaker: Jeweler
transcript.text: Are you interested in our diamond jewelry?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Let me see if I understand the concept here...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: ...I would give you thousands of dollars, and in return...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: ...you would give me a pebble you found on the ground.

transcript.speaker: Jeweler
transcript.text: These are no ordinary pebbles. Diamonds are very rare.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Rare? That's only because you made a marketing decision to restrict the supply.

transcript.speaker: Jeweler
transcript.text: Okay, okay, you figured us out. I'll give you a free bag of diamonds if you'll go away and keep quiet.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Great... Now I'm a party to this ugly little secret.

setting: A jewelry store counter
situation: A jeweler asks Dogbert if he wants to buy diamond jewelry. Dogbert reduces the deal to paying thousands of dollars for a pebble from the ground, and points out that diamonds are only rare because the industry deliberately restricts supply. The jeweler caves and bribes him with a free bag of diamonds to stay quiet.
punchline: Dogbert gets paid off in diamonds to keep the secret of artificial scarcity, then ironically notes that the bribe makes him complicit in the very scam he exposed.
summary: A shopper pierces the mystique of expensive gemstones and ends up bribed into silence, becoming part of the racket himself.

title: Dogbert's Miracle in the Peanut Butter

transcript.speaker: Television
transcript.text: Worshipers are flocking to the farm to witness the miracle. "I should charge for admission" quipped the farmer.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Guess what I found in the peanut butter.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Please, let it be a bug

setting: Dilbert's home, living room and computer desk
situation: Dogbert sits in an armchair watching a news report about a farmer who claims a saint's face appeared in a can of varnish, drawing crowds of worshipers. Dogbert then announces he has found something in the peanut butter while Dilbert works at his computer. Dilbert silently hopes the discovery is merely a bug.
punchline: Dilbert dreads that Dogbert has found another 'miracle' to exploit for profit, and hopes for the far less troublesome option of an ordinary bug in the food.
summary: After watching a news story about a profitable religious apparition, Dogbert hints that he has discovered something remarkable in the peanut butter, leaving his owner praying for something mundane.

title: Star Wars Theme Spreadsheet Multimedia

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.text: This morning I added my face plus the theme song from "Star Wars" to my budget spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I already forgot how I survived without it.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It can get pretty ugly when science and art collide.

setting: Dilbert's desk at the office, with a computer and video camera
situation: Dilbert proudly shows Dogbert his new multimedia setup, with a video camera pointed at his computer. He explains that he has added his own face and the Star Wars theme song to his budget spreadsheet, and says he can't imagine living without it. Dogbert dryly comments on the result.
punchline: Dilbert's pointless, gimmicky use of multimedia on a dull budget spreadsheet is something Dogbert wryly dismisses as an ugly collision of science and art.
summary: A gadget-happy Dilbert decorates a boring spreadsheet with video and movie music, and his dog responds with a withering one-liner.

title: Perpetual Certificates of Deposit Scam

transcript.speaker: Financial Advisor
transcript.text: For the timid investor, I recommend our "perpetual certificates of deposit."

transcript.speaker: Financial Advisor
transcript.text: They earn the highest possible interest. The only trade-off is that you can never withdraw it.

transcript.speaker: Financial Advisor
transcript.text: Ah, you've heard of our "flying debenture" product?

setting: A financial advisor's office, seated at a table
situation: Dilbert meets with a financial advisor who pitches a product for timid investors: a certificate of deposit that pays top interest but can never be withdrawn. Dilbert sarcastically suggests he might as well throw his money out a window. The advisor cheerfully responds that this is another product they sell.
punchline: The advisor treats Dilbert's sarcastic remark about throwing money away as a genuine product inquiry, revealing that his firm sells financial products that are effectively worthless to the customer.
summary: A cheerful money manager tries to sell a customer an investment he can never cash out, then eagerly pitches the customer's sarcastic jab as yet another offering.

title: Wrong Tape: Birth Video Mixup

transcript.speaker: Neighbor (man)

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Thanks for inviting us over.

transcript.speaker: Neighbor (man)

transcript.speaker: Neighbor (man)

transcript.speaker: Neighbor (man)

transcript.speaker: Neighbor (woman)

setting: Neighbors' living room
situation: Dilbert and Dogbert visit a couple who proudly want to show them a home video of their son's birth. As the VHS plays, the couple narrate a surgical scene, until the wife realizes they've put in the wrong tape, which is actually a video of an appendectomy.
punchline: The husband, still hoping it's the right tape, deadpans that the baby must just be unphotogenic, since the footage looks like surgery on an adult.
summary: A proud couple screens what they believe is their baby's birth video for their guests, but the surgical footage turns out to be somebody's appendix operation.

title: Dogbert's School Demands Tuition Upfront

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I've asked you to pay tuition in advance; that way if you're unsatisfied with the school, you'll have the added negotiating leverage of having already paid.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And thanks, Alice, for asking if tipping is customary.

setting: Dogbert's classroom at the School of Common Sense
situation: Dogbert welcomes his students to his School of Common Sense and explains that tuition must be paid in advance, sarcastically framing this as giving students negotiating leverage. In the last panel he happily collects cash from students' hands, thanking Alice for asking whether tipping is customary.
punchline: The school's lesson in common sense is contradicted by its own scam: paying upfront gives students no leverage at all, and Dogbert cheerfully pockets extra tips on top.
summary: A canine headmaster collects his students' money before teaching anything and spins the prepayment as a favor to them.

title: Making the Report Less Readable

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Good report, but change the word "use" to "utilize" in each case.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Change "help" to "facilitate" and replace "do" with "implementation phase."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hmm... it's still a bit too readable.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I could reduce the type size and run it through the fax.

setting: The Boss's office
situation: The Boss reviews Dilbert's report and demands that simple words be swapped for inflated jargon, such as "utilize" for "use" and "facilitate" for "help". When the result is still too clear for his liking, Dilbert deadpans an offer to shrink the type and fax it to make it even harder to read.
punchline: The Boss wants the report deliberately unreadable to seem important, and Dilbert sarcastically offers to degrade it further with tiny type and a fax.
summary: A manager keeps inflating a report with pompous buzzwords until his employee suggests making it physically illegible.

title: Ratbert's Dance Fails to Cheer Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Ratbert

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now I'm lonely and I have a dancing rat.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Kumbaya

setting: Dilbert's home, sitting in an armchair
situation: Dilbert sits slumped in his armchair, lonely because Dogbert is away. Ratbert offers to cheer him up with a dance number, hoping to bond and replace Dogbert as his best friend. He dances and sings Kumbaya while Dilbert remains unimpressed.
punchline: Ratbert's cheerful dance doesn't cure Dilbert's loneliness; it just leaves him lonely with a dancing rat as company.
summary: A pet rat tries to win over his gloomy owner with a song and dance, but only manages to make the evening more awkward.

title: Dogbert Denies Killing Goldie Fish

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You expect me to believe that Goldie flushed himself down the john??!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Surely you don't believe that I ended his ugly, stupid fish life in a fit of pet rivalry...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Explain how a fish can write a suicide note.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I've heard they have schools...

setting: Dilbert's home, beside the empty fishbowl
situation: Dilbert confronts Dogbert over the disappearance of his pet goldfish Goldie, refusing to believe the fish flushed itself down the toilet. Dogbert feigns innocence and denies killing the fish out of pet rivalry, but Dilbert produces a suicide note and challenges how a fish could have written it. Dogbert deflects with a pun.
punchline: Dogbert's answer that fish 'have schools' is a pun on schools of fish, glibly dodging the question of how a fish could write a note while implicitly confirming he forged it.
summary: A suspicious pet owner presents a damning note to his scheming dog, who answers with a groan-worthy fish pun instead of an alibi.

title: Waxing the Desk With Hair

transcript.speaker: Man in glasses
transcript.text: His name is Dilbert. He invented something that would make our entire product line obsolete.

transcript.speaker: Man in chair
transcript.text: Do you have a plan?

transcript.speaker: Man in glasses
transcript.text: Uh... I could wax your desk with my hair again.

transcript.speaker: Man in chair
transcript.text: It's just crazy enough to work.

setting: Executive's office
situation: A subordinate in glasses and a tie shows an executive a photograph of Dilbert, an engineer whose invention threatens to make the company's whole product line obsolete. When asked if he has a plan, the subordinate can only offer to wax the executive's desk with his hair again. The unseen executive approves, saying it is just crazy enough to work.
punchline: Faced with a serious competitive threat, the company's response is a ridiculous act of groveling that management approves of simply because it is crazy.
summary: An employee's only answer to a looming business disaster is an absurd, humiliating favor for the boss, and the boss finds it brilliant.

title: Ratbert Pours Out Existential Despair

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Bob, sometimes I wonder if there's a place in this world for a sensitive rat like me.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I can't live the hollow, meaningless shell of existence that others so ironically call "life."

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I want to make a difference to people.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Well, you ruined MY day.

setting: A plain pink background with a ledge, where Ratbert sits next to Bob the dinosaur
situation: Ratbert sits beside Bob the dinosaur and earnestly shares his gloomy thoughts about life feeling hollow and meaningless. He says he wants to make a difference to people. Bob, who has been listening to the whole depressing monologue, replies that Ratbert has indeed made a difference by ruining his day.
punchline: Ratbert's wish to make a difference is granted in the worst way, since his relentless moping has brought down his only listener.
summary: A melancholy little rat longs to affect people's lives and learns he has, but only by dragging his dinosaur friend into a bad mood.

title: Mother Nature Zaps Off-Key Robin

transcript.text: It's not mean; it's natural. Nature seems cruel but it's really beautiful.

transcript.text: For example, do you see that robin that's singing?

transcript.text: Yes?

transcript.speaker: Sound Effect

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Yet another example where keen perception doesn't pay off.

setting: Outdoor path beside a grassy hillside
situation: Dogbert greets Mother Nature, a robed figure with a laurel wreath and staff, and asks why she is so mean. She insists nature is natural and beautiful, then zaps a singing robin with lightning for being off-key. Dogbert points out she is smiling and enjoys being mean, and she zaps him too, leaving him singed.
punchline: Dogbert correctly sees that Mother Nature enjoys cruelty, but pointing it out gets him zapped, so being perceptive is punished.
summary: A cheerful nature goddess defends her harshness as harmony, but when Dogbert calls out her glee he ends up smoking and frazzled.

title: Mensa President Admits Intelligence Is Impractical

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Intelligence has much less practical application than you'd think.

setting: Office break area
situation: A coworker holding a coffee cup suggests Dilbert join Mensa, and reveals he is president of the local chapter. Dilbert asks why two supposedly brilliant people end up working at this company. The Mensa president replies that intelligence is much less useful in practice than people assume.
punchline: Even a genius-level IQ society's president concedes that being smart doesn't spare you from a mediocre office job, so intelligence is basically worthless in the real world.
summary: A Mensa chapter president explains to Dilbert that brainpower does little to improve one's career or workplace circumstances.

title: Dilbert Predicts Dogbert's Clueless Newsletter Tip

transcript.text: You're probably thinking up some clever little fact that the so-called clueless people would never realize on their own.

transcript.text: Let me see... "If you are the only one talking then it is a clue that no conversation is occurring and it is time to leave."

setting: Office cubicle, Dogbert at his computer
situation: Dilbert walks up to Dogbert, who is typing at his computer, and mocks his newsletter for clueless people. He guesses what clever tip Dogbert might be writing, and the tip he comes up with is that if you are the only one talking, no conversation is happening and you should leave. Dogbert silently keeps typing while Dilbert does all the talking.
punchline: Dilbert's own tip applies to himself: he is the only one talking, so by his own rule he is the clueless one who should leave.
summary: While lecturing a silent, busy Dogbert about his newsletter, Dilbert unwittingly recites advice that describes his own one-sided monologue.

title: Dilbert Meets Superior Techno-Bill

situation: Dilbert, wearing a belt loaded with gadgets, thinks proudly about how his personal technology makes him dominant over the other engineers, who bow before him. He wonders if anyone could top him, then turns to find Techno-Bill, who sports a helmet, antenna and a backpack of gear. Techno-Bill notices a paper fax trailing from Dilbert's belt and mocks it.
punchline: Dilbert's gadget-laden smugness is instantly deflated by someone with even more technology, who also treats Dilbert's gear as embarrassingly dated.
summary: A gadget-festooned engineer basks in his own tech superiority until a rival with even more devices shows up and humbles him.

title: Dogbert's Morbid Greeting Card Poem

situation: Dilbert asks Dogbert how his new line of greeting cards for death occasions is progressing. Dogbert says he is now working on the humorous angle. Dilbert reads the card he has made, a joke poem that mocks the deceased.
punchline: Dogbert's idea of a humorous sympathy card is a mean-spirited rhyme joking about the recipient's rigor mortis, which makes it completely inappropriate for a death occasion.
summary: Dogbert's attempt at funny sympathy cards produces a tasteless poem that jokes about a corpse being stiff.

title: Ratbert's Geodesic Insight Goes Wrong

Mid-announcement he lets out a yelp and kicks a leg up, then collapses on the floor, dazed. Dogbert calmly comments that this is what happens when inspiration strikes the wrong spot.
punchline: The sudden flash of insight is treated as a literal shock that hits Ratbert in the wrong part of his body, such as his backside, instead of his brain.
summary: A scientific epiphany zaps a small rodent in an embarrassing place, leaving a dog to wryly explain the mishap.

title: Dogbert Becomes a Doctor for Power

situation: Dogbert announces he has decided to become a doctor and explains his reasoning: patients must flatter doctors or risk being jabbed with big needles for little reason. Dilbert, sitting in the armchair, dryly agrees that other professions lack this kind of leverage, comparing it to office supplies.
punchline: Dogbert's motive for becoming a doctor is the power to make people grovel and then stab them with needles, and Dilbert's stapler remark deadpans that office jobs offer no comparable ability to hurt people with impunity.
summary: Dogbert picks medicine as a career because it lets him intimidate people with needles, and Dilbert quietly notes that his own desk gear can't compete.

title: Dogbert Suggests Lysol for Husband

Dogbert suggests she treat him with Lysol as if he were mildew, and she deadpans that she already tried it and it just made him dizzy.
punchline: The wife has already tried disinfecting her husband like household mildew, showing how little she thinks of his personality and how little she needs Dogbert's advice.
summary: A woman who married for a fancy car complains her husband is as lively as mold, and the counselor's absurd cleaning-product advice turns out to be something she has already tried.

title: Dogbert's Very Short Provocative Book

He promptly adds that he should become a media sensation for the idea and ends the book there. Then, in a thought bubble, he muses that he is too efficient to fill an entire book.
punchline: Dogbert's book is finished in two paragraphs because he gets straight to the point, and his real aim is to become a famous media sensation through a deliberately outrageous claim.
summary: A computer-typing dog drafts a shockingly short book built around an outrageous proposal and then laments that he is too concise to stretch it out.

title: Fast-Track Dropped Over Haircut

situation: The Boss approaches Dave at his computer and says he has heard Dave has started cutting his own hair. He then removes Dave from the management fast-track program because of it. Alone in the last panel, the Boss thinks he was lucky to catch the problem early.
punchline: Management treats a trivial personal habit like cutting your own hair as a disqualifying flaw, showing how arbitrary and petty promotion criteria can be.
summary: A manager yanks an employee off the executive career ladder because of a do-it-yourself haircut and congratulates himself for the timely catch.

title: Dogbert Steals Ratbert's Chips Philosophically

Ratbert is so distraught that he drops the bag, and Dogbert takes the chips.

summary: A scheming dog gets a snack from his friend by convincing him that free will is an illusion, then uses that same idea to excuse the cruelty.

title: Dogbert's Sarcastic Battle Pep Talk

transcript.text: Today, bold memos will be written, dangerous meetings will be attended, and many a photocopied image will be captured for eternity.

transcript.text: If it weren't for sarcasm, my life would sound pathetic.

The epic tone is applied to mundane office chores like writing memos, attending meetings and photocopying. Dilbert admits that sarcasm is the only thing making his life sound less pathetic, and Dogbert cheerfully takes credit.
punchline: Dogbert's mock-heroic narration only works as sarcasm, since a typical office worker's day of memos, meetings and photocopies is truly unglamorous and pathetic.
summary: While Dilbert dresses for work, Dogbert turns his dull office routine into a warrior's epic, and Dilbert concedes that the irony is the only thing making his life sound bearable.

title: Dilbert Accused of Petting Neighbor's Cat

punchline: Dilbert treats his dog's brief contact with a cat like a spouse's infidelity, complete with a lame excuse ('more of a pat than a pet') and a threat of a trial.
summary: A man sniffs out evidence that his dog has been fraternizing with the neighbor's cat and responds with the melodrama of a betrayed partner.

title: Lazy Beaver's Useless Daytime Planner

transcript.speaker: Beaver
transcript.text: I got this daytime planner to organize my day more efficiently.

transcript.speaker: Beaver
transcript.text: But all it does is sit there.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Looks like you got a bad one.

setting: Outdoors in a grassy area, with a tree stump serving as the beaver's desk
situation: A lazy beaver explains to Dogbert that he looks for shortcuts and tricks to get his work done. He shows off a daytime planner he bought to organize his day, then complains that it just sits there doing nothing. Dogbert deadpans that he must have gotten a bad one.
punchline: The beaver expects the planner to do his work for him, and Dogbert sarcastically implies the product is defective rather than pointing out that the beaver has to actually use it.
summary: A slothful beaver blames his organizer for not magically managing his schedule while Dogbert dryly plays along.

title: Dogbert Watches Solar Flare News

situation: Dogbert sits in an armchair watching a television news broadcast. The anchor reports on solar flares, then CNN's Wolf Blitzer is shown on the scene, reporting that it is another hot day on the sun. Dogbert responds with a thought bubble.
punchline: Dogbert is annoyed by the sun's blazing heat and calls it a bunch of show-offs, as though it were flaunting its temperature at everyone else.
summary: A dog watching the evening news mutters a grumpy retort at the sun for flaring up and making a spectacle of itself.

title: Climbing Stairs to Dogbert's Command Center

transcript.text: Pant! Are you Dogbert, wheeze, pant, the new leader, pant, of the vegetarian movement?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: I have a pant, pant, warning from the pant, cow and egg industry... pant, you must ERK!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: In retrospect, it was pretty clever of us to rent a third floor command center with no elevator.

characters: Messenger from the cow and egg industry
setting: Dogbert's third-floor office, a command center for the vegetarian movement
situation: A winded man in a suit staggers into Dogbert's office to deliver a threatening warning from the cow and egg industry. He collapses mid-sentence from exhaustion. Dogbert, feet up on his desk, remarks on how smart it was to pick an office with no elevator.
punchline: The office's lack of an elevator turns out to be a defense mechanism, as the exhausting stairs incapacitate or kill anyone coming to threaten Dogbert.
summary: An out-of-breath visitor bearing a threat keels over before he can deliver it, and Dogbert credits the stairs-only building for his security.

title: The Not-So-Anonymous Boss Survey

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, do you have a minute?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The company is doing a survey of employee attitudes about their bosses.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's totally anonymous, so you don't have to fear any retribution.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Oops! It looks like your questionnaire is a bit dog-eared.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll put my phone number on the confidential envelope in case you need me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You can use this green marker pen.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Oh, and I took the liberty of checking off your ethnic background as Eskimo. It's just a statistical thing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: 1. Does your boss clearly communicate your objectives?

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle
situation: The Boss hands Dilbert a company survey about employee attitudes toward their bosses and insists it is totally anonymous. He then undermines the anonymity at every turn: he has already opened and handled the questionnaire, writes his own phone number on the envelope, supplies a distinctive green pen, and pre-checks Dilbert's ethnic background. Dilbert is left to read the first question about whether his boss communicates clearly.
punchline: The Boss delivers a survey about himself while visibly sabotaging its anonymity, so any honest answer would be easily traced back to Dilbert.
summary: A manager personally hands over a supposedly anonymous review of managers while doing everything possible to identify the respondent.

title: Secret Account Number Nobody Knows

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: BANK OF ETHEL - NOW A SECRET SWISS BANK

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'd like to withdraw two hundred dollars.

transcript.speaker: Ethel
transcript.text: What's your secret Swiss account number?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't have a secret account. It's just a regular account.

transcript.speaker: Ethel
transcript.text: Wrong. I changed all of the accounts into secret Swiss accounts.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Oh, okay, what's my secret account number?

transcript.speaker: Ethel
transcript.text: It's a secret.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then how do I get my money out?

transcript.speaker: Ethel
transcript.text: You're a bit slow in grasping the concept here.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, okay I'll just open a new account.

transcript.speaker: Ethel
transcript.text: Do you have any previous banking references?

setting: A small neighborhood bank, the Bank of Ethel, outside and at the teller window
situation: Dilbert tries to withdraw two hundred dollars, but the teller, Ethel, has converted every account into a secret Swiss account with secret numbers. She refuses to tell him his own account number because it's a secret, leaving his money inaccessible. When he gives up and tries to open a new account, she asks for previous banking references.
punchline: The bank's absurd secrecy policy makes customers' money impossible to access, and the teller treats Dilbert as dim for not understanding that, then asks for banking references from someone whose bank just locked him out.
summary: A bank rebrands itself as a secret Swiss bank so thoroughly that even customers can't learn their own account numbers or reach their money.

title: Dogbert Flushes Dilbert's Goldfish

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hope Dogbert doesn't get jealous of my new goldfish.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Flush

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Have you noticed that Goldie was looking a bit depressed?

setting: Dilbert's home living room
situation: Dilbert sits with his new goldfish in a bowl and worries in a thought bubble that Dogbert might be jealous of it. In the next panel Dilbert reads the newspaper in an armchair while a flush is heard offscreen. Dogbert then calmly asks whether Dilbert noticed the goldfish looked depressed.
punchline: Dogbert, jealous as Dilbert feared, has flushed the goldfish down the toilet and blandly disguises the killing as the fish's suicide from depression.
summary: A man's worry about his dog's envy is confirmed when the pet quietly disposes of the new fish and offers a deadpan excuse.

title: Dogbert's Newsletter for Clueless People

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's this?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm starting my own newsletter for clueless people.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Thanks to the technical marvel of desktop publishing, clueless people will now have the benefit of my immense wisdom.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How do you know who the clueless people are?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: They ask a lot of questions.

setting: Office or home workspace at a computer
situation: Dilbert finds Dogbert typing at his computer and learns he is launching a newsletter aimed at clueless people, made possible by desktop publishing. Dilbert asks how Dogbert can identify his target audience, and Dogbert answers that clueless people are the ones who ask lots of questions.
punchline: Dogbert's criterion for cluelessness is asking questions, which ironically describes Dilbert's own curiosity and implies Dogbert plans to profit from anyone who seeks information.
summary: Dogbert launches a self-important publication for the uninformed and defines his readership as anyone inquisitive enough to question him.

title: Guilt-Selling Girl Scout Cookies at Work

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: I'm taking orders for "Camp Girl Cookies" on behalf of my daughter.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: How many dozen can I guilt you into buying?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've always wondered, Ted, why do they sell cookies? Is it just for the money?

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: No, it's to help them build character by earning their own money.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Oh, so your daughter is doing some selling from door-to-door?

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: No, too dangerous. My wife and I are doing all the selling at work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, then aren't you only teaching your daughter to act helpless so other people will do her work?

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Just buy the stupid cookies!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Have you considered foster care for your kids?

setting: Office cubicle
situation: Ted, a coworker, comes to Dilbert's cubicle to collect orders for his daughter's Camp Girl cookie fundraiser. Dilbert questions the supposed purpose of the sale, building character through earning money, and points out that Ted and his wife are doing all the selling at work rather than the daughter. Ted loses his temper and demands he just buy the cookies.
punchline: Dilbert exposes the hypocrisy that parents selling cookies at the office teaches children nothing about earning money, only how to get others to do their work, and then sarcastically suggests foster care when Ted gets angry.
summary: A coworker's fundraising pitch collapses when Dilbert logically dismantles the supposed character-building purpose of having parents do the selling.

title: Knock-Knock Layoff Joke

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've decided to use humor in the workplace.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Experts say humor eases tension which is important in times when the workforce is being trimmed.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Knock-knock.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Who's there?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Not you anymore.

setting: Office
situation: The Boss announces to a group of employees that he will use humor in the workplace, explaining that it eases tension during layoffs. He then tells a knock-knock joke to a single employee, and the punchline is that the employee is being fired.
punchline: The Boss's 'humor' is a knock-knock joke used to deliver a layoff notice, making the firing cruelly clueless rather than tension-easing.
summary: A manager tries to lighten the mood around downsizing by telling a joke that turns out to be a termination notice.

title: Body Language Dodges Extra Work

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe Ted can answer that question...

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Uh-oh

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: They're trying to make me work. I'll have to use body language to discourage them.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh... never mind

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: It's working.

setting: Conference room during a meeting
situation: During a meeting, Dilbert suggests that Ted could answer a question. Ted privately worries he is being handed work and decides to discourage them with body language. He scowls and chews on a pen, and Dilbert quickly withdraws the suggestion.
punchline: Ted avoids being assigned work simply by looking menacing and unapproachable, and his colleagues back off immediately.
summary: A meeting attendee fends off a request for his input by putting on an intimidating scowl.

title: Boss's Morale-Building Fly Swatter Experiment

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hold still. I'm going to try a morale-building experiment.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Slap slap slap slap

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Thanks. I feel a lot better.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle
situation: The Boss approaches Dilbert at his desk holding a fly swatter and announces a morale-building experiment. He repeatedly slaps Dilbert with it while Dilbert sits there. The Boss walks away happy, saying he feels much better, while Dilbert is left bruised and baffled.
punchline: The boss's idea of a morale-building exercise only improves his own morale by abusing his subordinate, who gets nothing out of it.
summary: A manager beats an employee with a fly swatter for the sake of team spirit and walks off pleased with himself.

title: Kick Me Signs Boost Creativity

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: As part of my program to use more humor at work, I'm asking each of you to wear a "Kick Me" sign.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll check later to see if you're more relaxed and creative.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Later...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You seem to be taking unfair advantage of the situation, Alice.

setting: Office hallway
situation: The Boss announces a humor program and sticks "Kick Me" signs on his employees, saying he'll check later whether they are more relaxed and creative. Later, Alice is gleefully kicking a coworker in the backside while other employees stand around looking pained. The Boss scolds Alice for abusing the situation.
punchline: The Boss dreams up a ridiculous humor initiative that invites physical abuse, then is surprised and critical when Alice enthusiastically takes advantage of it.
summary: A manager's forced-fun scheme of wearing mocking signs predictably turns into an excuse for a coworker to kick her colleagues.

title: Elbonia Airlines Slingshot Diplomacy

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The President of Elbonia asked me to negotiate an end to their civil war.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Why you?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Elbonia

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: ...At his weight, we calculate that Elbonia Airlines will fling him right on the rebel leader.

setting: Dilbert's office, then a rebel hideout in Elbonia
situation: Dilbert tells Dogbert that the President of Elbonia has asked him to negotiate an end to the civil war, and he worries about flying on Elbonia Airlines. In Elbonia, two hooded rebels study a diagram of a slingshot and calculate that the airline will fling Dilbert, given his weight, directly onto their rebel leader.
punchline: Elbonia Airlines is literally a slingshot, and the rebels plan to use Dilbert's body as a projectile to take out their own leader, so his 'diplomacy' mission is really a weapon.
summary: A reluctant envoy heading to a war zone learns the hard way that the national airline is a catapult aimed at its target.

title: Dilbert Confronts Old Fourth Grade Teacher

transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.text: You know, Miss "Molepit," if my dog had your face I'd shave his hiney and make him walk backward.

transcript.speaker: Miss Mulput
transcript.text: Leave me out of this.

setting: Outdoor park path with grass and bushes
situation: Dilbert, out walking with Dogbert, recognizes his old fourth grade teacher, who doesn't remember him. He recounts how she once made him write an insulting line a thousand times for chewing gum, then reveals the punishment left him angry and vengeful. He finally delivers an insult of his own, shifting the insult onto his dog.
punchline: After a long, polite-seeming buildup about how his teacher's punishment shaped him, Dilbert finally gets his revenge by insulting her looks, mirroring the 'homely' line she once forced him to write, and dragging Dogbert into it.
summary: A grown-up Dilbert runs into the teacher who once punished him cruelly and repays her with a well-aimed insult about her face.

title: Boss Announces Dehumanizing Badges and Alfalfa

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: From now on you will wear identification badges at work. This symbolizes that people who look like you are often criminals.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Oh... and the cafeteria is closed. We'll just lay down some alfalfa in the break room.

setting: Office, during a staff announcement
situation: The Boss, holding a small device, addresses his employees, including Alice and Dilbert. He cheerfully announces that the company has a new way to dehumanize staff, introducing mandatory ID badges and explaining they imply the employees resemble criminals. He then adds that the cafeteria is closing and alfalfa will be put out in the break room instead.
punchline: The Boss openly admits to dehumanizing and insulting his workers as if it were good news, and caps it off by treating them like livestock fed alfalfa.
summary: A manager proudly unveils demeaning new policies, from criminal-style ID badges to feeding staff hay instead of lunch.

title: Ratbert's Hostile Fruit Bowl Painting

transcript.text: All I see is a bowl of fruit.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: The banana hates the apple.

setting: An office or studio where Ratbert paints at an easel while Dogbert sits at a desk
situation: Ratbert stands at an easel with a palette and announces he is pouring his pain and hostility into his painting. Dogbert looks at the canvas and sees only a still life of a bowl of fruit. Ratbert, scowling, insists that the banana hates the apple.
punchline: Ratbert's supposedly angst-ridden art is just an ordinary fruit still life, so he has to explain the emotional conflict that only he can perceive, with the banana and apple as absurd enemies.
summary: A tiny artist claims his painting is full of rage, but his skeptical friend sees only fruit until the artist reveals a feud between two of the pieces.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Let's say you fall into more than one of those categories...

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Engineers...

setting: Office hallway
situation: A female co-worker collects money for Mary's birthday gift and says the amount is up to each person, then lays out the unwritten donation norms. They range from ten dollars for men hoping to woo Mary to a faked contribution made by ruffling the envelope. Wally pretends to put money in while Dilbert looks on, and the collector privately sighs about engineers.
punchline: The collector's cynical rundown of gift-giving etiquette ends with Wally ruffling the envelope to fake a five-dollar donation, confirming her low opinion of engineers.
summary: A colleague passing around an envelope for a coworker's present cynically explains what different people are expected to give, and one cheapskate fakes his share.

title: Dilbert's Date Has Puppetitis

situation: Dilbert is on a date with a woman who explains she caught a disease called puppetitis from a previous date. She laughs and shows that her hand has become a talking puppet, which then invites Dilbert to join them.
punchline: Dilbert's dating life in the nineties is so bizarre that a contagious puppet disease is the last straw, and the puppet hand creepily invites him to catch it too.
summary: A dinner date reveals she has a contagious puppet-hand condition and her hand eerily tries to recruit Dilbert.

situation: Dogbert tells Dilbert he has analyzed his finances to help him pick a Christmas gift, concluding that Dilbert's lack of a social life and a second mortgage would free up $50,000 for Dogbert's present. Dilbert calmly replies that he bought Dogbert a hat because it was on sale. A disappointed Dogbert walks off musing about beating someone with a yule log.
punchline: Dogbert's greedy demand for a $50,000 gift is met with a cheap on-sale hat, leaving him so annoyed that he fantasizes about violence with a yule log, a dark twist on holiday cheer.
summary: Dogbert schemes to pry a huge Christmas present out of his owner, only to be rewarded with a discount hat and a sour holiday mood.

situation: Dogbert, wearing a cheap antenna headband as an alien disguise, tells Dilbert he plans to announce to the media that he is a space alien with unstoppable powers so that the world's nations will surrender. Dilbert accuses him of thinking people are idiots, and Dogbert holds up a photo of himself from before the disguise.
punchline: Dogbert's flimsy antenna headband is supposed to make him look like a space alien, and the photo shows he looked like an ordinary dog before it, implying he thinks the public is gullible enough to fall for a trivial costume.
summary: A scheming dog in a silly antenna costume plans to bluff the world into surrendering by posing as an extraterrestrial, betting on human gullibility.

Dilbert then arrives at the group, where the men are sipping cinnamon snap tea, and regrets not reading the book first.
punchline: The supposedly manly drum group turns out to be a gentle tea-sipping gathering, showing Dilbert should have researched before joining something based on a book he never read.
summary: After committing to a macho drumming retreat inspired by an unread book, Dilbert finds a crowd of mild men drinking herbal tea and wishes he had done his homework.

situation: Dogbert hosts a TV segment about ignorant people and interviews two men seated at a table. One man complains that the Federal Reserve increased the money supply but his own bank balance didn't change. Dogbert, holding a microphone, sympathizes with him.
punchline: Dogbert agrees with the man's absurd complaint, so the supposed expert host is just as clueless about economics as the people he is mocking.
summary: A talk-show dog introduces a segment on the economically ignorant, then proves he fits right in by sympathizing with a man puzzled that his bank account never grew.

He threatens to kill Dilbert with untraceable poison if he tells the press about his UFO abduction. Dilbert complains about the poor value for his tax dollars, and the general responds by offering him a breath mint.
punchline: Dilbert complains that his taxes are paying for a government thug threatening to murder him, and the general cheerfully ignores the complaint and offers a breath mint, as if the visit were routine customer service.
summary: A menacing military man warns a man to keep quiet about alien kidnapping, then casually treats his complaint as a minor matter.

punchline: The telemarketer asks if it's an inconvenient time, so only a person who is busy gets left alone, and the honest answer of 'no' guarantees he will be pestered again.
summary: A candid sales call about dubious savings ends with the caller backing off only because the person he phoned was perfectly available.

punchline: The card's message is absurdly blunt and addressed to the deceased rather than the mourners, yet Dogbert deadpans that it might be overly sentimental.
summary: Dogbert unveils a sympathy card whose entire message is a flat apology to the corpse and wonders if it's too touchy-feely.

situation: Dilbert finds a small gray robot, Ruebert, tinkering in his lab. Ruebert explains he is building a feminine robot to nurture and serve him, and that he asked the National Organization of Women to help program it. He then cheerfully asks Dilbert if he likes surprises, implying the programming will not go as intended.
punchline: Asking a women's rights organization to help program a robot meant to be a subservient female companion is a terrible idea, so the robot's servant is bound to be a nasty surprise.
summary: A robot builds a docile female companion and enlists the very group least likely to make it obedient.

title: Dogbert's Backhanded Intelligence Pep Talk
