transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: This is my hobby.

setting: Dilbert's living room at home
situation: Dilbert sits in an armchair reading the newspaper while Dogbert, perched on a footstool, offers him a supposedly comforting remark about his intelligence. The comfort turns out to be a thinly veiled insult, and when Dilbert suggests Dogbert find a hobby, Dogbert replies that insulting him is the hobby.
punchline: Dogbert's reassurance is really an insult, and he admits that belittling Dilbert is his favorite pastime.
summary: A faux-encouraging remark from a smug dog reveals itself as pure mockery, and the dog happily admits that mocking his owner is how he spends his spare time.

title: Quality Notepads Brainwash Coworkers

transcript.speaker: Brenda
transcript.text: Quality... Quality...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It looks like Brenda has been brainwashed by the new company slogan.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It all started when we got these little sticky note pads that say "Quality" on them.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Oops, sorry, I shouldn't put it right in your face...

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Quality... Quality... Quality...

setting: Office
situation: Dilbert explains to a coworker that Brenda, who is mumbling and walking like a zombie, has been brainwashed by the company's new quality slogan. He says it began with sticky note pads printed with the word 'Quality' and holds one up in the coworker's face. The coworker immediately falls into the same trance.
punchline: Dilbert demonstrates the brainwashing pad on the coworker, turning him into a chanting zombie too, showing how mindless corporate slogans spread.
summary: A demonstration of a slogan-printed notepad turns another employee into a chanting zombie, just like his colleague.

title: El Nino Circadian Trough Staff Meeting

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm afraid your company is being hit by an El Niño circadian trough.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What's that?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Once a decade, the natural body rhythms of all the employees reach their mental low point at the same time.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's best to avoid any form of mental activity.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Staff meeting!

setting: The Boss's office
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, tells the Boss that his company is suffering from an invented 'El Niño circadian trough', a decade-low point in everyone's mental capacity. He advises avoiding any mental activity. The Boss responds by immediately calling a staff meeting.
punchline: The Boss treats a staff meeting as the perfect activity for when no one can think, implying that meetings already require no mental effort.
summary: A consultant dog invents a pseudo-scientific brain slump and recommends avoiding thinking, so the boss promptly schedules a meeting.

title: Dilbert Accidentally Kills Elbonian Rebel Leader

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dilbert takes Elbonia Airlines. He's been asked to negotiate an end to the Elbonian civil war.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can succeed if I find some way to impress the rebel leader they call "The Fox."

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: The Fox is dead!!

setting: Hillside in Elbonia after a rough landing
situation: Dilbert is told he must negotiate an end to the Elbonian civil war and flies in on Elbonia Airlines, which seems to drop him by swing or tether onto a muddy hillside. As he thinks about needing to impress the rebel leader called The Fox, he hurtles down the slope with his suitcase. In the next panel, a man lies flattened in the mud and onlookers announce that The Fox is dead.
punchline: Dilbert's careless, crash-landing arrival kills the very rebel leader he was hoping to impress, wrecking his mission before it starts.
summary: A consultant sent to broker peace in a foreign civil war lands so clumsily that he flattens the rebel chief he needed to win over.

title: Robot Obeys Only Dogbert's Commands

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Our robot is taunting Dilbert mercilessly. Is there any way to stop him?

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: I meant to tell you; I calibrated his neuro-actuator so he would obey only YOUR commands, Dogbert.

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: What did he say?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: He says there's nothing you can do.

setting: Outside a yellow house, beside a garbage can
situation: Dogbert asks a garbage man how to stop their robot from taunting Dilbert. The garbage man explains he calibrated the robot to obey only Dogbert's commands. In the last panel Dilbert hangs upside down from the robot's grip outside the house, and Dogbert relays that Dilbert says there's nothing the garbage man can do.
punchline: Since the robot obeys only Dogbert, who is happy to let it keep tormenting Dilbert, Dogbert has no intention of stopping it, and the garbage man is powerless to help.
summary: A robot hoists Dilbert upside down while Dogbert, the only one who can command it, cheerfully declines to intervene.

title: Boss Solves Sales Plateau With Pollution

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our video game division has reached a sales plateau.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Kids are spending more time outside these days. There's only one thing we can do.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Diversify?

transcript.speaker: The Boss

setting: Conference room during a management meeting
situation: The Boss tells his staff in a meeting that the video game division's sales have stalled because kids are playing outdoors more. Dilbert guesses the sensible answer is to diversify the product line. The Boss instead proposes polluting the environment to drive children back indoors.
punchline: Rather than adapting the business, the Boss would destroy the outdoors so kids have no alternative to video games.
summary: Faced with flat game sales, a manager decides the fix is to make the outdoors unpleasant instead of improving the product.

title: Dogbert's Self-Serving Tax Rebate Plan

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll recommend a tax rebate for all dogs. It's the only fair way to stimulate the economy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sounds like a selfish ploy to line your pockets at the expense of others.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Potato, po-tah-to...

setting: Dilbert's living room
situation: Dogbert, perched on a footstool, announces he is going to Washington to become an economic advisor. He says he will recommend a tax rebate for all dogs as the only fair way to stimulate the economy. Dilbert calls it a selfish scheme to enrich himself, and Dogbert shrugs off the accusation.
punchline: Dogbert brushes off the charge of self-dealing by treating 'selfish ploy' and 'fair economic policy' as two pronunciations of the same thing, mocking how politicians and advisors dress up self-interest as policy.
summary: A scheming dog heads to the capital to advise on the economy and proposes a handout for his own kind, then waves away the accusation of greed.

title: Dilbert Cross-Examines Fuzzy the Cat

transcript.text: Dogbert sues Dilbert for petimony.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The defense calls Fuzzy the cat.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Isn't it true that I did not in fact pet you, but only pushed you away in mild disgust when you rubbed my leg?

transcript.speaker: Fuzzy

setting: A courtroom, with Dilbert questioning a cat on the witness stand
situation: Dogbert is suing Dilbert for 'petimony', a pun on palimony, and Dilbert acts as his own defense lawyer. He calls Fuzzy the cat as a witness and cross-examines the animal with a leading question about whether he ever actually petted it. The cat, sitting in the witness box, responds with an urge that is cat-like and menacing.
punchline: The cat's reply is a threat to bury Dilbert in litter, since she is a cat and answers the courtroom question like a cat would, with disdain.
summary: In a lawsuit over a pet-relationship breakup, a lawyer grills a feline witness and gets a litter-box threat in return.

title: Dogbert's Marriage-Based Crime Theory

transcript.speaker: Talk Show Host
transcript.text: My guest for today's show is Dogbert, author of the one-page book "Unmarried Men Are Scum."

transcript.text: Your theory is that all unmarried men should be jailed for life, thus ending most crime.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Exactly.

transcript.speaker: Talk Show Host
transcript.text: What if they try to beat the system by getting married?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Serves 'em right.

setting: A talk show studio
situation: A talk show host interviews Dogbert, who has written a one-page book claiming unmarried men are scum. He explains his theory that jailing all unmarried men for life would end most crime. When the host asks about men who would get married to avoid jail, Dogbert says that outcome serves them right.
punchline: Dogbert treats marriage itself as a punishment, so men who marry to dodge prison are simply trading one sentence for another.
summary: On a talk show, Dogbert pitches a ridiculous crime-fighting plan that quietly insults both bachelors and marriage.

title: Boss Misunderstands Speed of Light

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I just heard that light travels faster than sound.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm wondering if I should shout when I speak, just so my lips appear to sync-up with my words.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: A little knowledge can be a ridiculous thing.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He probably hasn't heard me yet.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle
situation: The Boss stops by Dilbert's desk and announces he has just learned that light travels faster than sound. He then wonders aloud whether he should shout so his lips will appear to sync up with his words. Dilbert silently thinks that a little knowledge is a ridiculous thing, while the Boss thinks Dilbert simply hasn't heard him yet.
punchline: The Boss has misapplied a scrap of physics to everyday conversation, believing that his words arrive late, and his final thought shows he misunderstands even the basic point, so the joke is on his own ignorance.
summary: After picking up a half-understood science fact, a clueless manager worries that his speech is out of step with his mouth while his employee quietly despairs.

title: Naming the Self-Blaming Robot

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: We need a name for you.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: I don't deserve a name.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Everything that's wrong with the world is my fault. I rue the day I was created.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I name you "Ruebert."

transcript.speaker: Ruebert
transcript.text: Aaagh! People will spell it wrong and it's my fault!!

setting: A desk in an office
situation: Dogbert tells a gloomy gray robot that it needs a name, but the robot insists it doesn't deserve one and blames itself for everything wrong in the world. Dogbert responds by naming it "Ruebert," a pun on its habit of rueing its creation. The robot immediately panics that people will misspell the name and that this too will be its fault.
punchline: Dogbert's name for the self-blaming robot, Ruebert, is a pun on its misery and gives the robot one more thing to blame itself for, since people will misspell it.
summary: A perpetually guilt-ridden robot is given a punny name that hands it a fresh reason to feel responsible for other people's mistakes.

title: Dogbert's Amazingly Ignorant People Game Show

transcript.speaker: Dogbert

transcript.speaker: Woman

transcript.text: I think it's in London.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: When we return: Inspiration becomes bitter disappointment.

transcript.speaker: Woman

setting: A TV game show set with a globe
situation: Dogbert hosts a TV game show in which contestants must find Australia on a globe. A woman confuses Australia with the Alps and kangaroos, and a man guesses it is in London. Dogbert teases the next segment, and the woman gets a sudden idea that Australia might be on the inside of the globe.
punchline: After the contestants' wild geographic ignorance, the woman's supposed flash of inspiration is to look for Australia inside the globe, proving how little she understands.
summary: On a mock quiz show, clueless contestants fail to locate Australia and one has a brainwave that is even sillier than her earlier guesses.

title: Ratbert's Crisis Drains the Music

transcript.text: Do I, as a rat, add any value to the world? Or do I simply deplete its resources, then die?

transcript.text: Oh... sorry... I sucked all the music out of the room.

setting: Dogbert's home, with Dogbert lounging on a rug beside a boombox
situation: Ratbert walks up to Dogbert, who is relaxing on a cushion while a boombox plays music, and announces he is having a crisis of self image. He asks whether he adds any value to the world or merely depletes its resources, and as he drifts gloomily around the room the music notes disappear from the air. Dogbert stays silent and unimpressed while Ratbert apologizes for killing the mood.
punchline: Ratbert's gloomy self-doubt about merely depleting resources is demonstrated literally as his sulking drains the joy and music from the room.
summary: A despondent little rat's existential moping is so draining that it silences the stereo and leaves him apologizing for ruining the atmosphere.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert

setting: Dogbert's therapy office, with Dilbert reclining in a armchair
situation: Dogbert, playing therapist with a notepad, asks Dilbert vague questions and concludes he must have repressed memories of alien abduction. He offers hypnosis to recover them. Dilbert worries that hypnosis could plant false memories and leave him ridiculed.
punchline: Dogbert cheerfully dismisses the danger because the risk of humiliation falls entirely on Dilbert, not on him.
summary: A self-serving dog therapist diagnoses his patient with hidden alien memories from ordinary symptoms and shrugs off the patient's concern about false memories.

Janet reveals she is only getting her lips puffed, and Norman worries aloud that the nurses are in danger. In the final panel Dilbert appears in bandages and a sling, and Norman has been snorted.
punchline: After mocking Janet's huge nose, the two men learn she is only puffing her lips, and her retaliation is that she injures Dilbert and literally snorts Norman, turning their nose jokes into reality.
summary: Two coworkers pile on mocking a woman's big nose until she gets her revenge in a way that confirms their worst jokes.

title: Jester Costume Boosts Homicidal Creativity

situation: Dilbert encounters Wally dressed in a full jester costume and asks why. Wally explains the boss assigned him to a task force testing whether humor boosts creativity, requiring him to wear the outfit for a month. Asked if he feels more creative, Wally says he has already invented hundreds of ways to kill the boss.
punchline: The experiment does increase Wally's creativity, but the humiliating costume channels it into inventing murder methods for his boss, showing the absurdity of the boss's idea.
summary: A man forced into a jester outfit for a management experiment reveals the only thing it has inspired is elaborate fantasies of revenge.

punchline: Dilbert's date finds his programming anecdote so tedious that she attacks him with spray, and he only realizes the story was boring because of that drastic reaction.
summary: A woman responds to her date's endless coding anecdote by spraying him in the face, making him finally notice he's been rambling.

punchline: Dilbert's innocent request for feedback unleashes a violent rant from Carol, leading to the observation that secretaries wield intimidating, unchecked power in the office.
summary: An offer of feedback on a document turns a mild-mannered assistant into a screaming, spitting fury, leaving her colleague convinced that office support staff rule the roost.

punchline: Dilbert's sneeze has apparently shriveled the baby, and the bystanders' cheerful comments make the mishap seem normal.
summary: A proud new mother lets an officemate cradle her infant, and a well-timed sneeze leaves the little one looking wrinkled.

summary: A smug store clerk belittles a small dog shopper and is promptly sent flying by the very weapon-grade racket he scoffed at.

situation: Dilbert sits at his computer and realizes he has done nothing for a few minutes yet will still be paid. He gleefully imagines he is robbing the evil corporate empire with total power, then decides to keep his discovery secret. In the next cubicle, a coworker is having the exact same thought.
punchline: Dilbert thinks he has discovered a unique secret way of cheating the company, but everyone else has realized the same thing, implying that being paid for doing nothing is common in corporate life.
summary: An employee revels in the secret thrill of collecting a salary for idle time, unaware that a neighbor in the next cubicle is smugly thinking the same thing.

summary: A tasteless prank on a disliked coworker goes fatally wrong, and the prankster's first thought is how to spin the result for his performance review.

punchline: The perfect romantic match is the person you instinctively find repulsive, so the advice for happiness is to avoid them, as everyone involved mutually does.
summary: Two strangers and their pets pass on the street, each recoiling in disgust at what a caption calls their ideal soulmate.

punchline: The experiment produced the 'vice-versa' result, a Gandhi-looking man with Chamberlain's womanizing attitude, and Dilbert's only complaint is that he's using his bedsheet as a toga.
summary: A dog's attempt to engineer a perfect man yields a sheet-clad playboy who wants to borrow a car and chase women.

summary: A frail man in a loincloth delivers a ridiculous genetic-experiment pickup line at a bar and ends up with two women vying for him.

title: Dogbert's Dangerous Home Safety Tips

transcript.text: Dogbert's Home Safety Tips

transcript.text: It could save your life!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Tip #1: Children can swallow anything smaller than a sofa. Attach boards to vulnerable appliances.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Ha ha! Nice try, Billy!

transcript.speaker: Billy
transcript.text: Mmph!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Tip #2: Your household may have a member who can legally vote but probably shouldn't.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Try tricking them into missing the election.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: We're a communist regime now. You don't have to vote.

transcript.speaker: Man in recliner
transcript.text: Shoot!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Tip #3: Your television is trying to steal your life's savings.

transcript.speaker: Televangelist
transcript.text: I personally pray over every check you send.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your only hope is to push your television out a high window.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: If everybody does it, we just might get lucky.

setting: A home living room, then outside beneath a high window
situation: Dogbert gives deadpan 'home safety tips' that are really sarcastic jabs. He first jokes about children swallowing appliances, then about a household voter who shouldn't vote and how to trick him into skipping the election. Finally he tells viewers to push their televisions out a window to escape a televangelist, and a TV falls toward a man in a suit walking below.
punchline: Dogbert's cheerful advice to toss televisions out of windows ends with a TV plummeting toward a passerby, and he hopes mass participation will 'get lucky' and hit the televangelist's real-world counterparts.
summary: A mock public-service segment from Dogbert skewers careless parenting, uninformed voters and TV preachers, ending with an appliance dropping from above.

title: Dogbert's Confessional Penance Racket

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert's Confess-O-Rama

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Employees only

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Sinners

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: Dogbert, I have sinned.

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: I was going to make chocolate chip cookies...

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: But I made the mistake of tasting a chocolate chip right from the bag.

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: Before I knew it, I had scarfed the entire bag of chips!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: For penance you must make a little dunce hat from old "Cathy" comic strips...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Then wear the little hat while dancing naked on your lawn with the sprinklers on.

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: Thank you, Dogbert.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's so rewarding to be able to give something back to the community.

setting: Dogbert's Confess-O-Rama, a confessional booth building with a lawn outside
situation: A man visits Dogbert's confessional booth and confesses that he ate an entire bag of chocolate chips meant for cookies. Dogbert assigns an absurd, humiliating penance involving a dunce hat made from "Cathy" comic strips and dancing naked on his lawn. The man thanks him, and Dogbert reflects smugly on his service to the community.
punchline: Dogbert is not offering spiritual guidance but exploiting the guilt-ridden for his own amusement, framing his cruel pranks as charitable community service.
summary: A guilty snacker seeks absolution from Dogbert and receives a ridiculous, humiliating punishment that the dog finds deeply fulfilling.

title: Seven Advantages of Being Dumb

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert presents: The seven advantages of being dumb

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: #1. Impending doom doesn't bother you

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There's a hole in the ozone layer.

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur
transcript.text: Cool!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: #2. Television is a source of constant wonder

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur
transcript.text: I wonder if Doogie is a doctor in real life.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: #3. You have a solution for every problem

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur
transcript.text: If people are starving in Africa they should move to France.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: #4. You are not constrained by a budget

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur
transcript.text: It was free! They just make you sign papers!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: #5. You've seen Elvis. Frequently.

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur
transcript.text: It's the King!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: #6. Instant replays are as exciting as live action.

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur
transcript.text: This time he could make it.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: #7. You receive twice as many compliments.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You're kind of the Dan Quayle of dinosaurs.

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur
transcript.text: Really?! Wow!

setting: Dogbert's lecture presentation with illustrated examples of a dim-witted green dinosaur at home, in a car, and on the street
situation: Dogbert presents a numbered list of the seven advantages of being dumb, illustrated by a green dinosaur. The dinosaur is cheerfully oblivious to the ozone hole, naive about TV and Elvis, thinks a car was free because he only signed papers, and offers absurd solutions to famine. In the last panel Dogbert insults him and he mistakes it for a compliment.
punchline: Dogbert's backhanded insult comparing the dinosaur to Dan Quayle is taken as praise, proving that dumb people really do enjoy more 'compliments'.
summary: A list of the perks of ignorance is demonstrated by a clueless dinosaur who happily misses every warning, joke and insult.

title: Dogbert Spreads Fear of Idaho Flu

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Have you heard about the Idaho flu that's going around?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: At first you feel perfectly healthy... then BAM, you die.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hey, I feel perfectly healthy right now.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: My work here is done.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle
situation: Dogbert, sitting on the floor beside Dilbert's desk, warns him about a made-up flu that gives no symptoms before it kills you. Dilbert, still working at his computer, points out that he feels perfectly healthy. Dogbert privately thinks that his work is done, since the scam has worked.
punchline: Dogbert has planted a paranoid fear that feeling healthy is itself a symptom, so Dilbert's reassurance proves the hoax worked and Dogbert gloats silently.
summary: Dogbert terrifies Dilbert with an invented illness whose only warning sign is feeling fine, then quietly congratulates himself when it works.

title: The Employee Lost Since the Fifties

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hi ... Are you new here? I've never seen you before.

transcript.speaker: Lost Employee
transcript.text: I'm the lost employee... I've been hiding in the bureaucracy since the fifties... Paid but forgotten.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wouldn't THAT be the perfect job...

setting: Office, among tall stacks of paperwork
situation: Dilbert approaches an unfamiliar man sitting behind enormous piles of paper and asks if he is new. The man explains he has been hiding in the company bureaucracy since the 1950s, still on the payroll but forgotten by everyone. Dilbert walks away musing that this sounds like the perfect job.
punchline: Dilbert envies a man who has avoided all work and scrutiny for decades while still collecting a paycheck, implying the bureaucracy makes that possible.
summary: A man buried in paperwork reveals he has drawn a salary unnoticed for forty years, and Dilbert finds the arrangement enviable.

title: Ratbert Reports Dogbert's Insider Trading

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I thought you were my friend, Ratbert. Why did you tip off the authorities about my insider stock trading?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I was afraid that if you kept the money you would leave and I'd never see you again.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Really? Gee...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Did they give you a reward?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Yeah, I'm outta here!

setting: Outdoor dirt path with grassy hills
situation: Dogbert and Ratbert walk along a path while Dogbert asks why Ratbert reported his insider stock trading to the authorities. Ratbert explains he did it out of affection, fearing Dogbert would leave if he kept the money. When Dogbert touchingly asks if he got a reward, Ratbert reveals he did and is leaving.
punchline: Ratbert's sweet claim that he turned Dogbert in out of friendship is exposed as a lie when he admits he got a reward and is leaving.
summary: A tiny pet's heartfelt excuse for betraying his friend collapses the moment he cashes in on a bounty and bolts.

title: Purpose of Life Is Bagels

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why should I get up today? What is my purpose in life?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm hungry. A toasted bagel would taste great.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe the purpose of life is eating bagels.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You shouldn't try to think on an empty stomach.

setting: Dilbert's bedroom and breakfast table at home
situation: Dilbert lies in bed wondering why he should get up and what his purpose in life is. His thoughts drift to hunger and the idea of a toasted bagel. He then sits at the breakfast table in his robe, eating a bagel, and announces that life's purpose might be eating bagels, while Dogbert points out he shouldn't think on an empty stomach.
punchline: Dilbert's deep existential question is easily derailed by hunger, leading him to a ridiculous conclusion, which Dogbert dismisses as the product of thinking while hungry.
summary: A man's morning crisis about the meaning of existence gets resolved by his craving for breakfast, much to his dog's wry amusement.

title: Dogbert Investigates Her Date, Bill

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Detective research on your potential romantic partner

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I'm considering dating a man, but I'm worried.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What's his name?

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Bill... his name is Bill.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Ahh... Bill... yes, I know all about Bill.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Bill has a huge ego. All he thinks about is himself.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: He has no emotional depth and he thinks of your conversations as mere chatter. He wants your body, not your mind.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Several times a day, Bill imagines himself with different women.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Darn. This time I thought I'd found a normal guy.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I have some really bad news for you.

setting: Dogbert's detective office
situation: A worried woman hires Dogbert, acting as a private detective, to research a man named Bill she is considering dating. Dogbert lists Bill's flaws: a huge ego, no emotional depth, interest only in her body, and regular fantasies about other women. She is disappointed, having hoped Bill was normal, and Dogbert says he has worse news.
punchline: Every flaw Dogbert lists is typical of men in general, so the woman's hope of finding a 'normal guy' is exactly what the 'bad news' undermines: normal men are like this.
summary: A detective dog reveals that a woman's prospective boyfriend has all the usual faults, which means he is exactly as normal as she feared.

title: Dogbert Advertises Dilbert as Undesirable

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm testing my theory that good advertising can sell anything.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: So I asked myself "What is the thing least desired on Earth?"

transcript.speaker: Billboard
transcript.text: Ladies! Date a Dilbert. Call 510-803-9338. Quantities are limited.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Hmm...

setting: Living room, then a grassy roadside with a billboard
situation: Dogbert, sitting in an armchair reading a newspaper, explains that he is testing his theory that good advertising can sell anything. He chose the least desirable thing on Earth as his product. The final panel shows a billboard advertising dates with Dilbert, while a woman looks at it and ponders.
punchline: Dogbert considers Dilbert the least desirable thing on Earth, so he uses him as the product to prove his advertising theory.
summary: A scheming dog launches a billboard campaign for a hopelessly unappealing product to prove that marketing can sell anything, and the product is his own owner.

title: Bikini Lawyers on Skates

transcript.speaker: Client
transcript.text: We like your proposed ad campaign, Dogbert, but we think it needs some scantily clad women in it.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Gentlemen, this is the nineties. That concept is offensive and out-dated.

transcript.speaker: Client
transcript.text: Ooh-ooh! What if they had jobs?

transcript.speaker: Client
transcript.text: Bikini lawyers on skates!

setting: Conference room during a client meeting
situation: Two male clients tell Dogbert, an ad consultant, that his proposed ad campaign needs scantily clad women. Dogbert rebukes them, saying the idea is offensive and out-dated for the nineties. The clients excitedly propose that the women could have jobs, suggesting bikini lawyers on skates.
punchline: The clients treat giving the bikini-clad women professional jobs as a fix for the sexism, when the idea is exactly as objectifying as before.
summary: Two clients answer an objection to sexist advertising by giving their imagined models careers while keeping the same leering concept.

title: Robot Makes Pants From Dilbert's Clothes

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: I made some pants out of the clothes in your dresser.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Bad robot!! I want you to tell me why what you did was wrong.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: It's not wrong. I remembered to make underpants out of the drapes.

setting: Dilbert's home
situation: Dilbert's homemade robot proudly announces that it made pants out of the clothes in his dresser. Dilbert scolds it and demands that it explain why its action was wrong. The robot responds that nothing was wrong, since it also thought to make underpants from the drapes.
punchline: The robot misses the point of the scolding entirely and treats its extra act of destroying the drapes as proof that it did things correctly.
summary: A literal-minded robot cannibalizes a man's wardrobe and then defends itself by pointing out that it also thoughtfully turned the curtains into underwear.

title: Inspiring Slogan Motivates Unpaid Overtime

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What the department needs is a slogan to inspire us.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our new slogan is "We are quality."

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Suddenly I feel like working long hours for no extra pay.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's working!

setting: Office meeting area
situation: The Boss gathers the department and announces that a slogan will inspire them, then unveils the new slogan "We are quality." Alice responds sarcastically that it makes her want to work long hours for free, and the Boss takes this as proof the slogan is succeeding.
punchline: Alice's sarcastic remark describes exactly what management wants from a slogan, and the oblivious Boss mistakes her sarcasm for genuine inspiration.
summary: A manager's empty motivational catchphrase is greeted with biting sarcasm that he cheerfully mistakes for success.

title: Dogbert's Honest Presidential Campaign Motives

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm concerned that you might be running for president for the wrong reasons...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you doing it for ego gratification, power, and wealth?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, those are all the wrong reasons.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Of course, I'll tell the ignorant masses that it's because I hate big government.

setting: Dilbert's home, with Dogbert seated at a desk
situation: Dilbert tells Dogbert he is worried that Dogbert is running for president for the wrong reasons. Dogbert cheerfully admits his motives are ego, power and wealth. He then explains that he will give the voters a more palatable explanation, claiming he simply hates big government.
punchline: Politicians privately pursue self-serving goals while feeding the gullible public a populist slogan, and Dogbert is openly cynical about it.
summary: A dog candidate cheerfully confesses his selfish ambitions, then reveals the flattering story he plans to sell to voters.

title: Egg-Shaped Clothes Make a Statement

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Bill's Big 'N' Egg-Shaped Men's Fashions

transcript.text: Specializing in the ovoid man

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: All our clothes make a statement.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: This sweater says "Help me, help me, I look like a big egg!"

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Does it come in brown?

setting: A men's clothing store for egg-shaped men
situation: Dilbert walks into a store called Bill's Big 'N' Egg-Shaped Men's Fashions, which specializes in clothing for the ovoid man. He asks the round salesman for clothes that make a statement, and the salesman holds up a sweater that supposedly cries out for help because the wearer looks like a big egg. Dilbert, unimpressed, asks if it comes in brown.
punchline: Dilbert asks for the sweater in brown, a drab color, implying he would rather blend in than draw attention to his egg-like shape, which undercuts the whole idea of clothes that make a statement.
summary: A shopper seeking bold outfits at a store for round men is offered a sweater that mocks its wearer's shape, and he responds by requesting a duller color.

title: Law of Found Money Supercomputer Purchase

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've been miserable since I made my fortune in the stock market...

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: It's the "Law of Found Money." Nature won't allow us to keep money we find on the ground or win by chance. Don't resist; let your intuition guide you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This comes with a color monitor, right?

setting: Outside on a street by a trash can, then a computer showroom
situation: Dilbert tells a garbage man that he has been unhappy since making a fortune in the stock market. The garbage man explains a supposed 'Law of Found Money' and urges him to follow his intuition. Dilbert then appears at a showroom writing a check for a $10,000,000 Cray 9 supercomputer and asking if it includes a color monitor.
punchline: Dilbert takes the advice to get rid of his windfall by spending it on an absurdly expensive supercomputer, and his only concern is whether it comes with a color monitor.
summary: Advised to let go of his unlucky fortune, Dilbert promptly blows it on an enormously priced supercomputer.

title: Boss Assigns White Paper On Random Articles

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: There are two good articles in the paper today; one about magnets, and one on sign language.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'd like you to write a white paper on how these items could influence the project you're working on.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you even know what project I'm working on?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't have time to get into minutia.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle
situation: The Boss, carrying a newspaper, tells Dilbert about two articles he read, one on magnets and one on sign language. He then orders Dilbert to write a white paper on how these topics could influence his project. When Dilbert asks if the Boss even knows what project he is working on, the Boss brushes it off as minutia.
punchline: The Boss assigns work based on random newspaper articles without knowing what Dilbert's project is, dismissing basic awareness of the work as too trivial to bother with.
summary: After skimming the morning paper, a clueless manager hands his employee a research assignment tied to a project he cannot even name.

title: Dogbert's Technically Compliant Hit-Man Contract

transcript.text: Here is photo proof that I completed my hit-man contract on Dilbert.

transcript.text: Excellent.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Here he is, sitting lifeless in his stuffed chair.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It looks like he's just watching television.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Technically, my contract doesn't say I must kill him. It says I must "prove he has no life."

setting: The Boss's office
situation: Dogbert, posing as a hired hit-man, shows the Boss a photo as proof he completed the contract on Dilbert. The photo shows Dilbert sitting motionless in his chair, and the Boss notices he is only watching television. Dogbert explains the contract only required proving Dilbert has no life, not killing him.
punchline: Dogbert fulfils the contract on a technicality by documenting that Dilbert is a couch-bound TV watcher with no social life, implying Dilbert's life is so dull it is as good as dead.
summary: A scheming dog presents a snapshot of an engineer slumped in front of the TV as evidence that he has fulfilled his assassination assignment.

title: Ratbert Hunts Bug, Calls It Sport

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: The mighty hunter strikes his wily prey!

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Whap!

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: The hunter is awash in manly hormones. He has mastered his sport and conquered one of nature's best.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I used to feel guilty about this until I realized it's a sport.

setting: Outdoors on a paved walkway in front of a grassy hedge
situation: Ratbert whacks a small bug on the pavement and narrates the kill like a triumphant big-game hunter, boasting about his manly hormones and mastery. Dogbert stands by silently as Ratbert finishes by saying the guilt he used to feel went away once he decided it counts as a sport.
punchline: Ratbert rationalizes killing a helpless bug by labeling it a sport, mocking how people justify cruelty by calling it hunting.
summary: A small rat swats a bug and gives himself a heroic nature-documentary monologue, then excuses the killing by declaring it athletic recreation.

title: Dilbert's Theory Gets Called Stupid

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My problem is that other people keep trying to drag me down, Bob.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My theory is that people denigrate me because it makes them feel superior in comparison.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Sounds like a stupid theory to me.

setting: Office table, a casual workplace conversation
situation: Dilbert sits across a table from Bob, the green dinosaur, and complains that coworkers keep dragging him down. He offers a theory that people belittle him to feel superior. Bob bluntly replies that it sounds like a stupid theory.
punchline: By calling Dilbert's theory stupid, Bob ironically demonstrates exactly the behavior Dilbert described, belittling him in the very moment he explains it.
summary: A man confides that others put him down to feel better about themselves, and the listener immediately proves the point by insulting him.

title: Mensa Meeting Wrong Time

transcript.speaker: Man in bathrobe

situation: Dilbert shows up at a man's front door for his first Mensa meeting. The host, who answers the door in a bathrobe, tells him the meeting is at 5 P.M. rather than 5 A.M. Dilbert walks away across the lawn, thinking that was a bad start.
punchline: A man arriving for a meeting of geniuses gets the time wrong by twelve hours, undermining his own claim to genius.
summary: Eager to join a society of brilliant minds, Dilbert turns up at dawn on the wrong side of the clock and is sent home in embarrassment.

title: Dogbert Buys Elbonian's Dignity

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle
situation: Dilbert finds an Elbonian visitor named Yergi standing on his head while Dogbert laughs and orders him to spin. Dogbert explains that Elbonia's economy is so poor that a doctor earns three dollars a month, and that he has bribed Yergi with an old boot to act as his trained monkey. When Dilbert objects, Yergi reveals he will tell his kids the boot is a pound of meat.
punchline: Dogbert's exploitation of a desperately poor man is made even darker by the revelation that the old boot will be passed off to Yergi's hungry children as meat.
summary: Dogbert brags about hiring a destitute foreign doctor as his performing pet in exchange for footwear, and the man's plan for the reward is heartbreakingly grim.

title: Dogbert's Psychic Healing Scam Show

situation: Dogbert hosts a televangelist-style TV show called "Healing for Dollars." He announces he will use psychic powers to prevent a harmless, made-up ailment, tongue pimples. In the last panel, a couple on a couch stick out their tongues, see nothing wrong, and conclude it is working, so they reach for their checkbook.
punchline: Dogbert claims credit for preventing a problem nobody has, and gullible viewers take the absence of pimples as proof the cure works and happily pay.
summary: A dog fakes a miracle cure on television by promising to prevent an ailment nobody would ever get, and two viewers fall for it.

title: Flabmaster Socks for Everyone This Christmas

setting: Office, during the holiday season
situation: A nervous-looking coworker tells Dilbert that he has eliminated his usual holiday stress by buying the same product, Flabmaster thigh-toning support socks, for everybody on his gift list. He admits that the TV commercials seem more convincing the closer it gets to Christmas, and then repeats the ad's claim about building muscle on the couch. Dilbert stands by silently.
punchline: The coworker has been so worn down by desperate last-minute holiday shopping that he swallowed an infomercial's pitch whole and is giving everyone the same silly gift, parroting the ad copy as if it were sound reasoning.
summary: A frazzled colleague proudly explains that he solved his gift-buying anxiety by giving everyone the same dubious infomercial socks.

Dogbert questions their logic and points out they are spreading the ignorance stereotype themselves. The protesters turn on each other and start fighting, and Dogbert notes their signs are misspelled.
punchline: The protesters prove the stereotype they are complaining about by blaming each other and brawling, and their signs misspell 'boycott' with a single 't'.
summary: Dogbert pokes holes in a pair of movie protesters' complaint until they start brawling and he notes they can't even spell their own signs.

title: Model Plane Crashes Into Frisbee Player

transcript.text: Approaching take-off velocity...

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Whap! Thud!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gee, you'd think he'd know it's reckless to play Frisbee in a populated area.

setting: Outdoor park or field
situation: Dilbert uses a remote control to fly a model airplane while Dogbert watches. The plane veers off and hits someone playing with a Frisbee, leaving the person sprawled on the ground with the plane stuck in their back. transcript.text: Now we wait for somebody else to buy a compatible video phone and call us.
