transcript.text: The amazing thing is that society couldn't advance without people like you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think I saw something.

setting: Dilbert's home
situation: Dilbert proudly carries home a box containing the first video phone in the city. He sets it up and realizes he must wait for someone else to buy a compatible phone before he can call anyone. Dogbert sarcastically praises him as an early adopter while Dilbert stares at the blank screen, hoping he saw a flicker of activity.
punchline: Dogbert's sarcastic praise for early adopters underscores that Dilbert paid for a useless gadget, and his hopeful 'I think I saw something' shows how desperately he wants it to work.
summary: A man buys a cutting-edge gadget that is worthless until others adopt it, and his dog mockingly flatters his role in progress.

title: Dogbert Recounts Dilbert's Embarrassing Memories

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Remember the time you laughed at your own joke so hard that you inhaled and snorted at the same time?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Then you choked on your own spit, which caused you to lurch over and bonk your head on the coffee table...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm ignoring you.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Who says your life is boring?

setting: Dilbert's living room at home
situation: Dilbert sits in an armchair reading a newspaper while Dogbert, lounging with his feet up, reminds him of an embarrassing incident where he laughed at his own joke, choked, and bonked his head. Dilbert responds by trying to ignore him from behind his newspaper.
punchline: Dogbert implies Dilbert's life is so dull that his most memorable moments are humiliating accidents, and he is entertained by them.
summary: While his owner tries to read in peace, a dog gleefully recounts the man's most mortifying slapstick moment and then suggests it proves his life is anything but dull.

title: Old Programmers Outdo Each Other Hardship

transcript.speaker: Older programmer
transcript.text: When I started programming, we didn't have any of these sissy "icons" and "windows."

transcript.speaker: Older programmer
transcript.text: All we had were zeros and ones -- and sometimes we didn't even have ones.

transcript.speaker: Older programmer
transcript.text: I wrote an entire database program using only zeros.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You had zeros? We had to use the letter "O."

setting: Lunch table in an office break room
situation: Several engineers eat lunch while an older programmer brags about how primitive computing was when he started. Each coworker tries to top the last with more extreme deprivation. Dilbert finishes by claiming they had to substitute the letter "O" for the digit zero.
punchline: It parodies the 'Four Yorkshiremen' one-upmanship sketch, with programmers competing over who had it worse, ending in an absurd claim that even zeros were unavailable.
summary: Veteran techies at lunch trade exaggerated tales of how little they had to work with in the early days of programming.

title: Borrowing the Planet From Strangers

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Nature is so wonderful...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: They say we don't leave the planet to future generations, we borrow it from our children.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's even better than that.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: We don't have children, so we're borrowing the planet from complete strangers!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And there's no collateral. We can use up the planet, have great lives and leave an empty smoking shell to the strangers!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I tell you, people have completely overlooked the positive side of this environment situation.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But someday I want to have children.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Let's hope they're not as selfish as you.

setting: Outdoor walking path through a park or woods
situation: Dilbert and Dogbert take a walk in nature while Dogbert muses about the saying that we borrow the planet from our children. He gleefully argues that since they have no children, they are borrowing it from strangers with no collateral and can trash it freely. Dilbert objects that he wants kids someday, and Dogbert replies that he hopes they aren't as selfish as Dilbert.
punchline: Dogbert's cynical case for exploiting the environment backfires on Dilbert, who is told that the children he hopes to have should hope not to inherit his selfishness, even though it was Dogbert's selfish logic all along.
summary: While strolling outdoors, a smug dog explains why having no kids makes wrecking the environment a bargain, then turns the insult on his human friend.

title: Robot Bride Rejects Her Only Option

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: My mate is complete! I will now have eons of marital bliss!

transcript.speaker: Female Robot
transcript.text: I don't think so, Gomer. I'm going to shop around... maybe find somebody more enlightened than a can opener.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: It's Ruebert, not Gomer, and I'm the only other robot in existence!

transcript.speaker: Female Robot
transcript.text: I'm in hell.

setting: Dilbert's workplace or lab, where he has built two robots
situation: Dilbert stands by while a newly built male robot proudly announces that his robot mate is finished and that he expects eons of marital bliss. The female robot, newly activated, says she plans to shop around for someone more enlightened than a can opener, only to learn that the male robot is the only other robot in existence. She realizes she is stuck with him and thinks she is in hell.
punchline: The female robot's plan to shop around for a better partner collapses because the only other robot is the can-opener-like one she is rejecting, leaving her with no choice.
summary: A freshly built robot couple discovers that the bride's dating pool contains exactly one candidate, whom she finds unimpressive.

title: Rich Now, Rejected Earlier Dating

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gee, Mary, you weren't willing to date me BEFORE I made millions in the stock market.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm afraid you see me as just a big, talking wallet.

transcript.speaker: Mary
transcript.text: You're much more than that.

transcript.speaker: Mary
transcript.text: For example, you also wear thick glasses.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Too little, too late.

setting: A restaurant table on a date
situation: Dilbert is on a dinner date with Mary, a woman who previously refused to date him but now will that he has made millions in the stock market. He accuses her of seeing him as just a wallet, and she tries to reassure him by saying he is more than that, then offers his thick glasses as another thing she likes.
punchline: Mary's attempt to prove she values more than his money backfires because the only other quality she can name is his thick glasses, which is hardly a compliment.
summary: A newly wealthy man calls out his date's sudden interest, and her clumsy reassurance only confirms his suspicion.

title: Dogbert Plans Demagogue Career

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I've decided to become a demagogue.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll find some issue that appeals to the emotions and blind prejudices of the masses, then I'll whip it into a media frenzy and become a national figure.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: For example, unmarried men are responsible for most of our violent crimes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's because we tend to have pets.

setting: Dilbert's office desk
situation: Dogbert announces to Dilbert that he plans to become a demagogue by inflaming public prejudice into a media frenzy. He offers a sample issue, claiming unmarried men commit most violent crimes. Dilbert, seated at his computer, responds with a deadpan comment about pets.
punchline: Dilbert, an unmarried man with a dog, sarcastically takes Dogbert's baseless claim as an accusation against himself, implying the real culprits are pets like Dogbert, who is the one plotting the scheme.
summary: A scheming dog rehearses how to stir up public outrage with a bogus statistic, and his unmarried owner dryly points out who is really to blame.

title: Garbage Man Debunks Squirrel Prediction Model

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I know that my computer model is accurate, but nobody believes me when I predict that squirrels will conquer the Earth.

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: Of course, you're aware that according to "chaos theory" any complex iterative model is no better than a wild guess, even if the logic is perfect.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're making that up.

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: You caught me; I'm really a giant spy squirrel in disguise.

setting: Outdoors beside a trash can
situation: Dilbert complains to a garbage man that no one believes his computer model predicting that squirrels will conquer the Earth. The garbage man calmly cites chaos theory to argue that complex models are no better than wild guesses. When Dilbert accuses him of inventing that, the garbage man cheerfully admits he is a giant spy squirrel in disguise.
punchline: The garbage man's dismissal of Dilbert's model turns out to be self-serving, since he confesses to being a spy squirrel, which suggests Dilbert's prediction may be right after all.
summary: A man's doubted forecast of a rodent takeover gets brushed off by a sanitation worker who then casually reveals his true identity.

title: Dogbert's School for Jerks Sorting

transcript.speaker: Sign
transcript.text: Dogbert's School for Jerks

transcript.speaker: Student
transcript.text: Hey!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: We'll begin by sorting you into the three major jerk categories for specialized instruction.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Look at this picture of supermodel Cindy Crawford.

transcript.speaker: Student
transcript.text: Whoa! Hubba! Snort!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Anybody who said "hubba" stand over there. You are what is called "jerks around women."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Now, somebody catch this ball, please.

transcript.speaker: Students
transcript.text: Foul! You fouled!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Anybody who yelled "foul" is a "sports jerk." Stand over there.

transcript.speaker: Student
transcript.text: It was a foul.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: So, whoever is left must be...

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Hurry up. I'm late for court.

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: You're a lawyer too?

transcript.speaker: Another man
transcript.text: I was going to say "hubba".

setting: Dogbert's School for Jerks, a classroom with a stool
situation: Dogbert runs a school for jerks and sorts the students into categories using traps. He tricks them into revealing themselves by showing a supermodel picture and throwing a ball. The students left over are lawyers who are in a hurry to get to court.
punchline: The third category of jerk is lawyers, and the last man admits he only avoided the first category by being too slow to say "hubba".
summary: A canine instructor traps his pupils into self-identifying as two kinds of jerks, and the leftover group turns out to be attorneys.

title: Minimizing the Boss's Layoff Pain

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need an outside consultant like you to help with lay-offs.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My main concern is to minimize the pain and hardship that goes with this.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: With generous severance pay?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, I think that would only make my pain and suffering worse.

setting: The Boss's office
situation: The Boss hires Dogbert as an outside consultant to help carry out layoffs, saying his main concern is reducing pain and hardship. Dogbert suggests generous severance pay as the obvious way to ease the burden on laid-off employees. The Boss rejects it because the pain he cares about is his own.
punchline: The Boss's concern about 'pain and hardship' is entirely about himself, not the employees being fired, so he rejects severance pay because it would cost him more.
summary: A manager seeking help with firing staff reveals that the suffering he wants to avoid is strictly his own.

title: Dogbert Buys Lenin's Body Cheap

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Wow! You bought Lenin's body?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Only ten dollars.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Now I have to decide what to do with it.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: You could build a museum.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I was thinking of using him as a coffee table.

setting: A room with pink walls, apparently in the Soviet Union or a similar location, with a bookshelf and a uniformed guard standing by
situation: Ratbert is amazed to learn that Dogbert has bought the preserved body of Lenin for only ten dollars, with a uniformed guard standing nearby. Dogbert says he must now decide what to do with it, and Ratbert suggests building a museum. Dogbert has a far less reverent plan in mind.
punchline: Dogbert dismisses the dignified museum idea and plans to treat the revered communist leader's embalmed body as a piece of living-room furniture.
summary: After snapping up a famous embalmed leader at a bargain price, a scheming dog skips the grand display idea and opts for something far more domestic and disrespectful.

title: Dilbert Haggles With Lucky Airlines

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Lucky Airlines? I demand payment for the luggage I lost when we crashed into the mountain.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, technically it's not "lost." . . . Well, yes, I did eat your complimentary peanuts . . .

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Help me out here . . . so far, I've agreed to hot-wax their tarmac.

setting: Dilbert's home, on the phone
situation: Dilbert phones Lucky Airlines to demand compensation for luggage lost when his flight crashed into a mountain. The airline's replies push back on his claim, and he ends up conceding points, including having eaten their peanuts. By the end he is asking the airline to help him find a concession it will accept, since so far he has only agreed to hot-wax their tarmac.
punchline: Dilbert's complaint backfires so badly that he has already conceded to absurd chores like waxing the runway, while the airline hasn't offered him anything.
summary: A passenger who survived a plane crash ends up bargaining himself into doing favors for the airline instead of collecting compensation.

title: Supercomputer Predicts Evil Squirrel Takeover

transcript.speaker: Reporter
transcript.text: This man used his supercomputer to predict the future of the world.

transcript.speaker: Reporter
transcript.text: Within five years, evil squirrels will conquer the world and make us all slaves in their nut mines.

transcript.speaker: Reporter
transcript.text: The squirrels should love this guy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's based on actual math.

setting: Outdoors or a press interview with a news reporter holding a microphone
situation: A news reporter introduces Dilbert as the man who used a supercomputer to predict the future. She announces his absurd forecast that evil squirrels will enslave humanity in nut mines. She jokes that the squirrels will love him, and Dilbert defensively insists the prediction is based on real math.
punchline: Dilbert defends a ridiculous prediction as legitimate simply because it came from a supercomputer and mathematical modeling, showing how computed results can be absurd yet trusted.
summary: A reporter gleefully relays an engineer's computer-generated forecast of squirrel world domination, and he stubbornly insists the numbers back it up.

title: Dogbert's Faith Healer Hair Scam

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What did you do to your hair?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's for my new television show, "Healing for Dollars." People send more money if you have this kind of hair.

transcript.speaker: Wife
transcript.text: It might be a trick.

transcript.speaker: Husband
transcript.text: That's what I thought until I saw his hair.

transcript.speaker: Television
transcript.text: Checks or money orders

setting: Dilbert's home, then a living room couch in front of a TV
situation: Dilbert notices Dogbert's strange, puffed-up hairdo and asks about it. Dogbert explains it is a costume for his new televangelist show, because donors give more to someone with that look. A rural couple watching the show on TV debate whether it is a trick, and the husband says the hair convinced him.
punchline: Dogbert cynically exploits gullible viewers, who are persuaded to send money by the televangelist's ridiculous hair rather than any real evidence of healing.
summary: Dogbert styles his hair like a televangelist to fleece trusting viewers, and a couple watching at home is won over by the hairdo alone.

title: Vegetarians Seek Charismatic Leader Dogbert

transcript.speaker: Vegetarian
transcript.text: Dogbert, we need you to become the charismatic leader of our vegetarian movement.

transcript.speaker: Vegetarian
transcript.text: We tried to pick a leader from our ranks, but most of us are ... uh... well...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Scrawny wimps?

transcript.speaker: Vegetarian
transcript.text: Yeah, but deceptively healthy.

setting: Dogbert's home, with Dogbert sitting in a red armchair
situation: A bespectacled, mustached man representing a vegetarian movement asks Dogbert to become their charismatic leader. He explains they could not pick a leader from among themselves because most members are, awkwardly, physically unimpressive. Dogbert bluntly supplies the word 'scrawny wimps' and the man grudgingly agrees, adding that they are 'deceptively healthy'.
punchline: The vegetarians admit their own members are too weak and unimpressive to lead, and can only offer the feeble defense that they are secretly healthy.
summary: A group of meat-avoiding activists recruits Dogbert as their figurehead because their own members lack any commanding presence.

title: Marketing's Weekly Unicorn Barbecue

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dilbert is transferred to Marketing

transcript.speaker: Marketing Employee
transcript.text: Every Tuesday we barbecue a unicorn.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Employee
transcript.text: Make mine rare. Ha ha! Get it? Rare?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm not sure I believe this is the "best part."

setting: Outdoor barbecue in the Marketing department
situation: Newly transferred to Marketing, Dilbert joins a line for the department's weekly barbecue, where a colleague explains they grill a unicorn every Tuesday. A marketing employee jokes about ordering his portion rare, and the chef serves Dilbert a plate holding a unicorn's spiral horn tip.
punchline: Dilbert is served the unicorn's horn and doubts it is the "best part," implying Marketing hands newcomers the worthless scrap while being cheerfully fake about it.
summary: A new arrival in Marketing is given a ceremonial barbecue helping that turns out to be the least appetizing bit of a mythical animal.

title: Office Workers Are Prairie Dogs

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Prairie dogs

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Office workers

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Prairie dog workers

transcript.speaker: Prairie Dog
transcript.text: Man, I'm swamped.

setting: A desert prairie and an office with cubicles
situation: The strip compares prairie dogs popping out of their burrows with office workers peering over their cubicle walls, which look much alike. In the final panel, prairie dogs with glasses and office-worker traits pop out of their holes, and one complains of being swamped, as if it had a desk job.
punchline: Office workers peeking over cubicle walls resemble prairie dogs in their holes, so a prairie dog doing office work would naturally complain about being swamped.
summary: Cubicle dwellers popping up over partitions are shown to be basically prairie dogs with jobs, and one even grumbles about his workload.

title: Team Rope Exercise Ruins Instructor

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: At the "Rivers and Trees" management course.

transcript.speaker: Instructor
transcript.text: This next exercise is always a favorite.

transcript.speaker: Instructor
transcript.text: Using only a rope, your team must figure out how to cross the muddy patch without getting your feet dirty.

transcript.speaker: Instructor
transcript.text: I could have been a forest ranger, but no-o-o-o...

setting: Outdoor management training course beside a muddy path
situation: A cheerful instructor at a management training course hands a rope to a group of participants and tells them to cross a muddy patch without getting their feet dirty. The team apparently solves the problem by using the instructor himself, who ends up bound with the rope and lying face-up in the mud, lamenting the career he missed.
punchline: The team's creative solution to not getting their feet dirty is to tie up the instructor and walk across him, leaving him to regret not becoming a forest ranger.
summary: A trainer's favorite team-building puzzle backfires when the participants turn him into a human bridge over the mud.

title: False Compliments Trick Ratbert

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I've been using false humility to weasel compliments out of people...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: But I know YOU're way too smart to fall for that trick, Ratbert.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Actually, I'm as dumb as toast.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Then I found I could use false compliments to make people insult themselves.

setting: Sitting on an armchair at home
situation: Dogbert tells Ratbert that he has been using false humility to fish for compliments, then flatters Ratbert by saying he is far too smart to fall for that trick. Ratbert responds by declaring that he is actually as dumb as toast. Dogbert reveals that he has moved on to using false compliments to get people to put themselves down.
punchline: Dogbert's flattery of Ratbert was itself the trick, and it worked instantly, getting Ratbert to insult himself.
summary: Dogbert flatters his small friend and gets him to run himself down, demonstrating a new manipulation technique in real time.

title: Suggestion Box Under a Blanket

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I just received your employee suggestion.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We'll handle it the usual way -- by making you sit under a wet blanket surrounded by imbeciles.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: At least there's a process.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Explain your suggestion again.

setting: Office, in the Boss's presence and then in a group around Dilbert's desk
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that he received his employee suggestion and explains the company's standard way of handling suggestions: forcing the suggester to sit under a wet blanket surrounded by imbeciles. In the last panel Dilbert sits covered by a blanket while coworkers crowd around and ask him to explain his suggestion again.
punchline: Dilbert's sardonic consolation that 'at least there's a process' underscores that the company reliably follows a procedure for suggestions, even though it is absurd and punishing.
summary: A manager's formal routine for reviewing a worker's idea turns out to be a humiliating ritual, and the employee can only take comfort in its predictability.

title: Dogbert's Clues for the Clueless

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Bob, here's a copy of my new newsletter for clueless people.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: "Dogbert's Clues for the Clueless: 1. Professional wrestling is all faked. 2. Nobody ever lost weight on a home exercise device."

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: "3. Looks are more important to happiness than brains. 4. If people don't comment on your new hairdo, they hate it."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's not healthy to read them all at once, Bob.

setting: A plain room with a purple-grey wall
situation: Dogbert hands Bob a copy of his new newsletter of tips for clueless people. Bob, a green dinosaur, reads aloud a list of blunt, cynical observations about wrestling, exercise gadgets, appearance and hairdos. Dogbert then warns him that reading them all at once is unhealthy.
punchline: Dogbert's cynical truths are so harsh that he warns the reader they are dangerous to absorb in one sitting, as if the truth itself were bad for your health.
summary: A dog hands a dinosaur a newsletter of grim home truths, then cautions him against taking in too many at once.

title: Elves Insult Dilbert Over Donuts

transcript.speaker: Elf
transcript.text: The humans are not afraid of our elf magic. We must gain their respect through verbal intimidation.

transcript.speaker: Elf (off-panel)
transcript.text: Hey, Bozo! We're talking to you, Chubby!

transcript.speaker: Elf
transcript.text: And then Karl says "Do you think you're going to eat ALL of those donuts?"

transcript.speaker: Elf (thought)
transcript.text: Shut up.

setting: A break room or lunch counter, with a box of donuts on the counter
situation: A group of elves decides to earn human respect through verbal intimidation and heckles Dilbert, who sits quietly with a box of donuts. Later the elves, now wearing donuts around their bodies, retell the exchange, with one quietly thinking that the heckler should shut up.
punchline: The elves have clearly eaten the donuts themselves and are wearing them, so the one mocking Dilbert for eating donuts is the real culprit, while a fellow elf privately wishes the heckler would stop.
summary: Tiny elves mock a man for his donuts, only to be revealed as the ones who have been stuffing themselves with them.

title: School for People Without Common Sense

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm going to open a school for people with no common sense.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Who would pay to go to a school that teaches something that can't be learned?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Except maybe people with no common sense...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Bingo.

setting: Dilbert's living room
situation: Dilbert sits in an armchair reading a newspaper while Dogbert, perched on a footstool, announces plans to open a school for people lacking common sense. Dilbert objects that nobody would pay to be taught something unlearnable, then realizes the customers would be exactly the people who lack it. Dogbert confirms with a single word.
punchline: Dilbert's objection answers itself: people without common sense are exactly the ones who would pay for a pointless school, which is Dogbert's whole business plan.
summary: Dogbert's scheme to sell lessons in an unteachable skill turns out to have a ready market of gullible customers.

title: Dilbert Invents Self-Strangling Shoelace Knot

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm going to start jogging again.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why does everybody tie their laces in the same type of knot?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: From an engineering perspective, there are plenty of good alternatives to the standard knot.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is how innovation begins; one man who refuses to accept the conventional wisdom.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ha ha! I'll invent my own knot! A rebellious, audacious knot!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Like this and this and this! Ha ha ha!!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Many people wonder why there haven't been more engineers in the Olympics.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Call the Boy Scouts.

setting: Dilbert's bedroom at home
situation: Dilbert announces he will start jogging again, then wonders why everyone ties their shoelaces the same way. Inspired by the idea of innovation, he invents his own elaborate knots. He ends up hopelessly tied up on the floor while Dogbert comments dryly.
punchline: Dilbert's rebellious engineering approach to shoelaces leaves him bound helplessly on the floor, so he has to call the Boy Scouts, who know knots, while Dogbert mocks the idea of engineers as Olympic athletes.
summary: Convinced he can improve on ordinary shoelaces, an engineer ties himself into an inescapable tangle and needs rescuing.

title: Shallow Christmas Gift for Poor

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm collecting money for a gift to a poor family this Christmas.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What are you buying for them?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: A CD player.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Thank you for making this the most shallow gesture of my life.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'll add your name to the card.

setting: Office cubicle
situation: Wally approaches Dilbert's desk with an envelope, collecting money for a Christmas gift for a poor family. When Dilbert asks what the gift is, Wally says a CD player. Dilbert sarcastically says it's the most shallow gesture of his life, and Wally cheerfully offers to put Dilbert's name on the card.
punchline: Wally is oblivious to Dilbert's sarcasm about the absurdly impractical gift, taking his complaint as a reason to add Dilbert's name to the card.
summary: A coworker passes the hat for a charity present that turns out to be a pointless luxury, and he misses the sarcasm in the reply.

title: Dogbert Interviews Historically Ignorant Man

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: On today's episode of "Dogbert's Amazingly Ignorant People" we talk to people who don't know history.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: How many people perished because of World War II?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The answer is fifty million.

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: Oh... Rounding.

setting: Outdoor sidewalk beside a grassy hill
situation: Dogbert holds a microphone and hosts a street-interview segment on people who are ignorant of history. He asks a passerby how many people died in World War II, and the man guesses 400. When Dogbert gives the real figure of fifty million, the man brushes off his enormous error as mere rounding.
punchline: The man's guess is off by a factor of about 125,000, yet he passes it off as a harmless rounding error, showing the absurd overconfidence of the ignorant.
summary: A microphone-wielding dog quizzes a bystander on wartime death tolls and gets a wildly low guess that the man tries to excuse as approximation.

title: Dogbert, Industrial Spy for Hire

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: My code name is Dogbert. I'm an industrial spy.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What makes you think my company needs your services?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's pretty obvious that you won't survive on your wits alone.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: There's a rumor that Xypon Inc. is developing a tactical nuclear weapon to use against you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What exactly will you do for us?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You give me fifty thousand dollars, then I disappear for a month and do secret spy things.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll return with information that only a spy or a regular newspaper reader could know.

transcript.speaker: Rival Boss
transcript.text: How good are they, Agent Dogbert?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: They're a bit gullible.

setting: The Boss's office, then the rival company Xypon Inc.'s office
situation: Dogbert pitches himself as an industrial spy to the Boss, scaring him with a rumor that a competitor is building a nuclear weapon and asking for fifty thousand dollars. His plan is to disappear for a month and return with ordinary newspaper information. In the last panel it is revealed he is also working for the rival company, Xypon Inc., and is happily collecting money from both sides.
punchline: Dogbert is a double agent who is fleecing both competing companies, and the gullible Boss is the mark.
summary: A canine con artist sells worthless espionage to one company while secretly taking the competitor's money too.

title: The Bureaucracy Savant New Hire

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: How's the new guy doing?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He's extremely productive.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We think he's one of those bureaucracy savants.

setting: Office hallway and a coworker's office
situation: Wally asks Dilbert how the new guy is doing, and Dilbert replies that he's extremely productive. In the last panel, the new employee is shown at his desk gleefully flinging papers into the air while Dilbert explains he must be a bureaucracy savant.
punchline: The new hire's frantic, joyful paper-shuffling makes him look productive, but it is only a savant-like talent for generating bureaucratic busywork, mocking the idea that paperwork equals real output.
summary: A cheerful newcomer tosses papers around his desk, and his coworkers marvel at his freakish gift for paperwork.

title: Dogbert Grudgingly Wears Christmas Crown

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Why should I open it? You already told me it's just a stupid hat.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Open it anyway.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hey, it's not really a hat; it's a crown.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm not happy. I'm only humoring you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Merry Christmas, little friend.

setting: Dilbert's home on Christmas
situation: Dilbert gives Dogbert a wrapped Christmas present and urges him to open it even though Dogbert has been told it's just a stupid hat. Dogbert opens it and finds a golden crown, which Dilbert points out is not really a hat. Dogbert puts it on but insists he is not happy and is only humoring Dilbert.
punchline: Dogbert, who thinks of himself as a would-be ruler, is secretly pleased with a crown but pretends to be unimpressed while wearing it anyway.
summary: A grumpy dog reluctantly unwraps a gift from his owner and ends up wearing a royal headpiece while denying any delight.

title: Floyd Chewed My Clothes Off

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What happened to you?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I asked Floyd a question.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Floyd hates his job, so he takes it out on co-workers. He almost chewed my clothes off.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How'd you stop him?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: He went into synthetic shock; it's not healthy to eat too much of this stuff.

setting: Office hallway
situation: Dilbert meets a bald, bespectacled coworker whose shirt is torn and shredded. The coworker explains that a miserable colleague named Floyd takes out his job hatred on others by chewing at their clothes. He escaped because the synthetic fabric made Floyd sick.
punchline: The coworker survived a clothes-eating attack only because his cheap synthetic shirt was too unhealthy for Floyd to keep chewing.
summary: A ragged employee recounts how a disgruntled colleague nearly devoured his outfit until the fabric itself drove the attacker off.

title: Dogbert the Market-Crashing Space Alien

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: As my antennae clearly prove, I'm a space alien with incredible powers.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert (on TV)
transcript.text: I call on the nations of the world to surrender. Otherwise, I will cause your stock markets to fall.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Later

transcript.speaker: TV Announcer
transcript.text: The market fell five points today. Analysts blame interest rates and aliens.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Yes!

setting: A TV news interview, then Dilbert's living room watching television
situation: Dogbert, wearing antennae, tells a TV news crew he is a space alien with incredible powers and threatens to make stock markets fall unless nations surrender. Dilbert watches the broadcast at home, and later the news reports a five-point market drop, blaming interest rates and aliens. Dogbert celebrates as if his threat caused it.
punchline: Dogbert claims credit for an ordinary market drop that analysts partly blame on aliens, showing how easily a bluff can look like real power.
summary: A dog in antennae threatens the world's markets on live television and then gleefully takes credit when they dip.

title: Dogbert's Insulting Model Evaluation Service

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Excuse me, would you like to take advantage of our "Model Evaluation Service"? Only ten dollars.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Me? Gosh, I've never thought of myself that way. Yes, I would love to be evaluated.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You're hideous... That's ten dollars.

setting: A city sidewalk
situation: Dogbert stops a woman walking along the sidewalk and offers a ten-dollar 'Model Evaluation Service.' Flattered, she eagerly agrees to be evaluated as a potential model. Dogbert bluntly tells her she is hideous and then demands payment.
punchline: Dogbert profits by selling a service whose honest result is a brutal insult, and the flattered customer still has to pay for it.
summary: A canine street hustler charges a delighted stranger for an appraisal that turns out to be a cruel one-word verdict.

title: Quality Program Turns Employees Into Zombies

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Quality... Quality... Quality...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's working. All the employees are brainwashed.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've done it! I've transformed the very fabric of the corporate culture!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Things sure have changed around here.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Yeah, for example, my arms are tired.

setting: Office hallway and workplace
situation: Employees walk through the office with arms stretched out in front of them like zombies, chanting 'Quality' after a company quality initiative. The Boss smugly thinks the employees are brainwashed and celebrates transforming the corporate culture. Dilbert remarks that things have changed, and Wally replies that his arms are tired.
punchline: The Boss's grand 'cultural transformation' has only produced mindless zombie-walking and sore arms, mocking quality programs that change employee behavior superficially without any real benefit.
summary: After a quality drive turns the staff into outstretched-arm chanting zombies, the boss gloats about his triumph while the only noticeable change is fatigue.

title: Dogbert Teaches Scissor Safety Badly

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert's School of Common Sense.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Todd, show the class how you hand these scissors to Russell.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Don't run! Don't run!

transcript.speaker: Russell
transcript.text: Aaagh!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Sorry, Russell. It's the teacher's fault; he didn't even ask if I need left-handed scissors.

setting: Dogbert's School of Common Sense classroom
situation: Dogbert, acting as a teacher, asks a student named Todd to demonstrate handing scissors to Russell. Todd apparently runs with the scissors and Russell falls, leaving only his legs sticking up. Todd then offers an excuse that blames the teacher for not asking whether he needed left-handed scissors.
punchline: A lesson meant to teach common sense ends in a scissors accident, and the student responds by shifting blame onto the teacher with an absurd excuse.
summary: A scissor-handling demonstration at a school for common sense goes horribly wrong, followed by a comically misplaced excuse.

title: Flight Attendant's Cannibalism Safety Briefing

transcript.speaker: Flight Attendant (off-panel)
transcript.text: This will be our most memorable vacation yet.

transcript.speaker: Flight Attendant
transcript.text: ... and in the event of a snowy mountainside crash, the young and feeble passengers are completely edible.

transcript.speaker: Flight Attendant (off-panel)
transcript.text: But Captain Bob promises he won't make that mistake again.

setting: Inside a passenger airplane, then an exterior view of planes near a snowy mountain
situation: Dilbert sits in an airplane seat wearing a life vest while the flight attendant gives a cheerful safety announcement. She casually explains that in a mountainside crash the young and feeble passengers can be eaten. The final panel shows several crashed planes on a mountain, implying the pilot has crashed before.
punchline: The safety briefing cheerfully reveals that the pilot has a history of crashing into mountains, and that the airline's survival plan is cannibalism.
summary: A chirpy in-flight announcement turns grim when passengers learn the plane's pilot has previously crashed into mountains and that survivors may need to eat each other.

title: Dogbert Debates Beer Commercial Feminist

transcript.speaker: Larry King
transcript.text: Tonight on "Larry King Live" we have a dog who makes sexy beer commercials, plus an angry feminist.

transcript.speaker: Feminist
transcript.text: His commercials encourage discrimination against women by portraying us all as sex objects.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Are you saying men are so dumb, they get their views on life from beer commercials?

transcript.speaker: Feminist
transcript.text: I call them like I see them.

setting: A television talk show studio
situation: A talk show host introduces Dogbert, who makes sexy beer commercials, and an angry feminist as his guests. The feminist accuses Dogbert's commercials of encouraging discrimination by portraying women as sex objects. Dogbert counters that her complaint implies men are so dumb they take their views on life from beer ads.
punchline: The feminist's own argument forces her to admit that men are dumb enough to be shaped by beer commercials, so her reply of 'I call them like I see them' confirms Dogbert's insult.
summary: A talk show guest accuses a dog's beer ads of demeaning women, but his clever rebuttal turns her argument into an admission that men are gullible.

title: Dilbert Applies For A Date

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Here are the flowers and the non-refundable date deposit.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This diskette has my dating history, personal references, and full financial disclosure.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When may I expect the rejection notice?

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I can give you a verbal now...

setting: A woman's doorway at her home
situation: Dilbert arrives at a woman's door and hands her flowers, a non-refundable date deposit, and a diskette containing his dating history, references and finances, as if applying for a job. He then asks when he can expect her rejection notice, and she says she can give him a verbal rejection right away.
punchline: Dilbert treats a date like a bureaucratic application process, so the woman bluntly rejects him on the spot, sparing him the formal paperwork.
summary: A painfully awkward man approaches a first date like a formal application, only to be turned down at the door.

title: Combing Ear Hair Over Bald Head

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm feeling confident today with what appears to be a full head of hair.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Nobody suspects that I'm actually combing the hair that grows in my ears over the top of my otherwise bald head.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's amazing how clueless these people are.

setting: Conference room during a meeting
situation: The Boss sits at a conference table with two coworkers and thinks to himself, in thought bubbles, about his confidence in his apparently full head of hair. He reveals that the hair is really ear hair combed over his bald head. He then smugly concludes that everyone around him is clueless.
punchline: The Boss thinks his coworkers are clueless for not noticing his ear-hair comb-over, when the obviously fake hairdo is almost certainly fooling no one and he is the clueless one.
summary: A smug manager privately congratulates himself on a disguise that is almost certainly obvious to everyone at the table.

title: Dogbert's Dating Statistics Advice

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I have a solution for your dating dilemma.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: At your age there are more single men than single women.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Worse yet, all of the single women are dating married men or serial killers.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: But the statistics eventually favor men.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Really? How?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: At age 80 there are three times as many available women as men because men die younger.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you saying I should wait until I'm old... and date 80-year-old women?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: No. I wouldn't wait...

setting: Dilbert's workspace at his computer
situation: Dogbert offers Dilbert a solution to his dating problems and lays out gloomy statistics about single men and women. He explains that the odds only improve for men around age 80, when women outnumber men. Dilbert asks if he should wait that long, and Dogbert says he wouldn't.
punchline: Dogbert's 'solution' is to wait until age 80 for better odds, and then he undercuts even that by admitting he wouldn't wait, implying Dilbert's situation is basically hopeless.
summary: A dog offers his lonely owner a statistical remedy for his love life that turns out to be decades away and not even worth the wait.

title: Rat Choking on Carrot Hoax

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Hey, Dogbert, everybody is talking about you at the lab.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Really?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: The "cow and egg" industry is going to discredit your vegetarian movement. They paid us to prove meat is healthy.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What's your role?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I play the rat who ironically chokes to death on a carrot during the news conference.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Great... I'll have to see that on CNN about a jillion times.

setting: Outdoor path beside a grassy hedge
situation: Ratbert, a lab rat, tells Dogbert that the cow and egg industry has hired the lab to discredit Dogbert's vegetarian movement by proving meat is healthy. Dogbert asks what Ratbert's part is, and Ratbert explains he will stage a death by choking on a carrot at a news conference.
punchline: The industry-funded smear campaign relies on a staged, ironic carrot-choking death of a lab rat, and Dogbert sarcastically anticipates it being replayed endlessly on the news.
summary: A lab rat reveals he has been hired to fake a vegetable-related death as part of a meat industry plot against a vegetarian cause.

title: Dogbert Sells Saint Ted Peanut Butter

transcript.speaker: Reporter
transcript.text: People have traveled from all over to see the miracle of the peanut butter.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Step right up... just ten bucks to see the face of Saint Ted appearing in my jar of peanut butter.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Ooh! And I see Elvis in the Jello!

transcript.speaker: Man in cap
transcript.text: Only the King moves like that!

setting: Outdoor roadside attraction, then a kitchen with an open refrigerator
situation: A TV reporter announces that crowds have traveled to witness a miracle in a jar of peanut butter. Dogbert stands on a ten-dollar pedestal, taking cash from eager customers to see the supposed face of Saint Ted. In the last panel, a couple at home find Elvis in the Jello in their own refrigerator.
punchline: People are so gullible about supposed miracles that Dogbert profits from a jar of peanut butter, and the craze spreads to people seeing Elvis in their own Jello.
summary: A con-artist dog charges admission to a supposedly holy jar of peanut butter while the public's miracle-spotting mania spills into home refrigerators.

title: Friday Is Your Day in the Well

transcript.speaker: Marketing Guy
transcript.text: When you work in marketing, you use the research well to test new ideas.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Guy
transcript.text: Any day but Friday you can shout your question into the well and an answer will come back.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why not Friday?

transcript.speaker: Marketing Guy
transcript.text: Friday is your day in the well.

setting: Outdoors beside a stone well, in a marketing department's 'research' area
situation: A robed, laurel-wreathed marketing employee shows Dilbert the 'research well' that marketing uses to test new ideas by shouting questions into it. Dilbert leans over the well and asks why this doesn't work on Fridays. The marketer reveals that Friday is when the employee takes a turn being in the well.
punchline: Marketing's 'research' is just people hiding in a well giving answers, and Dilbert has been volunteered to be the one down there on Fridays.
summary: A marketer proudly introduces a literal well as the department's research tool, only to reveal that the newcomer must play the voice inside it once a week.

title: Dogbert's Lawyer Calls Dilbert Ugly

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert sues Dilbert for petimony

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can't we handle this amicably, without lawyers?

transcript.speaker: Lawyer
transcript.text: I've been advised that you're ugly.

setting: A conference table in a legal negotiation or deposition room
situation: Dogbert is suing Dilbert for 'petimony,' a pet version of alimony. Dilbert asks if they can settle things amicably without involving lawyers, but Dogbert's lawyer, in the middle panel, contemplates quietly with his hand on Dogbert's head, then responds with a petty insult about Dilbert's looks.
punchline: Dilbert's plea for an amicable settlement is met with a ridiculous, non-legal personal insult, showing that lawyers escalate conflicts rather than resolve them.
summary: A man trying to avoid a lawsuit from his dog is rebuffed when the dog's attorney simply insults his appearance.

title: Dilbert Seeks Cosmic Joy, Finds Stubble

transcript.speaker: Guru
transcript.text: You must renounce all physical pleasure before you can achieve true cosmic joy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Renounce it?! Heck, I don't think I've ever had a physical pleasure!

transcript.speaker: Guru
transcript.text: And you must shave your head...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Oh, I get it; then you can rub the little stubble as it grows in!

setting: A spiritual guru's meditation space, with Dilbert seated before him on a mat
situation: A robed, flower-garlanded guru sits cross-legged and tells Dilbert he must renounce all physical pleasure to reach cosmic joy. Dilbert protests that he has never had any physical pleasure to give up. When the guru adds that he must shave his head, Dilbert cheerfully concludes the point is to enjoy rubbing the growing stubble.
punchline: Dilbert is so starved of pleasure that he turns the guru's ascetic requirement of a shaved head into a newfound physical pleasure, defeating the whole purpose of renunciation.
summary: A holy man demands total abstinence from earthly delights, but a pleasure-deprived engineer finds a loophole in the haircut rule.

title: Dogbert's Smear Campaign Revealed

transcript.speaker: TV Announcer
transcript.text: The Canine Tax Rebate Bill was passed by Congress today.

transcript.speaker: TV Announcer
transcript.text: The bill's author, Mister Dogbert, successfully pinned the label "Dog Kicking Liberal" on all who opposed him.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Was that ethical?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Tha-a-at's it. You're on the list.

setting: Dilbert's living room, watching television
situation: Dilbert relaxes in an armchair watching a news report saying Congress passed a bill written by Dogbert, who defeated his opponents by branding them "dog kicking liberals." Dilbert asks whether that tactic was ethical, and Dogbert responds by adding him to his enemies list.
punchline: Dogbert answers a question about ethics by retaliating against the questioner, proving the smear tactics were exactly as unethical as implied.
summary: After a news story reveals Dogbert won legislative support through name-calling, Dilbert's mild objection earns him a spot on the dog's list of enemies.

title: Practicing a Victory Celebration Pose

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What happened?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Nothing. I'm just practicing in case something good ever happens to me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll yell "Yes!" and pump my arms in a distinctive way.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now I'm working on incorporating this spinning motion.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes!!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It looks like you've got the "distinctive" part down.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes!

setting: Dilbert's home, indoors and then the backyard
situation: Dogbert is relaxing on a mat listening to music when Dilbert suddenly shouts "Yes!" Dilbert explains he is rehearsing a victory celebration for if something good ever happens to him, and adds a spinning kick to his arm-pumping. The move sends him out a second-story window, and he lands face-down on the lawn.
punchline: Dilbert's rehearsed celebration for a good event that never comes ends in a painful fall, and Dogbert sarcastically notes that the move is certainly distinctive, while Dilbert, flat on the ground, still yells "Yes!"
summary: A man rehearses an elaborate victory dance for a future triumph and accidentally tumbles out a window, proving his own bad luck.

title: Dilbert Predicts Dogbert's Anger

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm using my new supercomputer to create a model that can predict your entire life.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You see, everything, including your brain chemistry, is subject to predictable patterns of cause and effect...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That's ridiculous. It implies that we have no free will.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Next, you start getting really mad at me.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle with a supercomputer cabinet
situation: Dilbert sits at his computer next to a large supercomputer and tells Dogbert he is building a model to predict Dogbert's whole life. He explains that brain chemistry follows predictable cause and effect. When Dogbert objects that this denies free will, Dilbert calmly says Dogbert's next step is to get really mad at him.
punchline: Dogbert's indignant objection to the idea of determinism is exactly the reaction Dilbert predicted, which supports his point that behavior is predictable and free will may be an illusion.
summary: A man with a powerful computer claims human behavior is predictable, and his dog's outraged denial turns out to be part of the forecast.

title: Dilbert's Best Account Attacks Him

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: So... Dilbert, welcome to the Sales Department. I'm Tina, your new boss.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hi

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: As the new guy, you get the customers who despise our products and want to hurt us personally.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: I hate you! I hate you!

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: You'll be selling to the small business market. He's your best account.

setting: Sales department office
situation: Dilbert is welcomed to the sales department by his new boss Tina, who explains that as the newest salesperson he gets the customers who hate the company's products. In the last panel an angry small business customer is already physically attacking Dilbert, grabbing him and screaming that he hates him, while Tina calmly calls him Dilbert's best account.
punchline: Tina describes a customer violently assaulting Dilbert as his best account, implying that the rest of his sales territory is even worse.
summary: A new salesperson is handed the company's most hostile clients, and the first one is already throttling him while his cheerful manager looks on.

title: Diplomat Dilbert Insults Elbonian Proverb

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: You crushed our leader. Now you must be the new rebel leader.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm a diplomat, on a peace mission.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: A wise Elbonian once said "In a race between a rock and a pig, don't varnish your clams."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's stupid.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: What kind of diplomat are you??

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: First day on the job... gimme a break.

setting: Barren hillside in Elbonia
situation: Dilbert arrives in Elbonia carrying a suitcase, having accidentally flattened the rebel leader. The Elbonians declare he must now lead their rebellion, but he insists he is a diplomat on a peace mission. When an Elbonian offers a nonsensical proverb, Dilbert bluntly calls it stupid and then excuses his poor diplomacy as first-day inexperience.
punchline: A supposed diplomat immediately insults the locals' nonsensical wisdom and then pleads that it's his first day on the job.
summary: A rookie envoy to a foreign land fails at tact within seconds of meeting the locals and asks for leniency.

title: Hair in Soup Lab Scam

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Waiter, there's a hair in my soup.

transcript.speaker: Waiter
transcript.text: It looks like one of yours. I'm sure it wasn't there when I served it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It is NOT one of mine!

transcript.speaker: Waiter
transcript.text: Sir! You insult my integrity!

transcript.speaker: Waiter
transcript.text: I shall send the hair to our lab for analysis.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Fair enough.

transcript.speaker: Waiter
transcript.text: They'll need a clump of your hair for comparison.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ouch!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You have to be tough with these waiters or else they'll walk all over you.

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: Does it seem odd to you that the restaurant has its own lab?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They must have a lot of problems with hairy food.

transcript.speaker: Waiter
transcript.text: The lab says they need a few more clumps of your hair...

setting: Upscale restaurant dinner table
situation: Dilbert, on a date, complains to a waiter about a hair in his soup. The waiter blames Dilbert's own hair, takes offense, and offers to send the hair to the restaurant's lab, yanking out a clump of Dilbert's hair for comparison. Dilbert naively accepts it, and the waiter keeps returning for more clumps.
punchline: Dilbert obliviously falls for an obvious scam, believing the restaurant has a legitimate lab while the waiter simply keeps pulling out his hair.
summary: A gullible diner lets a waiter pluck his hair again and again for supposed lab testing after finding a strand in his soup.

title: Hairy Dilbert Fears Midlife Crisis

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Things have been strange since the mishap with my hair growth formula.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have a strong urge to buy sunglasses and drive a Porsche...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And I worry that people won't take me seriously.

setting: A therapist's office
situation: Dilbert lies on a therapist's couch, his face and body covered in thick, spiky hair after a mishap with a hair growth formula. He confesses that he now wants sunglasses and a Porsche, and fears that nobody will take him seriously. The therapist scribbles notes, and her notepad shows a doodle labelled 'hair'.
punchline: The hair-growth mishap has given Dilbert the hairy look and urges of a stereotypical midlife-crisis man, and his worry about not being taken seriously is itself a symptom of that cliché.
summary: A bristly, hair-covered Dilbert tells his therapist that his bad hair experiment has left him craving flashy midlife-crisis accessories.

title: Dogbert Installs Guilt Module in Robot

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: We need to do something about your total lack of ethics and social conscience.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I had Dilbert build this guilt module for your control board. It has the synthesized shame of every major belief system.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Later

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Frankly, I liked him better before.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: I am unworthy to roll in your spittle.

setting: Dogbert's lair and Dilbert's cubicle
situation: Dogbert tells his robot minion that it lacks ethics and a social conscience, then fits it with a guilt module Dilbert built, containing the shame of every major belief system. Later the robot is crushed by guilt and grovels, saying it is unworthy to roll in Dogbert's spittle, while Dogbert tells Dilbert he preferred the robot before.
punchline: Dogbert's attempt to give his robot a conscience backfires, leaving it so overwhelmed by guilt that it becomes pathetically self-abasing, and Dogbert realizes he preferred the amoral version.
summary: A scheming dog upgrades his robot with a dose of moral shame and quickly regrets how whiny and servile it becomes.

title: Dilbert Dismisses Date's Choking Fit

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: Mphf! Aack! Cough! Hmp! Gurgle!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If you're pretending to choke to death to end our date early, it won't work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Like I haven't seen that trick a jillion times.

setting: A restaurant table during a date
situation: Dilbert is on a dinner date when the woman across from him starts coughing and gagging. Dilbert calmly accuses her of faking a choking fit to escape the date early. She slumps onto the table, and then sits up again, arms crossed and scowling, as he claims to have seen the trick many times.
punchline: Dilbert is so used to dates trying to flee that he mistakes a real choking emergency for an excuse, and his boast about seeing the trick a jillion times shows how often his dates have bailed on him.
summary: A man brushes off his date's apparent choking as a ploy to cut the evening short, boasting that he has seen every escape trick before.

title: Dogbert Recruits Inept Running Mate

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Ratbert, I'm looking for a vice president for my ticket.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I need somebody who is so inept and simple-minded that I always look good in comparison.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I don't understand.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Okay, okay, you've got the job.

setting: Outdoor dirt path beside a grassy field
situation: Dogbert walks with Ratbert and tells him he is searching for a vice president to join his election ticket. summary: A sanitation worker reads Dilbert's crumpled notes from the trash and expertly diagnoses the mistake in his quantum invention.

summary: An image-obsessed junior manager turns down a simple lunch invitation to protect his career prospects, leaving Dilbert dismayed that such a person is destined to lead him.

summary: A meeting with no purpose kicks off with a rant about how meetings leave no time for real work.

punchline: The invention works so well that Dilbert is now hairy all over, a result of testing it carelessly on his whole body rather than a small patch of scalp.
summary: An inventor's miracle hair tonic succeeds, but a sloppy test leaves him bristling with hair from head to toe.

punchline: Dilbert follows absurd advice just because it came from someone wearing a chef's hat, and Dogbert only clarifies the instructions after the whole pot of spaghetti has been thrown at the wall.

summary: A worker driven to incoherence by overwork is rewarded by management with a promotion, though he may be too addled to notice.
