transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Stay back, I've got a compass!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wireless fax!

transcript.speaker: Unknown
transcript.text: Aagh!

setting: Office
situation: Dilbert, wearing a belt loaded with gadgets, mocks Wally for owning only a pager and a calculator watch and demands that Wally yield to his technical superiority. A narrator then describes the confrontation as a nature-documentary-style ritual battle between male engineers, which plays out as the two shouting gadget names at each other.
punchline: Engineers' fight for pack dominance is a pathetic, nerdy showdown where the weapons are gadgets and the 'attacks' are shouted product features.
summary: Two coworkers settle a status contest by brandishing their gadgets like animals in a wildlife documentary.

title: Doctor Dogbert's Ambassador Class Healthcare

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You have a mild flu, and normally you would survive.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: However, in this brief visit I've developed no real empathy for you, so I've decided to let you die.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Is there anything I can do?!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Well... unless you can afford my new "Ambassador Class" service.

setting: A hospital or doctor's examination room
situation: Dogbert, acting as a doctor, tells a patient in a hospital gown that he only has a mild flu but that he has decided to let him die because he feels no empathy for him. When the desperate patient asks if there is anything he can do, Dogbert reveals that a premium paid service tier could save him.
punchline: Dogbert manufactures a life-threatening situation in order to upsell a premium 'Ambassador Class' service, mocking pay-for-better-care healthcare and tiered customer service.
summary: A cynical canine physician threatens to withhold treatment from a flu patient until he is offered a pricey upgrade package.

title: Insider Trader Sentenced to Biography

transcript.speaker: Judge
transcript.text: I find you guilty of stealing millions in an insider trading scheme.

transcript.speaker: Judge
transcript.text: Let's see... according to my sliding scale of justice, the punishment at your income is... Hmm...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm sentenced to be the subject of a Kitty Kelly biography.

setting: A courtroom
situation: A judge in a courtroom finds Dogbert guilty of stealing millions through insider trading. The judge consults a sheet of paper to look up the sentence on his 'sliding scale of justice' based on the defendant's income. Dogbert then announces that his punishment is to be the subject of a Kitty Kelley biography, while Dilbert sits nearby.
punchline: The wealthy criminal's sentence is not prison or a fine but a gossipy, unflattering celebrity biography, mocking how justice is lenient on the rich and how such biographies are treated as a punishment.
summary: A judge hands a rich financial criminal an absurdly light sentence that amounts to having his life story written by a notorious tabloid biographer.

title: Too Prepared With Career Graph

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...Therefore, I recommend that we switch to the new technology... Any questions?

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Dilbert, are you willing to bet your career on this?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes, I would definitely bet my career.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You would too if you had my career.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have a view graph which anticipated your question.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This chart tracks my declining sense of self-worth as my career progresses.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: At the low-point, here, I'm reduced to answering imbecilic questions while pointing a little stick at the wall.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: How did the presentation go?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There's such a thing as being too prepared.

setting: Conference room during a presentation, then Dilbert's home
situation: Dilbert presents a recommendation to switch to new technology and is asked by a panel whether he'd bet his career on it. He responds with sarcasm, then pulls out a view graph charting his declining self-worth, which ends at the point he's answering dumb questions with a pointer. Afterward Dogbert asks how it went.
punchline: Dilbert prepared a chart anticipating the insulting question, using it to lay bare how his career has demoralized him, which proves he overdid the preparation.
summary: A presenter answers a loaded question about risking his career by unveiling a graph of his own plummeting self-esteem.

title: Boss Channels Bozo the Clown

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Uh... Dilbert, about that assignment I gave you last month...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Remember how you thought it was a silly and ridiculous assignment?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yeah?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well, it turns out that I've been spontaneously channeling the spirit of Bozo the Clown.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle
situation: The Boss approaches Dilbert's cubicle to revisit an assignment he gave a month earlier. He reminds Dilbert that Dilbert thought it was silly and ridiculous, then reveals, now dressed as a clown with a red nose and a polka-dot tie, that he was apparently channeling Bozo the Clown when he made it.
punchline: The Boss's absurd, supernatural excuse for a bad assignment shows him dodging responsibility for his poor judgment while admitting Dilbert was right.
summary: A manager sheepishly confirms his employee's suspicions about a foolish task by blaming it on an unexplained clown spirit that took over his mind.

title: Leading a Revolution of Vegetarians

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Vegetarians, we must march to the Capitol to protest the killing of animals!

transcript.speaker: Vegetarian 1
transcript.text: That's a mile away.

transcript.speaker: Vegetarian 2
transcript.text: Can we drive instead?

transcript.speaker: Vegetarian 3
transcript.text: Or maybe write letters?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Never lead a revolution of people who only own plastic and wooden shoes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I try to avoid it.

setting: A meeting hall for a vegetarian group, then Dilbert's living room
situation: Dogbert, standing on a stool, rallies a group of vegetarians to march to the Capitol and protest animal killing. The audience immediately objects that the march is too far and suggests driving or writing letters instead. Afterward Dogbert tells Dilbert, who is reading a newspaper, a lesson learned about leading such a group.
punchline: Vegetarians who avoid leather and wear only plastic and wooden shoes are too impractical or soft to follow through on a physical protest march, which makes them hopeless revolutionaries.
summary: A would-be revolutionary dog discovers his vegetarian followers would rather drive or write letters than walk a single mile.

title: Hairy Dilbert Fears Bigfoot Hunters

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've been so depressed since the fiasco with the hair growth formula.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hope nobody thinks I'm Bigfoot and tries to shoot me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You know, "Hair today, gun tomorrow." Heh-heh-heh.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm thinking about shooting you myself.

setting: Dogbert's office or therapy setting, with Dilbert reclining in an armchair
situation: Dilbert, now covered in hair from a failed hair growth formula, lounges in an armchair and laments his depression to Dogbert. He worries that hunters might mistake him for Bigfoot, then makes a pun about it. Dogbert, tired of the joke, deadpans that he is considering shooting Dilbert himself.
punchline: Dilbert's terrible pun "hair today, gun tomorrow" is so bad that Dogbert threatens to shoot him, which fulfills the very fear Dilbert just voiced.
summary: After a hair-growth experiment leaves him resembling a sasquatch, a gloomy Dilbert cracks a groan-worthy pun that nearly drives his listener to violence.

title: Video Phone Dating Filter Backfires

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This video phone will be a big help for dating.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This way I can weed out the unattractive prospects in seconds.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Isn't there a camera on your end too?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No system is perfect.

setting: Dilbert's office desk with a video phone
situation: Dilbert is excited about his new video phone and explains that it will let him quickly screen out unattractive dating prospects. Dogbert points out that the prospects can see him too through a camera on his end. Dilbert, facing away, concedes that the system has a flaw.
punchline: Dilbert's plan to judge others' looks overlooks that he would be judged too, and his weak admission that no system is perfect implicitly acknowledges he wouldn't pass his own test.
summary: A man hopes new video technology will let him reject unattractive dates instantly, until his dog notes that the same technology lets them see him.

title: Saliva-Soaked Binder Pages Stick Together

transcript.speaker: Bearded Coworker
transcript.text: Let me show you where the information is in your binder.

transcript.speaker: Bearded Coworker
transcript.text: First, I'll need a good load of saliva on my page-turning hand.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Slurp slurp

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe you can show me in your binder.

transcript.speaker: Bearded Coworker
transcript.text: Can't... somehow my pages got all stuck together.

setting: Office desk, sitting over open binders
situation: A bearded coworker offers to show Dilbert where information is in Dilbert's binder. He first licks his fingers to turn pages, and Dilbert, disgusted, asks to be shown in the coworker's own binder instead. The coworker then admits his own pages have stuck together, presumably from his saliva.
punchline: Dilbert tries to avoid the coworker's germ-laden, saliva-coated hand touching his binder, but the coworker's own binder is ruined by his habit, so the unhygienic approach backfires.
summary: A colleague's gross habit of licking his fingers to flip pages makes Dilbert recoil, only to find the man's own documents are glued shut by the practice.

title: Ratbert's Hate Book Disguised as Science

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I'm following in your footsteps so I can be a demagogue too.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Your book "Unmarried Men Are Scum" was so successful that I decided to write my own hate book disguised as science!

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I call it "Moles Are Morons."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Were you aware that moles have a strong underground movement?

setting: Dogbert's home, in front of his armchair
situation: Ratbert tells Dogbert he wants to follow his example and become a demagogue, having been inspired by Dogbert's successful hate book. He announces his own pseudo-scientific hate book, "Moles Are Morons." Behind him, a group of moles wearing sunglasses has appeared, and Dogbert warns him they are well organized.
punchline: Ratbert's hate book targets a group that turns out to be an organized, dangerous underground movement, with the pun on "underground" implying he is about to be in trouble.
summary: A copycat rodent pens a bigoted pseudo-science book about moles, only to learn his targets have an underground network and are lurking right behind him.

title: Dogbert's Seminar on Faking Sensitivity

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Today's lesson is just for men.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Lights please.

transcript.speaker: Slide
transcript.text: Acting sensitive even when you're not

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Click

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: As males, we know that women can only tolerate us when we act phony.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: This is what happens when a woman is subjected to honest male opinions.

transcript.speaker: Woman on slide
transcript.text: Aaagh!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Click

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Fortunately, even the most ridiculous lies can sound sensitive.

transcript.speaker: Man on slide
transcript.text: Nice hairdo.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And new research shows that women want empathy in conversation, not male suggestions.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: This discovery frees you to think about other things while they talk.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Click

transcript.speaker: Man on slide (thought)
transcript.text: Sports

transcript.speaker: Man on slide
transcript.text: Ooh... how sad

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Questions?

setting: A darkened lecture room with a projector screen
situation: Dogbert gives a slide presentation to an audience of men about how to get along with women. He explains that honest opinions upset women, that fake compliments sound sensitive, and that women only want empathy, so men can safely daydream while pretending to listen. The final slide shows a man thinking about sports while saying a sympathetic phrase to a woman.
punchline: Dogbert's cynical advice reduces male sensitivity to a sham: nod and say sympathetic things while secretly thinking about sports.
summary: A lecturing dog teaches men to fake caring conversation while their minds wander to athletics.

title: Dogbert's Poll Shows Zero Fame

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: The poll results are in.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: You still have low name-recognition outside of the living room... But some guy in the kitchen thinks he's heard of you.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Don't be discouraged, uh... uh...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Dogbert!

setting: Living room at Dilbert's home
situation: Ratbert reports poll results to Dogbert, who is sitting in an armchair. He explains that Dogbert's name recognition is limited to the living room, with only one vague mention from someone in the kitchen. While trying to console him, Ratbert can't remember Dogbert's name, and Dogbert has to supply it himself.
punchline: The pollster trying to encourage Dogbert about his name recognition forgets Dogbert's name, proving how obscure he really is.
summary: A tiny pollster delivers dismal fame statistics to a dog and then undercuts his own consolation by blanking on the dog's name.

title: Boss Bores Staff With Cliches

transcript.speaker: The Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Nothing ventured, nothing gained. If you're not part of the solution you're part of the problem.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How can we use our strengths against our competitors' weaknesses?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We could bore them to death with your clichés.

setting: Office meeting room
situation: The Boss addresses his team at a meeting, reeling off one empty business platitude after another. When he asks how the company can use its strengths against competitors' weaknesses, Dilbert answers that they could bore the competition to death with the Boss's clichés.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically points out that the Boss's endless stream of meaningless clichés is the only 'strength' the company has, and that it is tedious enough to kill.
summary: A manager spouts hollow motivational slogans until an employee suggests his speeches themselves could be used as a weapon against rivals.

title: Supreme Ruler Embraces Moral Corruption

transcript.speaker: Reporter
transcript.text: Now that you're the supreme ruler of Earth, will you become morally corrupt?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Yes, that's my plan. It's really the only way to enjoy a job like this.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And of course I'll be raising taxes just to see the expressions on your faces.

setting: A press conference with a podium and microphone
situation: Dogbert, now the supreme ruler of Earth, stands at a podium while reporters question him. Asked whether power will morally corrupt him, he cheerfully admits that is his plan. He then adds that he will raise taxes purely to enjoy the reporters' reactions.
punchline: Dogbert openly admits that corruption is the only perk of ruling, and that he will raise taxes purely for amusement, showing the absurdity of power without accountability.
summary: A newly crowned world leader cheerfully confirms to the press that abusing his power is the whole appeal of the job.

title: Dilbert's House Becomes Dogbert's Jail

transcript.text: Dogbert's jail for the rich and famous

transcript.speaker: Inmate
transcript.text: Man, you're the wrong guy to talk to during "happy hour."

setting: Dilbert's house, converted into a jail
situation: A caption reveals Dogbert's jail for the rich and famous. A wealthy inmate in a bathrobe holding a cocktail asks Dilbert what he is in for. Dilbert explains he actually lives there and that his dog turned his house into a for-profit jail without asking, and the inmate brushes him off as the wrong person to chat with during happy hour.
punchline: Dilbert's genuine complaint is dismissed because the inmate treats him as a downer interrupting cocktail hour, and Dogbert has quietly profited from seizing Dilbert's home.
summary: A man's pet turns his home into a profit-making prison for celebrities, and the pampered inmates just want to enjoy their drinks rather than hear his grievance.

title: Dogbert's Late Time Management Lecture

transcript.text: Sorry I'm an hour late, but I was giving another lecture across town... In effect, I'll complete two jobs while you sit in the dark like stunned cattle.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I don't mean to rub it in, but moooo...

setting: Darkened lecture hall with a stage
situation: Dogbert, holding a microphone on a stage, opens his time management lecture series but shows up an hour late. He explains he was giving another lecture across town, so he effectively completed two jobs while the audience waited in the dark. He then mocks the audience by mooing at them.
punchline: The supposed time management expert is unapologetically late, exploits his audience's wasted time as proof of his efficiency, and insults them by comparing them to cattle.
summary: A self-styled time expert keeps his audience waiting an hour, then boasts about his productivity and taunts them like livestock.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Stuff stuff

transcript.text: The best I can do is to make it quick.

transcript.speaker: Shirt
transcript.text: Aaagh!!

setting: Dilbert's laundry area at home, beside a washing machine
situation: Dilbert carries laundry to the washing machine, and a dress shirt with wildly elaborate washing instructions begins talking to him. As the shirt's demands get more absurd and it complains of being hurt, Dilbert grimly stuffs it into the machine anyway.
punchline: Dilbert ignores the shirt's impossible demands and its pleas, deciding the kindest option is to shove it in the washer and end its suffering quickly.
summary: A fussy garment's absurd care requirements and cries of pain are answered by its owner with a quick, merciless dunk into the washing machine.

title: Quality Notepads Misspelled Quality Initiative

transcript.text: That's why I've had these little note pads made that say "Quality."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Isn't it spelled with a "U"?

setting: Conference room during a meeting
situation: The Boss tells his team at a meeting that the company needs drastic changes to keep up with competitors. His answer is to hand out little notepads printed with the word "Quality." Dilbert points out that the word on the notepad is misspelled.
punchline: The Boss's idea of a drastic quality improvement is a gimmicky notepad, and the notepad itself shows poor quality because the word is spelled wrong.
summary: A manager answers the need for dramatic change with branded stationery, and an employee notices that the slogan on it is misspelled.

title: Dilbert Misreads Coworker's Monthly Friend

transcript.speaker: Alice

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's funny... I would think you'd be in a good mood if a friend were going to visit.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: She looked puffy, but she struck like a cobra.

setting: Conference room during a meeting, then a bandaged Dilbert next to Dogbert
situation: At a meeting table, Alice warns that her "friend" is about to visit, a euphemism for her menstrual cycle. Dilbert takes the word literally and wonders why she isn't cheerful about a friend coming over. In the last panel he is rumpled with a injured arm, telling Dogbert how Alice attacked him.
punchline: Dilbert's naive literal reading of a euphemism earns him a vicious attack from Alice, whom he compares to a cobra that looked harmless but struck.
summary: A clueless engineer takes a coworker's euphemism at face value, says so aloud, and ends up battered by her fury.

title: Boss Admits Transfer Is Just Teasing

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, you're being temporarily transferred to the field sales organization.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Normally we use these assignments to round somebody out for management. But in this case I'm just yanking your chain!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're over-communicating again, sir.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Plus, I hate the manager of sales.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he is being temporarily transferred to field sales. He explains that such assignments normally groom someone for management, but this time he is only toying with Dilbert. Dilbert says he is over-communicating, and the Boss adds that he also dislikes the sales manager.
punchline: The Boss cheerfully reveals that a major job transfer is merely a pointless prank, and then compounds it by disclosing a petty grudge, oversharing exactly as Dilbert says.
summary: A manager announces a staff reassignment, then gleefully confesses it is a gag and piles on an unrelated personal grudge.

title: Dogbert Defends Astrology, Dilbert Mocks Ancients

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's amazing that people believe in astrology... as if the stars could affect your personality.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Well, seasonal differences in diet, sunlight and natural rhythms could affect expectant mothers, which could have predictable results on fetal brain development.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Maybe the ancients simply used the stars to measure the timing of these patterns.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If they were so smart, why didn't they invent watches?

setting: Outdoors on a rocky hillside
situation: Dilbert and Dogbert are on a rocky outcrop. Dilbert scoffs that people believe in astrology, so Dogbert offers a plausible scientific explanation involving seasonal effects on fetal brain development, and suggests the ancients used stars as a calendar. Dilbert dismisses the idea by asking why such smart people never invented watches.
punchline: Dilbert dismisses a well-reasoned argument with a flippant, absurd retort, showing how people cling to their prejudices instead of engaging with evidence.
summary: A skeptic's scorn for astrology is met with a thoughtful scientific rationale, which he brushes aside with a glib question about watches.

title: Ratbert's Pathetic Toilet Paper Friend

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I've developed a plan to make you pity me and then welcome me in your family.

transcript.text: I built Timmy the toilet paper man. Timmy will be my only friend. It will be so pathetic and heart-rending that you will have to love me.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Dilbert seems to have very little respect for Timmy.

setting: Dilbert's home, near his computer desk
situation: Ratbert tells Dilbert, who is working at his computer, that he has a plan to win pity and a place in the family. He shows off Timmy, a toilet paper roll he built into a little man, as his only friend. In the last panel Timmy is a bare cardboard tube, with Dogbert sitting on a rug nearby, and Ratbert observes Dilbert's lack of respect for Timmy.
punchline: Ratbert's plan to be adorably pathetic with a toilet paper friend ends with Timmy used up and reduced to an empty cardboard tube, showing Dilbert used him for his intended purpose.
summary: A lonely lab rat builds a paper-roll companion to tug at heartstrings, only to find his creation put to its natural use.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Is the California drought my fault?

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Global warming?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert

transcript.text: Cows are destroying the Earth?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert

setting: A rocky, barren hilltop outdoors
situation: A guilt-ridden robot asks Dogbert whether it is responsible for heart attacks, the California drought, and global warming. Dogbert reassures it each time by blaming cows. When the robot finally asks if cows are destroying the Earth, Dogbert implies the cows are a coordinated force.
punchline: Dogbert's deadpan suggestion that cows are secretly organized turns the robot's anxiety into an absurd conspiracy theory about cattle.
summary: A worried robot keeps asking what it is guilty of, and Dogbert keeps pinning every global problem on cows until he hints at a bovine master plan.

title: Dogbert's Driving School Pen Problem

transcript.speaker: Customer

transcript.text: Uh oh.

setting: Dogbert's Driving School office
situation: A man who has failed his driving test nine times asks Dogbert for help. Dogbert, who runs the driving school, offers to take him on and tells him to sign the application form. The man then puzzles over how to use the pen, unable to remember what the pointy end is for, which makes Dogbert worry about his new student.
punchline: The student is so hopelessly inept that he can't figure out how a pen works, which shows why he failed the driving test nine times and makes Dogbert realize he has taken on a very difficult case.
summary: A serial driving-test failure signs up with Dogbert's school but cannot work out what the sharp end of a pen is for.

title: Boss Slams Employee's Head, Humor

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ha ha ha ha!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That loosened him up.

setting: Office cubicle
situation: The Boss stands behind Dilbert, who is working at his computer, and announces that he is using humor at work to ease tension and boost creativity. He then slams Dilbert's head down onto the desk while laughing. Dilbert is left dazed with his tongue hanging out, and the Boss thinks the prank worked.
punchline: The Boss's idea of workplace humor is a violent prank on his employee, and he cheerfully believes the dazed, concussed victim is now relaxed.
summary: A manager pledges to lighten the mood at work and then bangs an employee's head against his desk, pleased with the result.

title: Dogbert Hypnotizes Dilbert Into Drawing E.T.

situation: Dogbert, acting as a hypnotherapist, tells Dilbert, who is reclining in a chair, to draw the aliens that supposedly abducted him. Dogbert coaches him that they all look like E.T., and Dilbert wakes up amazed at his own drawing. Dogbert then ominously advises him to keep a bag packed because the aliens will return.
punchline: The hypnotist plants the answer in the patient's head, so the 'recovered memory' is just suggestion, and then Dogbert cynically scares him with a baseless warning.
summary: A dog therapist leads his hypnotized client to sketch a movie alien as his supposed abductor, then warns him to prepare for a return visit.

title: Water Draining on the Equator

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When you're north of the equator, water swirls clockwise down the drain . . .

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: South of the equator, it swirls counter-clockwise.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What's it do right on the equator?

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: On the equator

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Juan! It's just sitting there again!

setting: Outdoors on a grassy hill, then a kitchen on the equator
situation: Dilbert explains to Dogbert that water drains clockwise north of the equator and counter-clockwise south of it. Dogbert asks what happens exactly on the equator. The final panel shows a woman at a kitchen sink on the equator complaining to Juan that the water is just sitting there.
punchline: On the equator the water has no direction to swirl, so it just sits in the sink and doesn't drain at all.
summary: A science lesson about drain swirl direction ends with a household on the equator stuck with a sink that never empties.

title: Drawing Straws to Murder Floyd

transcript.speaker: Co-worker
transcript.text: Everybody pick a straw. The loser has to kill our abusive co-worker, Floyd.

transcript.speaker: Co-worker
transcript.text: Dilbert loses. He picked the blue straw.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I thought the short straw loses.

transcript.speaker: Co-worker
transcript.text: You're already a murderer; don't be a cheater too.

setting: Office, in front of green walls
situation: A group of co-workers, including Dilbert and Wally, hold a straw-drawing lottery to decide who must kill their abusive colleague Floyd. One co-worker announces that Dilbert lost because he picked the blue straw. Dilbert protests that the short straw is supposed to lose, and is told he is already a murderer so he shouldn't cheat as well.
punchline: The co-workers treat the murder as already decided and the only thing worth objecting to is bending the rules of the lottery, with Dilbert being declared guilty of murder before he has done anything.
summary: Office workers casually gamble over who will murder a nasty colleague, and the unlucky pick is scolded for disputing the rules.

title: Dogbert's Scribble Art Scam

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Another masterpiece.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What are you doing, Dogbert?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I discovered a highly efficient art form.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I've brilliantly combined the simplicity of charcoal with the simplicity of abstract expression.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The secret is to let your deepest inner feelings guide the charcoal.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Inner feelings?! What inner feelings? These are scribbles.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: All I see here is that a cynical dog thinks art buyers are a bunch of gullible morons.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Wow! I nailed that one!

setting: Dogbert's desk in an office
situation: Dogbert sits at a desk scribbling with charcoal and calls the results masterpieces. When Dilbert asks what he is doing, Dogbert pitches the scribbles as a profound abstract art form guided by inner feelings. Dilbert sees through it and says the drawing reveals Dogbert's contempt for art buyers.
punchline: Dogbert is delighted that Dilbert's insulting interpretation shows his scribbles conveyed exactly what he secretly meant, turning the critique into praise for his 'art'.
summary: A dog passes off random charcoal doodles as high art, and his friend's accusatory reading of them is taken as proof the piece worked.

title: Dilbert Lectures Elbonians on Civilization

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Elbonians hear me! You must end your futile civil war.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You've been loving your animals and fighting each other. A civilized country should slaughter the animals and simply discriminate economically against each other!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How did my speech go over?

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: I'm sold, but I think the Secretary of State was a bit put off.

setting: A muddy Elbonian village
situation: Dilbert stands in the mud before a crowd of Elbonians and urges them to end their civil war. He then advises them that civilized countries slaughter their animals and settle for economic discrimination against one another. Afterwards he asks an Elbonian how the speech went, and is told it went over fine except that the Secretary of State was offended.
punchline: Dilbert's idea of civilized conflict resolution is to replace violence with economic discrimination, and the pig-loving Elbonian Secretary of State is understandably insulted that he was told to slaughter his animals.
summary: A diplomatic visitor brings a warring muddy nation his idea of civilization, and it goes over about as well as you would expect.

title: Books Versus Television Debate Backfires

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You should read books instead of watching television all the time, Dogbert.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Why?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Books are more educational because they don't have any sound or pictures.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And books are challenging because it takes hours to read something that television could convey with one image.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And books make you think because they have more complex plots.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In fact, you can read entire books without even figuring out what the story was about.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now, compare all that with the junk you're watching.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I just watched the story of how DNA was discovered, then learned to bake a cake from scratch, and now I'm learning the causes of global warming.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What are you reading?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's called "The Poodle Who Killed."

setting: Dilbert's living room
situation: Dilbert lectures Dogbert, who is lounging on the couch with the TV remote, about how books are superior to television, listing absurd reasons that actually sound like drawbacks. Dogbert then points out all the useful things he has learned from TV, and asks what Dilbert is reading, which turns out to be a pulp novel.
punchline: Dilbert's arguments for books are really arguments against them, and Dogbert's TV viewing proves far more educational than Dilbert's trashy paperback.
summary: A man's sales pitch for reading over television collapses when his dog shows he learns more from the screen than the man does from his pulp novel.

title: Dogbert's Body Temperature Trough Consulting

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Every person has natural daily rhythms of mental peaks and troughs. We can use this knowledge to improve your performance.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: We use hourly body temperature readings to identify and avoid the troughs.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: One o'clock. We have encountered a severe trough. I fear it could be the dreaded "El Niño" trough.

setting: Office, consulting session with chairs
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, explains to the Boss that people have natural mental peaks and troughs and that hourly body temperature readings can help avoid the low points. He then takes the Boss's temperature with a thermometer in his mouth. Dogbert solemnly announces a severe trough at one o'clock while the Boss slumps back with the thermometer sticking out.
punchline: Dogbert dresses up a pointless, pseudo-scientific temperature routine with jargon, even naming the Boss's dull-wittedness after a weather phenomenon, to impress and bill a gullible client.
summary: A consultant dog pitches a body-temperature scheme for dodging mental slumps, then solemnly diagnoses his client with a weather-named trough.

title: Garbage Man's Negative Campaign Strategy

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The key to winning the election is voter turnout.

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: To be specific, you want everybody to stay home except you.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I've worked up a little ad campaign.

transcript.speaker: Poster
transcript.text: He touched the voting booth before you did.

transcript.speaker: Poster
transcript.text: And he never washes his hands

setting: Outdoors beside a garbage can, with a blue sky background
situation: Dogbert, sitting on a garbage can, tells a garbage man that voter turnout is the key to winning an election. The garbage man clarifies that the real goal is for everyone else to stay home. Dogbert then reveals a poster smearing the opposing candidate as a germ-ridden hand-washing slacker.
punchline: The candidate's real campaign strategy is voter suppression, using a fear-of-germs smear ad to discourage people from going to the polls.
summary: A scheming dog and a garbage man plot to win an election by scaring voters into staying away with a disgusting attack poster.

title: Parent License Written Test Fails

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: We'd better check it out.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Why do we need a license to become parents?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Something had to be done.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Under the old system all you needed to be a parent was a few body parts and a brain the size of a garbanzo bean.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: So I developed this written test to weed out the major bozos.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: If a baby cries, you should: A. Feed it B. Discipline it C. Call it "stupid"

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: You have to show it who's the boss.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: If a child gets poor grades you should: A. Tutor him B. Discipline him C. Call him "stupid."

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: What does "tutor" mean?

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: An acceptable nickname for a child is: A. Junior B. Ugly C. Stupid

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: Depends if it's a boy.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Well? Can we be parents?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: No. And you'll have to leave some body parts at the front desk.

setting: A government-style Parent Licenses office with Dogbert behind a desk
situation: A couple visits a Parent Licenses office run by Dogbert, who has created a written test to screen out unfit parents. The couple answers every question with the worst possible choice, such as disciplining a crying baby and picking 'stupid' as a nickname. Dogbert fails them.
punchline: The couple's wrong answers prove why licensing is needed, and Dogbert fails them and demands they surrender the very body parts that supposedly qualified them under the old system.
summary: Dogbert quizzes a clueless couple on child-rearing and rejects them after they give appalling answers to every question.

title: Tall Hair Fast-Track Manager Hire

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, I'd like you to meet Ben, our newest fast-track manager.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hi

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ben has no real experience but he's very tall, so we know he'll go far.

transcript.speaker: Ben
transcript.text: I also have executive style hair.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We think it will turn silver.

setting: Office
situation: The Boss introduces Dilbert to Ben, a new fast-track manager. He explains that Ben has no real experience but is very tall, so they expect him to go far. Ben adds that he has executive style hair, and the Boss says they expect it to turn silver.
punchline: The company promotes people on superficial traits like height and hair instead of experience or competence, as if looking like an executive is the qualification for management.
summary: A new manager is hailed as a rising star purely because of his height and distinguished-looking hair rather than any actual skill.

title: Dilbert's Discarded Robot Returns Smarter

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What happened with the robot you were building?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Nobody can make a robot. It's impossible.

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: Hmm... A perfectly good robot. Probably just needs a neuro-spectrum field calibration.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That whole robot project was bad for my ego as an engineer.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Hey! Guess who's way smarter than you!

setting: Dilbert's cubicle and a trash can outside
situation: Dogbert asks Dilbert about the robot he was building, and Dilbert claims nobody can make a robot and it's impossible. Meanwhile a garbage man pulls a working robot out of the trash, noting it just needs calibration. The robot then shows up in Dilbert's cubicle to taunt him about being smarter.
punchline: Dilbert insists building a robot is impossible after throwing his away, only for the working robot to return and rub in that it's smarter than him.
summary: After dumping his robot and declaring such machines impossible, an engineer is confronted by that very robot, repaired by a passing garbage man and eager to gloat.

title: Dogbert Sends Captain Bob Downhill

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Captain Bob, I think you're planning to eat the other survivors.

transcript.speaker: Captain Bob
transcript.text: Ha ha! Too bad your only hope is to send a message to the village at the base of this mountain.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: When you roll into town, tell them Dogbert sent you.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Whap!

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Zing

setting: A snowy mountainside where plane crash survivors are stranded
situation: Stranded survivors on a snowy mountain are confronted by Dogbert, who accuses the large, bearded Captain Bob of planning to eat them. Bob gloats that their only hope is to send a message to the village below. Dogbert then hits him with a snowball, and he rolls down the slope toward the village.
punchline: Captain Bob, a big round man, gets turned into a giant rolling snowball and becomes the message himself, delivered to the village by Dogbert's trick.
summary: A scheming pilot who plans to eat his fellow survivors gets knocked down the slope and sent rolling to town as an unwilling messenger.

title: Boss Routes Trivial Memo Downward

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Here's something else that's totally unimportant yet requires action.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll route it to a subordinate, thus inflating its perceived importance and destroying both morale and productivity.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What luck, I got two copies!

setting: The Boss's office, seated at his desk
situation: The Boss sits alone at his desk reading a piece of paper, shown only through his thoughts. He recognizes it as unimportant but decides to forward it to a subordinate, fully aware this will inflate its importance and harm morale and productivity. In the last panel he is delighted to find he received two copies.
punchline: The Boss knowingly damages morale and productivity by passing along junk, and then cheerfully treats a duplicate copy as good luck because it means he can pass on even more.
summary: A manager cheerfully admits to himself that forwarding pointless paperwork wrecks his staff's morale, then celebrates having a spare copy to send out too.

title: Bored Dilbert Insults Chatty Woman

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: ...So then I spent a year in Europe and blah blah blah blah.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hey, I think I can see your brain through your nose!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Anyway... you were saying..?

setting: A social gathering or party where people hold drinks
situation: At a party, a woman talks at length about her year in Europe while Dilbert holds a drink and listens. Dilbert abruptly interrupts with a bizarre, rude remark about seeing her brain through her nose. She looks stunned, and he calmly asks her to continue as if nothing happened.
punchline: Dilbert's deliberately absurd insult shows how little attention he was paying to her story, and he then casually invites her to carry on.
summary: A man tunes out a long travel story and jolts the speaker with a ridiculous insult before politely asking her to resume.

title: Rich Prisoner's Dental Floss Ladder

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: At Dogbert's jail for the rich and famous

transcript.speaker: Prisoner 1
transcript.text: Pssst... I'm planning an escape.

transcript.speaker: Prisoner 1
transcript.text: I've secretly built a ladder out of dental floss.

transcript.speaker: Prisoner 2
transcript.text: Ha! And they say the rich aren't clever.

setting: Dogbert's jail for the rich and famous
situation: Two inmates in brown prison robes talk quietly. One whispers that he is planning an escape and has secretly built a ladder out of dental floss. The other laughs and praises the cleverness of the rich.
punchline: The ladder is made of flimsy dental floss, which could never hold a person's weight, so the 'clever' rich prisoners are in fact foolish, and the remark about their cleverness is sarcastic.
summary: A pair of wealthy inmates congratulate themselves on an escape plan built around a ladder made of dental floss.

title: Marketing Has a Two Drink Minimum

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, I'm putting you on a rotational assignment...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You will be working in Marketing until further notice.

transcript.speaker: Sign
transcript.text: Marketing. Two drink minimum.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle, then the entrance to the Marketing department
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he is being moved on a rotational assignment to Marketing until further notice. In the last panel Dilbert stands at the entrance to Marketing, which is styled like a nightclub with a 'two drink minimum' sign, and people in party clothes hold drinks inside.
punchline: Marketing is portrayed as a cocktail lounge or nightclub, implying that marketing staff spend their time partying and drinking rather than doing real work.
summary: A manager reassigns an engineer to a department that turns out to be a cocktail party.

title: Dogbert Is Dilbert's Bad Luck

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've had nothing but tragedy since making a fortune in the stock market.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sometimes, Dogbert, it seems like our lives have preset balances of joy and pain; when one gets too high the other kicks in to compensate.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But through it all, I always have you, my friend.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: At least until my good luck kicks in.

setting: Dilbert's living room, sitting in an armchair
situation: A bandaged, battered Dilbert sits in his armchair with Dogbert on the ottoman. He laments that tragedy has followed his stock market windfall and philosophizes that joy and pain balance out in life. He thanks Dogbert for always being there, and Dogbert replies that this will last only until his own good luck arrives.
punchline: By Dilbert's own theory of balanced fortune, Dogbert's friendship counts as part of Dilbert's misfortune, so it will end as soon as Dogbert's luck turns good.
summary: After a lucky windfall is followed by a string of disasters, a wounded man credits his loyal dog for staying by his side, only to hear the dog's loyalty comes with an expiry date.

title: Dogbert Never Answers Dilbert's Questions

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Have you noticed that people rarely answer questions in conversation?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That reminds me of a story. One day I . . .

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: See? There! You didn't answer my question!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you think my questions are meant to be merely rhetorical?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You sure get worked up over the strangest things.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you doing this intentionally?!! Why won't you answer my questions??!!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Hey! There's a cloud that looks like a bunny!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It doesn't get any better than this.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why? Why? Why?

setting: Outdoor walk on a grassy hillside
situation: Dilbert and Dogbert take a walk outside, and Dilbert complains that people rarely answer questions in conversation. Dogbert keeps dodging every question Dilbert asks, changing the subject or ignoring it, which drives Dilbert into a frustrated rage. By the end Dogbert lies back watching clouds while Dilbert is flat on the ground screaming 'why?'.
punchline: Dogbert proves Dilbert's point by deliberately never answering any of his questions, and happily enjoys the clouds while Dilbert is driven to fits of frustration.
summary: A man complaining about unanswered questions is driven mad by his dog companion, who cheerfully ignores every question he asks.

title: Dilbert Fakes Celebrity Phone Calls

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Nobody ever calls on my new video phone so I routed the television signal to it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now I can pretend that celebrities are calling me all day.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ooh... Dolly Parton is calling. I'll bet it's for me again.

setting: Dilbert's home
situation: Dilbert explains that nobody ever calls his new video phone, so he has rerouted the television signal to it. He now treats the TV broadcast as incoming calls from celebrities. When Dolly Parton appears on screen, he walks over to answer, certain the call is for him.
punchline: Dilbert is so lonely and starved for contact that he fools himself into believing television stars are phoning him personally.
summary: A neglected video phone gets a second life when its owner pipes his TV into it and pretends famous people are ringing him up.

title: Dogbert Sues Dilbert for Petimony

transcript.speaker: Attorney
transcript.text: I'm an attorney for Mister Dogbert...

transcript.speaker: Attorney
transcript.text: He's suing you for "petimony." You allegedly pet the neighbor's cat...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: See... it was a pat, not a pet. Like this...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Oh look, it's "Garfield," your favorite...

setting: Dilbert's front doorway and home
situation: An attorney arrives at Dilbert's door with a legal paper, announcing that Dogbert is suing him for 'petimony' for allegedly petting the neighbor's cat. Dilbert tries to defend himself by distinguishing a 'pat' from a 'pet' and demonstrates the gesture. Meanwhile Dogbert, reading the newspaper, points out the Garfield comic as a dig at Dilbert.
punchline: Dogbert is suing Dilbert under a pun on 'palimony' for petting a cat, and he sarcastically undercuts Dilbert's defense by pointing to the Garfield comic, implying Dilbert's taste is as lazy as his defense.
summary: A lawyer serves Dilbert with an absurd pun-based lawsuit from his own dog over cat-petting, and Dilbert's hair-splitting defense gets mocked by Dogbert.

title: Dog's Fabricated Square-Dance Resume

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I was skeptical about hiring a dog as our new square-dance caller, but your resumé is impressive.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I didn't even know you could win a Pulitzer Prize for square-dance calling.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wow! And you're already in the Alberdeen Hall of Dung!

setting: Interview office, a desk in a pink-walled room
situation: The Boss, wearing a cowboy hat and western shirt, interviews Dogbert for a square-dance caller job. He reads Dogbert's resume aloud and is increasingly impressed by its absurd claims, including a Pulitzer Prize for square-dance calling and induction into a 'Hall of Dung'. Dogbert sits silently across the desk.
punchline: The Boss gullibly accepts a clearly fabricated resume full of ridiculous credentials without questioning any of it.
summary: A credulous hiring manager swoons over a dog's obviously made-up credentials, never noticing how absurd they are.

title: Hacking Techno-Bill's Gadgets Backfires

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Please don't hurt me, Techno-Bill!

transcript.speaker: Techno-Bill
transcript.text: Make your move.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My only chance is to use my cellular phone and modem to dial into his control module and set off all his systems.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Aaagh!

transcript.speaker: Sound effects
transcript.text: Beep beep. Rrring! Bzzz bzzz bzzz. Ding.

transcript.speaker: Techno-Bill
transcript.text: Fool! I have autodialing.

setting: A pink-background confrontation outdoors, with two gadget-laden engineers facing off
situation: Dilbert begs Techno-Bill, a man covered in electronic gadgets and a backpack, not to hurt him. Dilbert plans to use his cellular phone and modem to dial into Techno-Bill's control module and set off all his systems. Instead, Techno-Bill's own autodialing feature turns the attack around and Dilbert's gadgets all go off on him.
punchline: Dilbert's clever high-tech plan fails because Techno-Bill's gadgets have autodialing, which turns the attack back on Dilbert and sets off his own devices.
summary: A gadget duel between two engineers ends with the would-be hacker's own electronics going haywire thanks to his opponent's superior technology.

title: Video Phone Early Adopter Mirror

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Did anybody call on your new video phone yet?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Don't you think that the only people who will buy video phones are male techie dweebs like you?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Therefore, wouldn't it be cheaper to buy a mirror?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's hell being an early adopter.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle
situation: Dogbert asks Dilbert whether anyone has called his new video phone yet, and Dilbert admits nobody has. Dogbert points out that the only likely buyers of video phones are male techie dweebs like Dilbert himself. He concludes it would be cheaper to just buy a mirror, and Dilbert privately laments the pain of being an early adopter.
punchline: Since only geeks like Dilbert own video phones, the only person who could call him on one is someone who looks like him, so a mirror would serve just as well.
summary: Dogbert mocks Dilbert's lonely new gadget by suggesting its only possible caller is his own reflection.

title: Airport Built From Leaf and Bee

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: At the "Rivers and Trees" management course.

transcript.speaker: Instructor
transcript.text: Next, we have a creativity exercise.

transcript.speaker: Instructor
transcript.text: Your task is to build a commercial airport landing strip using nothing but a leaf and a dead bee.

transcript.speaker: Man in glasses
transcript.text: Look, we already voted. WE'RE design and YOU'RE construction.

transcript.speaker: Instructor
transcript.text: Time.

setting: Outdoor management training course in a grassy area with trees
situation: At a 'Rivers and Trees' management course, the instructor gives the participants an absurd creativity exercise: build a commercial airport landing strip using only a leaf and a dead bee. Before attempting anything, one participant announces that the group has already voted to split into design and construction teams, assigning the actual building to another group. The instructor simply calls time.
punchline: The managers spend their entire time on organizational politics and delegating the work rather than attempting the task, which shows how bureaucratic management thinking replaces actual creativity.
summary: A group at a corporate retreat wastes an impossible creative challenge by voting on who gets to design and who has to do the labor.

title: Money Can't Buy Happiness? Idiots

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Am I wrong or did you tell me you invested all of your money in stock options for a company called Zymed?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The radio says the stock price tripled on takeover rumors. You just made about ten million dollars.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But they say money can't buy happiness.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Apparently "they" are idiots.

setting: Dilbert's desk at the office
situation: Dogbert asks Dilbert whether he put all his money into stock options for a company called Zymed. Dogbert then reports that the stock tripled on takeover rumors, making Dilbert about ten million dollars richer. Dilbert, seated at his computer, repeats the saying that money can't buy happiness.
punchline: Dogbert dismisses the cliche that money can't buy happiness by saying the people who say it must be idiots, implying that being suddenly rich is plainly a good thing.
summary: A sudden stock windfall prompts Dogbert to mock the old saying about wealth and happiness.

title: Pilot Plans to Eat Survivors

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We're alive... we must have been thrown clear when the jet hit the mountain.

transcript.speaker: Captain Bob
transcript.text: I'm Captain Bob. Sorry about the crash. What are the odds I'd hit this same mountain on every flight?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We're in luck. Captain Bob knows how to survive these situations.

transcript.speaker: Captain Bob
transcript.text: Nice folks. I'll eat them last.

setting: Snowy mountainside after a jet crash
situation: Dilbert and Dogbert are half-buried in snow after their plane crashes into a mountain. The pilot, Captain Bob, cheerfully introduces himself and admits he has crashed into this same mountain on every flight. Dilbert is relieved that he knows how to survive, while the pilot walks off privately planning to eat the survivors.
punchline: Dilbert assumes the pilot's survival experience is good news, but the pilot's secret thought reveals his method is cannibalism, with Dilbert and Dogbert as the menu.
summary: After a mountain plane crash, a repeat-offender pilot's survival know-how turns out to mean eating his passengers.
